text:
A federal judge declined on Wednesday to intervene in a politically sensitive extradition fight over an ICE agent who is currently detained in Texas but is facing state charges in Minnesota for allegedly shooting an immigrant in Minneapolis earlier this year.

Texas hasn’t agreed to extradite the agent since he was arrested earlier this summer because the state said it was investigating whether the agent technically qualified as a “fugitive.”

A judge on Wednesday said he lacked authority over part of a lawsuit brought by Minnesota Democratic Gov. Tim Walz last week aiming to keep the agent, Christian Castro, behind bars for now because he didn’t find there was evidence that Texas Gov. Greg Abbott had violated federal law by not extraditing Castro yet, as Walz argued. Abbott hasn’t said if he will extradite Castro or not, and his attorneys say he’s still mulling the extradition request made to him in June.

At the same time, the clock has been ticking on a Texas policy that limits the number of days a fugitive awaiting extradition can be detained, and the agent could be released as soon as Thursday.

The state of Minnesota filed a lawsuit last week asking the federal court to order Abbott to hand over Castro and keep him behind bars until the extradition is completed.

Judge Fernando Rodriguez, Jr., an appointee of President Donald Trump, also handed Walz a loss by not directly ordering Texas to hand the agent over to officials in Minnesota to face charges for shooting the immigrant in Minneapolis.

“Minnesota cannot premise its causes of action on the allegation that Governor Abbott may” violate extradition laws in the future, Rodriguez, Jr. wrote in the ruling. “The record before the court … reveals that Governor Abbott has not denied the request for a rendition warrant.”

He continued: “Minnesota identifies no statutory or constitutional provision requiring Governor Abbott to complete his investigation and decide whether to sign the rendition warrant within a particular time period.”

Texas Rangers arrested Castro in Cameron County, Texas, on May 29 on a nationwide warrant. He faces four felony charges and a misdemeanor in Minnesota after the shooting of Julio Sosa-Celis during the height of Operation Metro Surge in the Minneapolis area. Prosecutors in Hennepin County, Minnesota, say Castro shot Sosa-Celis in the leg through the front door of a home, injuring him and endangering several other people who were also inside.

Castro is eligible for release from custody as soon as Thursday due to a Texas criminal procedure policy that puts a 90-day limit on the detention of fugitives awaiting extradition.

Cameron County Sheriff Manuel Treviño told CNN on Wednesday he’s waiting for further guidance from county attorneys on whether to release Castro.

When asked about the extradition battle last week, Abbott did not reference the state’s investigation into Castro’s fugitive status but accused Minnesota of fraud.

“While they’re making demands, I got a demand of my own, and that is, it’s time for Minnesota to step up and repay the United States of America and Americans for all the fraud that they’ve committed in their state under federal programs, and I will not respond to them at all until they step up and do what’s right and they acknowledge their fault in the fraud that took place and they fully repay the United States of America for the fraud they committed,” he said last week in Austin.

After the judge’s decision on Wednesday, Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison vowed to continue litigating the case, saying Abbott is “playing with constitutional fire.”

“Greg Abbott is turning Texas into a sanctuary state for violent criminals. But regardless of today’s ruling, Christian Castro will not escape justice in Minnesota,” Ellison said in a statement.

Mary Moriarty, the county attorney for Hennepin County, which issued the charges, said the country is on the “precipice” of having the “political views of governors make a difference in extradition.”

“This is not what was intended to happen by the founders. That’s why there’s an extradition clause in the Constitution,” Moriarty said in a Wednesday evening news conference.

CNN has attempted to reach Castro’s lawyer.

Minnesota, which sued Texas last week, argued that Castro posed a flight risk to Mexico due to a romantic relationship he has with a woman in Mexico. Judge Rodriguez on Wednesday recognized that Castro’s potential flight to Mexico would “impose a hardship on Minnesota’s prosecutorial efforts,” but said that concern alone was not enough to overcome the procedural issue he identified in the case.

“The threat of injury by itself does not create an issue ripe for adjudication,” the judge wrote.

If Castro were to go to Mexico, Moriarty said Wednesday evening “there is an international extradition treaty between Mexico and the United States, but that would require the help of the federal government.”

Texas has resisted the extradition so far because it took issue with Minnesota’s labeling of Castro as a “fugitive.” Castro was ordered back to his home base in Texas in January after the shooting, according to statements admitted to court from an ICE field office director. Abbott’s office argued extradition powers only apply to fugitives and that the state is still determining whether Castro’s move to Texas can be considered the act of a fugitive who’s fleeing from criminal liability.

“The court was right to reject Governor Walz’s absurd claim. The Constitution requires deliberate consideration of extradition requests and tasks Governor Abbott to ‘decide, upon such evidence as he may deem satisfactory’ whether ‘the person demanded is a fugitive,’” Andrew Mahaleris, press secretary for Abbott’s office, said in a statement Wednesday.

Meanwhile, Moriarty said they are all taking some time to consider next steps. “We want to be very thoughtful about how to move forward appropriately in this case.”

She also said, “Much depends on whether Castro does leave and go to Mexico.”

As the extradition fight plays out in Texas, the Justice Department has been considering a federal prosecution, but no decision had been made on Tuesday.

Justice Department spokeswoman Emily Covington told CNN this week that officials in the civil rights division have held conversations with local prosecutors in Minnesota. It is not clear what, if anything, the Justice Department will ultimately charge Castro with. Covington described the conversations as a standard part of any ongoing investigation.

Federal charges would mark a significant move for the Trump administration, which has vigorously resisted attempts to hold ICE officers accountable for other shootings.

Bringing a federal case against the officer wouldn’t on its own stop the Minnesota case from proceeding simultaneously.

CNN’s Whitney Wild contributed to this report.

This story was updated to include statements.

text:
PORTLAND, Maine — Maine’s Republican nominee for governor recently told a crowd of supporters that he would ask a top Department of Homeland Security official to send U.S. Marshals and Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to polling places in the state for this fall’s midterm elections, according to audio obtained by The Associated Press.

During an Aug. 20 event in Arundel, Bobby Charles told a group of supporters that he would ask Tom Homan, the White House border czar, to send federal agents to polling places in the weeks before Election Day. The audio was first reported by the Bangor Daily News.

“Here’s my secret,” Charles told members of a Maine Young Republicans chapter. “I have a friend named Tom Homan. Tom and I used to get on Fox all the time together. Tom’s an awesome guy.”

“I’m going to ask Tom, I’m going to actually — three or four weeks before the election, maybe three — I’m going to make an appeal for ICE and Marshals to be at our voting booths,” Charles said, according to the audio.

On Wednesday, he explained his comments by saying state and local authorities who manage elections should have an open line of communication with federal authorities if needed to “prevent violence at a voting place, in order to prevent intimidation at a voting place and in order to prevent illegality at a voting place.”

He said his point was that Maine authorities should do everything legally possible to prevent illegal voting in the state.

“Everybody who is legally entitled to vote should be free from any intimidation and should be able to vote,” he said in a statement released by his campaign. “Anybody who is not legally entitled to vote should not be voting.”

Charles’ comments come as President Donald Trump continues to sow doubt about the security of elections in the U.S. elections and takes unprecedented measures to intervene in election administration. The Constitution gives states, and sometimes Congress, the authority to set election rules but grants no such power to the president.

A central part of his attacks is to claim widespread fraud through voting by noncitizens. But those claims are vastly overstated. Voting by noncitizens is exceptionally rare and is punishable as a felony, with deportation as one potential penalty.

Nevertheless, Trump has been pushing Congress to pass a bill that would require voters to show documentary proof of citizenship to vote in the upcoming midterms and signed an executive order directing the Postal Service to send mail ballots only to those on an approved list of verified voters.

When reached for comment on Wednesday, DHS did not address whether department officials had held or planned to hold conversations with political campaigns about election security. DHS officials have previously said they do not have plans to send ICE agents to polling places.

“Elections exist for the American people, not illegal aliens, to choose their leaders,” a Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement to the AP.

Democratic state officials have been concerned about the possibility of immigration agents showing up near polling places on Election Day or during early voting.

In February, a DHS official told a group of secretaries of state that “any suggestion that ICE will be present at any polling location is simply not true,” according to several secretaries who were part of the conversation.

Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, a Democrat, said ICE agents are prohibited by law from being at polling places. Bellows ran for governor this year but lost the Democratic primary.

“The political rhetoric coming from Mr. Charles is just politics, but it won’t change the laws or the Constitution,” Bellows said.

The Maine Democratic Party also criticized Charles’ comments and described his plan as likely illegal. The party also criticized the timing of the comments as the state is continuing to wrestle with the killing of Biddeford resident Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero by an ICE officer earlier this summer.

The comments expose Charles as a “MAGA extremist” who will do Trump’s bidding, said Maine Democratic Party Executive Director Devon Murphy-Anderson.

“His plan to ask Trump’s border czar to send ICE agents to Maine polling places just weeks before Election Day is not only deeply alarming — it is likely illegal,” Murphy-Anderson said.

Federal law prohibits the military and federal agencies from putting troops or armed officers near polling sites, according to the Brennan Center.

The White House has dismissed concerns that federal agents would interfere with elections and noted that there was no disruption to the election process in last year’s elections, when Democrats performed well.

Charles is an attorney who served as U.S. assistant secretary of state under President George W. Bush. He will face Democrat Hannah Pingree, the former speaker of the Maine House of Representatives, in November.

While lauding police for quickly releasing their video, he interprets the Ogden officer as aiding the ICE agent.

text:
OGDEN — Ogden police are speaking out in response to the detention of a man on Tuesday by a federal immigration agent on an Ogden street as an Ogden police officer watched.

The encounter was caught on video by a passerby and posted to social media, prompting questions about the level of involvement of Ogden police in assisting Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials in their moves to crack down on illegal immigration. Police Chief Jake Sube and Ogden Mayor Ben Nadolski have emphasized that the city won't enter a cooperative accord with ICE, and the Ogden Police Department issued a statement Tuesday defending its role.

"The Ogden Police Department did not initiate the stop, did not conduct the arrest, did not ask for or run any information and did not assist with immigration enforcement," reads the statement, issued Tuesday night. "The officer's involvement was limited to maintaining safety and attempting to de-escalate an unusual and potentially escalating interaction."

The Ogden officer was on scene near 22nd Street and Porter Avenue responding to a report of an aggressive dog when an ICE agent was simultaneously tracking a suspect in the same area. Tuesday's statement, posted to the Ogden Police Department Facebook page, included video of the encounter from the police officer's body camera.

"This officer unexpectedly found himself in the middle of a situation he did not create, trying to determine the appropriate role for him to play while also recognizing the potential for the situation to escalate," Sube said. "Our officers are asked to navigate difficult situations like this in real time, make judgment calls and do the best they can to keep everyone safe, knowing those decisions may later be publicly scrutinized without the benefit of the full circumstances they were facing at the time."

The incident underscores the delicate role police sometimes have amid increased efforts under Pres. Donald Trump to detain and deport immigrants in the country illegally. While some agencies like the Weber County Sheriff's Office have entered into cooperative accords with ICE, known as 287(g) agreements, others, like the Ogden Police Department, have not.

"We are not part of the 287(g) program. We will not be a part of the 287(g) program. I hope you can hear that and see that I'm stating that very clearly," Sube said at a meeting last January of the Ogden City Council, after numerous residents spoke out against the federal crackdown. "We do not participate in ICE operations, in raids or sweeps."

Tuesday's police statement notwithstanding, Ogden resident Oshun Dayo, who's been vocal over the years about Ogden police issues, has his concerns. He posted a video made by a passerby who happened to be present when the ICE agent arrested the man and later reviewed the officer's body-camera video after the police department posted it. While lauding police for quickly releasing their video, he interprets the Ogden officer as aiding the ICE agent.

"Although I applaud OPD for being transparent with the body cam video, I also believe that the police officer was not just there to keep the peace; he played a role in assisting in the arrest," Dayo wrote in a public Facebook post on Wednesday. "So in my opinion, the police officer fully cooperated with the ICE agent and assisted in the gentleman's arrest that was in the car. He wasn't only an observer; he was an active participant."

Police say the man ultimately detained by the ICE agent had flagged down the Ogden officer, expressing concern that he was being followed by a black sports utility vehicle, the ICE agent's car. In the video, the police officer approaches the agent in his car to find out what's happening.

"But he's like, 'This guy is following me, and I don't know what's going on,'" the police officer tells the ICE agent.

The officer goes back to the car of the first man, who says he had been delivering food, and then the ICE agent approaches to arrest him, calling him Jonathan. In broken Spanish, the agent advises the man that he's in the country illegally and that he's going to be arrested. Jonathan attempts to roll up the window of his car.

"Don't do this, don't," says the Ogden officer. "Don't, don't, don't."

The immigration officer orders Jonathan to turn off his car, take off his seatbelt and open the locked door of his car.

"Why is he detaining me?" Jonathan asks in Spanish, still seated in his car.

"This is the police," the Ogden officer answers, also in Spanish, pointing to the ICE agent.

"It's ICE," Jonathan answers.

"Police," the Ogden officer responds.

The ICE agent keeps pressing Jonathan, who ultimately gets out of the vehicle. The agent handcuffs him and arrests him.

As the arrest unfolds, the Ogden officer can be heard discussing the turn of events to somebody, apparently on his police radio or a phone. He explains that the ICE agent had asked the officer to stop Jonathan's vehicle, which he didn't do, and that Jonathan had expressed concern about the agent following him.

The officer says he told the ICE agent he could remain on the scene "and make sure that nothing goes south here, but I can't help. So I just don't know what the extent of what we're allowed to do is."

text:
Federal authorities confirmed they have deported the wife of a U.S. Army sergeant headquartered at Fort Bliss.

Cristy Maryori Villafranca Trejo, a 29-year-old Honduran national with a 6-year-old daughter, was removed to Honduras on Monday. Army Sgt. Hedár Leonel Turcios Juárez confirmed the deportation to ABC News, and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) confirmed it as well.

"On Aug. 24, Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, an illegal alien from Honduras, was removed from the United States in accordance with our laws," a DHS spokesperson told the network.

Military.com previously spoke with Turcios, who said his spouse's deportation flight was delayed the previous week due to what DHS described as a "legal impediment." The agency confirmed that language to Military.com after the fact.

That attempted removal occurred Aug. 18 after his wife repeatedly told officers that a challenge to her 2017 removal order remained pending.

Villafranca's Arrest

DHS removed Villafranca after authorities held her since July 11 at Camp East Montana, an immigration detention facility at Fort Bliss—the same installation where Turcios serves as an E-5.

The agency, which oversees U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, arrested her as the family returned from a Walmart in El Paso, Turcios said. Villafranca had been the primary caregiver for the family's children while he worked, trained and deployed.

DHS described the arrest as a "targeted immigration enforcement operation." The department said Villafranca entered the United States illegally in 2016 and was released into the country during former president Barack Obama's administration.

Turcios claimed his wife entered with her son in 2016, was processed by immigration authorities, and released with an ankle monitor.

DHS previously said that her claims would be considered by the Justice Department.

Trump's Immigration Crackdown

Villafrance's case comes amid President Donald Trump's broader immigration crackdown since reclaiming office in 2024—arguably his biggest political campaign promise.

An Associated Press investigation published Aug. 5 identified more than 50 parents and spouses of active-duty service members detained since Trump returned to office.

At least six had been deported, and at least eight immediate family members remained in federal custody, according to the AP. DHS told the AP that it does not track such cases.

In response to the report, 60 Democrats sent a letter in August to DHS, the Department of Defense (DOD) and the Department of Veterans Affairs, vowing to investigate whether the DOD and DHS were working together to deport military service members and their families.

However, Trump has also made policies to support the military community.

In August, he created the Military Spouse Commission to support the lives and experiences of spouses of those enlisted in service.

The commission, helmed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's wife, Jennifer Rauchet, will provide recommendations to address themes including housing, employment, health care and childcare.

Turcios' Military Background

Turcio, who left Honduras in 2014, has served in the Army for three years. He was deployed to the Middle East for nine months in 2023.

"I truly want to keep serving this country," Turcios told Military.com.

He also told ABC News that he had hoped his military service would expedite his wife's naturalization process in their quest to make her a U.S. citizen.

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) guidance says that being the spouse, parent or child of an active-duty service member ordinarily weighs heavily in favor of parole in place when the applicant has no criminal conviction or other serious adverse factors.

"She has been my everything," Turcios said. "She was always there to support me."

"I'm not asking for special treatment," he added. "I'm not asking to be above the law. ... I'm just asking for my family to be together so I can continue with my military career."

text:
A federal appeals court ruled Wednesday that the Justice Department can proceed with most of its case against Rep. LaMonica McIver, who stands accused of assaulting an ICE officer during a scuffle last year at a migrant detention center.

The 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals did ask a lower court to go back and review one of the three counts in the indictment, but rejected the New Jersey Democrat’s challenge to two other counts, saying she can’t shield herself by claiming the scuffle was part of her official congressional duties.

Judge Cindy Chung, a Biden appointee, said that while Ms. McIver’s visit to the Delaney Hall migrant detention facility in Newark was part of her legislative duties, the physical confrontation was not.

“Count One charges Congresswoman McIver not for conduct relating to her entire visit to Delaney Hall, but for conduct during a specific interaction between her and Victim-1,” wrote Judge Chung, joined by Judge Stephanos Bibas, a Trump appointee.

They applied a similar logic to the second count of the indictment.

The third charge in the indictment, however, might implicate Ms. McIver’s legislative duties. The appeals court asked the district court to review that matter.

The appeals court did deny Ms. McIver’s claim that the prosecution against her was selective or vindictive. The lower court had ruled against the congresswoman, and Judge Chung said any appeal of that must come later, after a trial.

Judge Thomas Ambro, a Clinton pick, partially dissented from the decision, saying he would have asked the lower court to review the second count of the indictment as well as the third. He also said Ms. McIver should be allowed to explore whether the case was brought to punish her as a member of Congress.

The case has become a battleground over the executive branch’s ability to prosecute a member of the legislative branch.

The scuffle broke out when a group of Democratic politicians tried to enter Delaney Hall, which was opened over the objection of local officials in Newark.

After officers tried to get one of the group, Mayor Ras Baraka, to leave, several congressional Democrats moved to try to prevent his ouster.

During the scuffle that ensued, Ms. McIver was caught on video bashing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement employees with her forearm.

Ms. McIver said she was at the facility in Newark to conduct oversight as a member of Congress, in accordance with a law that specifically granted Congress members access.

After the confrontation, Ms. McIver and two other Democratic members of Congress did complete their oversight inspection.

The National Women’s Law Center Action Fund decried the appeals court’s ruling as a “grave miscarriage of justice.”

“What is happening to Rep. McIver is no accident: it is an intimidation tactic aimed at silencing a sitting member of Congress who stood up to protect her community members from human rights violations,” said Fatima Goss Graves, the fund’s president, in a statement.

Delaney Hall has become a flash point for the broader debate over President Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

text:
A federal judge in Houston ordered Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) authorities on Monday to release a witness to last month’s fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in the Texas city by agency officers.

U.S. District Judge Alfred H. Bennett granted Daniel Tirado Pantoja’s petition for writ of habeas, ordering ICE to release the man from Montgomery Processing Center in Conroe, Texas, where the agency has held him since the shooting.

Bennett, an appointee of former President Obama, wrote the continued detention of Tirado Pantoja, who is not a citizen of the U.S., would violate his right to procedural due process.

“After reviewing the authorities and the record, the Court determines release is the appropriate habeas relief for the unlawful detention in this case,” Bennett wrote in a three-page order, noting that Tirado Pantoja “has no criminal history, is not a flight risk, and does not otherwise pose a danger to the community.”

Bennett’s Monday order required ICE authorities to release Tirado Pantoja within 48 hours and provide a report on his status within 72 hours. The Hill has reached out to ICE and the Homeland Security Department for comment.

Tirado Pantoja, a Mexican citizen, was one of three passengers in a van Salgado Araujo was driving when ICE officers started to follow them on the road. An officer later fatally shot Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old father of three U.S. citizens whose family said was close to obtaining legal status.

Salgado Araujo owned a construction business and had lived in the Houston area for 35 years, per his family.

Federal officials have said Salgado Araujo was weaponizing his car against ICE officers before one officer shot him in self-defense. But passengers in the 52-year-old’s car and his family have disputed that account, saying ICE officers in unmarked vehicles trailed then surrounded them on the driver and passenger sides.

Rep. Sylvia Garcia (D-Texas), who represents parts of Houston, also said last month Salgado Araujo was not the target of the operation — citing a conversation she had with acting ICE Director David Venturella.

Last month, a different federal judge in Houston ordered ICE officials to release José Trinidad Rojas Pliego, another passenger in Salgado Araujo’s van. Victor Salgado, the brother of Salgado Araujo, was also in the van and remains in ICE detention.

Bennett wrote that ICE must release Tirado Pantoja in a public place and inform either his counsel or a friend of the time and location of his release three hours beforehand.

Under Bennett’s order, ICE authorities have to also return any identification documents they took from Tirado Pantoja during his detention.

If the federal immigration agency seeks to detain Tirado Pantoja again, the agency must demonstrate before an immigration judge there is “clear and convincing evidence” the man is a flight risk or a danger to the community, Bennett’s order notes.

In fiscal year 2025, approximately 3,000 unaccompanied children were released to sponsors in California.
Previously, in fiscal year 2024, almost 11,000 unaccompanied children were released to Californian sponsors.
Attorney General Bonta is committed to continuing to fight for children already within our borders who need more protection, not less.
In submitting this comment letter, Attorney General Bonta leads the attorneys general of Colorado, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawaiʻi, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, and Washington.
text:
OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta, leading a coalition of 19 attorneys general, submitted a comment letter opposing the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ (HHS) proposed rule that would add burdensome new requirements for sponsors of unaccompanied immigrant children. The coalition argues that the proposed rule’s requirements related to proof of identity and proof of income for potential sponsors will create barriers that will make it more difficult for immigrant family members and other qualified sponsors to sponsor unaccompanied children, decreasing the number of available sponsors and prolonging children’s time in federal custody.

“As Attorney General, I am dedicated to protecting all children within California's borders, including immigrant children” said Attorney General Bonta. “The changes proposed by HHS will achieve nothing but separating desperate families and increase the time kids are spending in immigration facilities. I urge HHS to reconsider this course of action and make the pathway to family reunification easier, not harder.”

Attorney General Bonta and the multistate coalition have a strong interest in protecting the rights of unaccompanied immigrant children. In fiscal year 2025, approximately 3,000 unaccompanied children were released to sponsors in California. Previously, in fiscal year 2024, almost 11,000 unaccompanied children were released to Californian sponsors. These children go on to become members of our communities, attending schools, participating in the workforce, and eventually having children of their own. Prolonging the time they spend in federal custody has proven to have adverse effects on their ability to thrive in communities after their release, as research shows that excessive time in immigration custody disrupts child development and is particularly harmful to their mental health and physical wellbeing.

In the comment letter, Attorney General Bonta and the coalition argue that the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) failed to provide adequate justification for the proposed rule’s changes to the proof of income and proof of identity requirements, which directly interfere with HHS’s and ORR’s obligations under the William Wilberforce Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act (TVPRA) and the Unaccompanied Children Program Foundational Rule (Foundational Rule). The TVPRA and the Foundational Rule, respectively, require that HHS and ORR place children in the least restrictive environment that is in the best interests of the child and to release children without unnecessary delay.

Attorney General Bonta is committed to continuing to fight for children already within our borders who need more protection, not less. In January 2026, Attorney General Bonta led an amicus brief opposing the Trump Administration’s efforts to terminate the Flores Settlement Agreement, which provides crucial protections for children in federal immigration custody and ensures the children in immigration custody are held in facilities licensed in and subject to oversight by the states in which they reside. He also filed a comment letter in May 2025 opposing a HHS interim final rule that removed key provisions from the Foundational Rule prohibiting ORR from disqualifying potential sponsors for unaccompanied children based solely on their immigration status and sharing immigration status information about sponsors with law enforcement and immigration enforcement entities.

In submitting this comment letter, Attorney General Bonta leads the attorneys general of Colorado, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawaiʻi, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, and Washington.

text:
A coalition of civil rights organizations and U.S. citizens filed a lawsuit challenging the Trump-Vance administration’s suspension of immigrant visa processing for people from 75 countries.

The ban, imposed by the U.S. Department of State, cited a so-called “public charge” risk as justification, which refers to the idea that immigrants from these countries would rely on government assistance. Plaintiffs argue that rationale is false and pretextual: the vast majority of immigrant visa applicants are ineligible for most government assistance programs, and Congress has made clear that accessing authorized public programs cannot be used to deny lawful immigration. The real effect of the ban is to cut off legal immigration from nearly half the countries in the world, disproportionately harming communities of color, separating families, and shutting out workers the U.S. economy depends on.

The plaintiffs include Catholic Legal Immigration Network (CLINIC) and African Communities Together, along with individual families directly harmed by the ban. Among them is a U.S. citizen grandmother in New York whose approved petitions for her four adult children and three grandchildren from Ghana were denied at their consular interviews. A Long Island father has been separated from his wife and young child, who traveled to Guatemala for a scheduled consular interview and are now stranded there indefinitely. A Colombian physician who was approved for an employment-based visa cannot receive it because Colombia is one of the 75 banned countries.

On August 21, 2026, the federal district court held that the ban exceeds the Secretary of State’s statutory and regulatory authority and violates the Immigration and Nationality Act’s prohibition on nationality-based discrimination in issuing a visa. In its decision, the court also vacated and set aside any visa denial based solely on the ban and ordered the State Department to restore lawful, case-by-case evaluation of visa applications.

Following reports that the U.S. Department of State ordered a mass “pause” on immigrant visa processing, citing a “training program” as a reason, on August 26, 2026, plaintiffs filed a motion to enforce the district court’s order.

description:

On July 21, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts granted emergency relief preventing the federal government from implementing unlawful USCIS policies.
The ruling came the day before thousands of TPS holders faced the imminent loss of their employment authorization under USCIS policies implementing portions of the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

text:
A coalition of immigrant advocacy organizations and labor unions filed a lawsuit challenging a series of unlawful U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) policies that threaten to strip tens of thousands of asylum seekers and Temporary Protected Status (TPS) holders of their ability to work, support their families, and remain safely in the United States. The lawsuit challenges several USCIS policies implementing portions of the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act that unlawfully impose new barriers on asylum seekers and TPS holders, putting thousands of people at immediate risk of losing work authorization, destabilizing their families, and, in the case of asylum seekers, potentially losing access to humanitarian protections guaranteed under federal law.

The challenged policies are:

The rejection of pending asylum applications and termination of work permits when applicants fail to pay a newly created annual asylum fee, without sufficient notice that payment is due, a grace period for late payment, or any way to appeal a rejection.

The elimination of a decades-old rule requiring the agency to process initial work permit applications for asylum seekers within 30 days, a change made without the notice-and-comment process required by law.

The implementation of new employment authorization policies for TPS holders unlawfully applies recent changes to the duration of TPS work permits retroactively, improperly cutting off work authorization for people who remain lawfully protected under TPS.

Plaintiffs in the case include the Venezuelan Association of Massachusetts, the National TPS Alliance, the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project, the Service Employees International Union, and 32BJ SEIU. They are represented by Democracy Forward, National Day Laborer Organizing Network, and the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project.

Plaintiffs argue that Congress has long recognized that people fleeing persecution and people who cannot safely return to their home countries deserve humanitarian protections under the law, and that the administration is attempting to dismantle those protections through unlawful agency action Congress never authorized, without basic due process. The lawsuit asks the court to strike down the challenged policies and prevent the government from stripping asylum seekers and TPS holders of their ability to work, support their families, and pursue the protections the law guarantees.

On July 21, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts granted emergency relief preventing the federal government from implementing unlawful USCIS policies. The ruling came the day before thousands of TPS holders faced the imminent loss of their employment authorization under USCIS policies implementing portions of the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

On August 5, 2026, the court granted plaintiffs’ request to temporarily block penalties for failure to pay a new annual asylum fee but declined to stay policies impacting work authorization for TPS holders.

The government filed a status report on August 19, 2026, alerting the court that USCIS extended TPS-based employment authorization for the great majority of the plaintiffs’ affected members. As a result, plaintiffs withdrew the emergency stay motion.

text:
Ohio immigrant advocates say the Trump administration is targeting political enemies after the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) filed a lawsuit Tuesday against the Franklin County Municipal Court.

The DOJ wants a federal court to order Franklin County to remove a new rule, prohibiting federal officials from detaining people at the courthouse without a warrant. The lawsuit said Immigration Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested about 12 people at the court in recent years before the rule was put in place.

The lawsuit was met with criticism from Columbus Mayor Andrew Ginther and other city officials Tuesday.

Ohio Immigrant Alliance Executive Director Lynn Tramonte told WOSU on Wednesday that policies like this weren't needed before the second Trump administration. She said common sense under President Donald Trump has been thrown out the window, forcing places like the Franklin County Municipal Court to put measures in place.

"ICE and the Trump administration have said that the only thing that matters is enforcing a paperwork violation. And state and local governments are saying that's not true. We have important business too," Tramonte said.

Tramonte argued that without rules like this, immigrants may fear showing up to court for routine proceedings like traffic court, divorce cases or even as key witnesses for criminal trials. She said the lawsuit is the latest in a trend of rising anti-immigrant policies as ICE begins to target Haitian refugees and other immigrants around Ohio.

"In the mornings, ICE agents go to McDonald's and gas stations hunting for people. We're definitely feeling the effects of the huge budget that Congress has given ICE," Tramonte said.

Tramonte said she doesn't think the timing of the lawsuit is intentionally coinciding with the arrest of Haitian refugees in Ohio following the end of Temporary Protected Status, but rather the wider immigration crackdown under Trump.

"I think it's been a constant rise of anti-immigrant policies, lawsuits, tactics, attacks and we've seen it since the 2024 campaign," Tramonte said.

The DOJ's main argument is that the federal government's authority supersedes that of a local government like Franklin County.

Tramonte said Ohioans don't want the DOJ coming in and telling local communities how to operate.

WOSU requested an interview with the DOJ, but have not received a response.

title: The D.C. Circuit's Growing Wait After Oral Argument - Legalytics
description:
Federal judiciary statistics show that, among cases terminated on the merits during the year ending September 30, 2025, the D.C.
Circuit took a median of 5.4 months to move from oral argument to its final opinion or order.
Circuit appeal can leave federal grants frozen, agency personnel decisions unsettled, regulatory obligations uncertain or an injunction governing executive action in place.
A review of 219 matters argued before the court during calendar year 2025 provides a closer look at that wait.
In fiscal year 2015, the court reported a median argument-to-disposition interval of 3.7 months, compared with 2.1 months nationally.
text:
Share

When lawyers argued before the D.C. Circuit in 2025, the court was considering disputes over the attempted downsizing of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the President’s power to remove members of independent agencies, access to billions of dollars in federal climate grants, and the procedures available to migrants facing removal. These were appeals with immediate consequences for federal programs, regulated businesses and the structure of the executive branch. They also produced some of the court’s longest and most sharply divided opinions.

The wait for those decisions has been growing. Federal judiciary statistics show that, among cases terminated on the merits during the year ending September 30, 2025, the D.C. Circuit took a median of 5.4 months to move from oral argument to its final opinion or order. The national median was 3.2 months. No other regional circuit reported a longer median interval.

An unresolved D.C. Circuit appeal can leave federal grants frozen, agency personnel decisions unsettled, regulatory obligations uncertain or an injunction governing executive action in place. The timing can affect reserves, compliance plans, settlement leverage and preparations for rehearing or Supreme Court review.

A review of 219 matters argued before the court during calendar year 2025 provides a closer look at that wait. It also permits a preliminary examination of who sat on the panels, whether panel composition corresponded with decision time and where partisan divisions became most visible. The results show a court whose panels generally reflected the Democratic-leaning composition of its bench, although the relationship between panel partisanship and decisional speed was considerably less straightforward.

A Timing Gap That Has Widened

The D.C. Circuit has long required more time after argument than the national appellate median, but the distance between the two has increased. In fiscal year 2015, the court reported a median argument-to-disposition interval of 3.7 months, compared with 2.1 months nationally. By fiscal year 2025, those figures had risen to 5.4 and 3.2 months, respectively.

text:
The Trump administration is expanding its immigration crackdown to legal pathways into the United States, temporarily halting immigrant visa appointments worldwide while consular officers undergo new training and prepare to revoke visas from some foreign nationals who entered legally before seeking asylum.

Earlier this week, the State Department announced it is preparing to revoke B-1 business and B-2 tourist visas from some foreign nationals who entered the United States as temporary visitors and later sought asylum. (TNND)

The State Department says immigrant visa appointments at U.S. embassies and consulates are being adjusted as officers undergo what the agency calls “in-depth training” aimed at strengthening screening of applicants.

State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said the goal is to ensure consular officers have the resources needed to properly evaluate visa cases, including whether applicants pose security concerns or are likely to follow the terms of their visas.

“Each one of these determinations is made on a case-by-case basis,” Pigott said.

The worldwide initiative comes after a federal judge blocked an earlier, broader policy that suspended immigrant visa issuance for nationals of 75 countries the administration considered at higher risk of relying on public assistance.

The National Immigration Law Center, which challenged that policy, praised the court's decision and called the restrictions an “unlawful and racist ban” that caused “immeasurable harm” by separating families.

Pigott defended the administration's broader approach, saying the State Department has an obligation to protect Americans and ensure taxpayer-funded benefits are protected.

The administration is also targeting some visas already issued.

Earlier this week, the State Department announced it is preparing to revoke B-1 business and B-2 tourist visas from some foreign nationals who entered the United States as temporary visitors and later sought asylum. Reports indicate as many as 200,000 people could be affected.

Pigott said the administration is focused on cases in which officials determine an applicant intended to seek asylum and remain permanently in the United States when applying for a temporary visa.

“If that person has applied for that temporary visa with the intent to apply for asylum and stay in this country permanently, they have misrepresented themselves to the consular officer,” Pigott said, characterizing such cases as fraud.

The moves are part of a broader effort by the administration to tighten legal immigration pathways.

This week, the Department of Homeland Security proposed a new roughly $103,000 fee for many new H-1B work visa petitions. Earlier this summer, DHS finalized new limits on how long some foreign students and journalists can remain in the country before seeking an extension.

The State Department says it has already revoked more than 175,000 visas this year, including visas held by foreign nationals accused of criminal activity or other violations.

text:
ACLU-NJ Statement on Appellate Court's Refusal to Dismiss US v. McIver

For Immediate Release: August 26, 2026

NEWARK – In a divided opinion, the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit today refused to reverse lower court rulings in U.S. v. McIver. The ACLU of New Jersey, along with the National Women’s Law Center and the NAACP Legal Defense Fund, had filed an amicus brief in support of Rep. LaMonica McIver, who is facing federal charges stemming from a congressional oversight visit of Delaney Hall, an immigration detention center in Newark. The brief urged the appellate court to dismiss the indictment because the charges brought against Rep. McIver are acts of political retribution.

In response to the ruling, Amol Sinha, executive director of the ACLU of New Jersey, issued the following statement:

"Congresswoman McIver visited Delaney Hall to carry out congressional oversight of an immigration detention facility, an essential function of accountability that she has the legal authority to do. As ICE continues to brutalize our communities with impunity, Rep. McIver is being targeted by the federal government because she disagrees with President Trump on some of the most pressing issues of our time, including immigration policy. Weaponizing the DOJ to target a sitting Member of Congress undermines our system of checks and balances and threatens our democracy. We will continue to urge the court to dismiss the charges against Rep. McIver."

text:
MIAMI — On Aug. 18, ICE removed Rafael José Quero Silva, a known human rights violator who participated in the detention and torture of political dissidents during the Maduro regime, to Venezuela following a Department of Justice immigration judge’s order of removal.

ICE arrested Quero Silva, an illegal alien from Venezuela, Feb. 27, 2025, in Miramar. He entered the United States June 20, 2016, at Miami International Airport but failed to depart in accordance with the terms of his admission.

“ICE officers continue to remove human rights violators to their home countries,” said ERO Miami Field Office Director Matthew Elliston. “This removal reflects the outstanding work of ICE Miami, HSI Miami, FBI Miami and the Human Rights Violators and War Crimes Center. We are committed to public safety and national security, and to ensuring the United States does not become a safe haven for individuals who participated in persecution, torture or other serious human rights abuses.”

“HSI remains committed to working with our law enforcement partners to identify, investigate, and hold accountable human rights violators who seek refuge in the United States,” said HSI Miami Special Agent in Charge Jose R. Figueroa. “This case reflects our unwavering commitment to protecting the integrity of our immigration system and ensuring that individuals who participated in persecution or torture cannot evade justice.”

Prior to entering the United States, Quero Silva served as a colonel in the Bolivarian National Guard of Venezuela, known as the GNB, commanding the 47th Detachment in the city of Barquisimeto. He was involved in, and had knowledge of, the excessive use of force, detention and torture of anti-Maduro protesters by GNB members under his command. Reports indicate that in 2013, Quero Silva directly oversaw the torture of at least 74 peaceful demonstrators. While in the custody of Quero Silva’s 47th Detachment, these political protesters were subjected to electric shocks, severe beatings with nightsticks and frozen water bottles, threats of rape, and other physical, psychological and sexual abuse.

The case was supported by ICE Miami, HSI Miami, and the Human Rights Violators and War Crimes Center. The HSI-led Human Rights Violators and War Crimes Center furthers the government’s efforts to identify, locate and prosecute human rights abusers in the United States, including those who are known or suspected to have participated in persecution, war crimes, genocide, torture, extrajudicial killings, female genital mutilation, or the use or recruitment of child soldiers.

Since 2003, ICE has arrested more than 520 people for human rights-related violations of law under various criminal and immigration statutes. During the same period, ICE has obtained deportation orders against, and physically removed from the United States, 1,178 known or suspected human rights violators and facilitated the departures of an additional 208. The Human Rights Violators and War Crimes Center has issued more than 80,000 lookouts for potential perpetrators of human rights abuses and has stopped more than 415 human rights violators and war crimes suspects from entering the United States.

Christian Castro is charged in Minnesota with assault and falsely reporting a crime in the Jan. 14 shooting of 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis. Minnesota authorities have sought his extradition since his arrest, but he remains in custody in Brownsville, Texas, a city bordering Mexico.

Under Texas law and barring extradition, Castro must be released after 90 days of detention, which is Thursday.

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison filed a request for a temporary restraining order last week, asking a federal judge to prevent the sheriff in Cameron County, Texas, from releasing Castro, and to order Texas Gov. Greg Abbott to sign his extradition warrant.

WATCH: ICE agent kills Mexican immigrant in Houston in latest deadly enforcement encounter

Minnesota officials believe Castro could flee the country, citing calls he made from jail to a woman in Mexico, talking "about marrying her and buying a house in Mexico when he is released," according to the lawsuit.

Castro is accused of firing a gun through the front door of a Minneapolis home, shooting Sosa-Celis in the leg. Prosecutors say Castro also falsely accused Sosa-Celis and another man of attacking an ICE officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel.

At a federal hearing in Brownsville on Tuesday, attorneys with the Minnesota Attorney General's Office argued it would be hard to compel Castro to face charges in their state if he is released, and they fear Castro may flee the country, citing his phone conversations with a woman who lives in Mexico.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott said last week he would not respond to the extradition request, citing the ongoing investigation into fraud in government social service programs in Minnesota, which President Donald Trump used to justify his immigration crackdown there.

text:
ICE has arrested more people in Maine so far this year than in the previous two years combined, according to new data released by a national nonprofit.

The data also shows the vast majority of people detained did not have a criminal record.

According to the Deportation Data Project, roughly 2% of individuals detained in Maine between January and July of this year had a criminal history. Only one person had a violent criminal conviction.

"It's one person. You probably have a better chance of finding a needle in a haystack," said Ruben Torres, director of advocacy and policy for the Maine Immigrants' Rights Coalition.

The Deportation Data Project collects immigration data from the U.S. government and makes it publicly available. The Maine Immigrants' Rights Coalition published the Maine data in its own report.

Also read: Report: Most people arrested by ICE in Maine operation had not been convicted of crimes

The data shows a sharp increase in detentions this year, with roughly 482 arrests in Maine so far in 2026.

Torres says there have been about two arrests every day since May, forcing families to have difficult conversations.

"How do you tell a 4-, 5-, 6-year-old you're gonna be the man of the house if dad is arrested?" Torres said.

"What has been sold to the public as a need for public safety isn't being reflected in how the actions are being undertaken," he added.

DHS previously said it was targeting people it called the "worst of the worst."

Earlier this year, CBS13 reported that just half of the arrests made by ICE in Maine were targeted. The rest involved individuals who were near an ICE agent and suspected of being in the U.S. illegally.

In the newly released data, DHS removed that distinction.

When asked why, DHS did not directly answer the question but said in part:

"Many of the individuals that are counted as 'non-criminals' are actually terrorists, human rights abusers, gangsters and more; they just don't have a rap sheet in the U.S. Further, every single one of these individuals committed a crime when they came into this country illegally."

DHS also disputed the report's accuracy and said the data in question was not reviewed before it was released.

Also read: 'Operation Catch of the Day': ICE launches major enforcement effort in Maine

The data was obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests.

Torres hopes state and federal leaders use the information to push for significant immigration reform.

"Find ways to fund a functional immigration system. That way, going through the process actually means something for families," Torres said.

Based on the volume of calls to an immigrant hotline, Torres believes arrests are on pace to continue increasing through the end of the year.

He says he hopes making the data public will empower the community and promote government transparency.

text:
A federal appeals court declined to toss the case against Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-N.J.), even as the panel split over a matter in which she is accused of attacking law enforcement with her forearms in a scuffle with immigration officials.

The ruling on Wednesday from the 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals comes as McIver has pushed to get the case dismissed on various grounds, including that her visit to the Delaney Hall detention facility was carried out in her role as a legislative official and should be protected by prosecution under the Speech or Debate Clause.

The three-judge panel declined to toss the case on a number of grounds raised by McIver, finding that while her inspection of Delaney Hall was protected under the clause, her intervention in the arrest of Newark Mayor Ras Baraka (D) was not.

But one judge dissented, saying McIver’s “plausibly incidental contact” with one of the officers came as she was being impeded from carrying out her legislative duties by touring the controversial detention center.

He also touched on McIver’s claims that the case amounted to a selective prosecution, saying the lawmaker “presented enough [evidence] to obtain discovery on whether this prosecution ‘was intended to prevent [her] exercise of a fundamental right’” to conduct legislative oversight.

McIver lamented the ruling.

“I fundamentally believe that the court got it wrong here. To protect the people, their elected representatives must be authorized to conduct oversight of the executive branch without fear of retaliation,” she said in a statement.

“Today’s decision chills that authority and emboldens the Trump administration to continue persecuting our most vulnerable communities, those who try to defend them, and anyone who dares hold the president or his lackeys accountable.”

The pending arrest against Baraka — who no longer faces charges in the matter — ignited chaos between Democrats there to tour the facility and immigration officials on site.

McIver is accused of having “slammed her forearm into the body” of one immigration officer and “using each of her forearms to forcibly strike” a second.

The appeals court determined those actions were not protected by the clause.

“The Speech or Debate Clause does not provide a blanket protection over ‘all things in any way related to the legislative process,’” Judge Cindy Chung wrote in the majority opinion.

“The nature of the conduct charged in Count One is non legislative. Congresswoman McIver’s physical contact with Victim-1 was not ‘integral’ to the ‘deliberative and communicative processes by which Members participate in committee and House proceedings.’”

The ruling determined charges related to those two incidents should stand but remanded the case back to the district court to review a third count that broadly incorporated all “efforts to hinder, impede the arrest of the Mayor.”

A second opinion from Judge Thomas Ambro dissented in part, saying his colleagues were too quick to determine that some of her actions could not be considered tied to her legislative role, saying the second count faced by McIver was at least “ambiguously” legislative.

“When an Executive Branch official prevents a Member from entering a DHS [Department of Homeland Security] facility, she is denied effective access to an oversight inspection, the investigative tool federal law supplies Members in this context,” Ambro wrote, adding that “her access to the facility depended on circumventing him somehow.”

Ambro also said the court should at least grant McIver further discovery on whether she is being selectively prosecuted.

He wrote that among lawmakers’ protections are “freedom from fear that the Executive will use criminal prosecution to punish legislators for their oversight and political opposition.”

“My colleagues believe vindication of this right is beyond our jurisdiction. I disagree. And where, as here, a legislator has presented evidence that her prosecution was brought as an act of political retaliation, I would allow her discovery into the truth of the matter—not only for her own sake but to safeguard the independence of our legislative bodies,” Ambro wrote, saying she deserved to know “whether [the case] punishes her for doing her job as a Member of Congress with specific oversight responsibilities.”

McIver’s attorney, Paul Fishman, warned the Trump administration is likely to continue to bring charges against political foes.

“Congresswoman LaMonica McIver is innocent and we are confident that any jury will agree. But there should never have been an indictment at all, much less a trial,” he said in a statement.

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detained almost 50,000 people in July, marking its highest monthly arrest total during President Trump’s second term, newly released data shows.

According to numbers published in the Deportation Data Project — a joint project conducted by the University of California, Berkeley and University of California, Los Angeles — ICE arrested 49,571 people in July 2026. A Monday Associated Press analysis noted that the figure marked a surge in detainments, jumping by 15 percent from the month prior.

For the majority of 2026, detention numbers stagnated around the lower 30,000 range. Detainments in July jumped by 70 percent from when this plateau began in February.

Since the Trump administration’s February immigration crackdown in Minnesota, called Operation Metro Surge, ICE and Customs and Border Protection have expanded their enforcement across the country. The agencies have also invested heavily in their officers as President Trump rolls back deportation protections for several migrant groups.

Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, the wife of Army Sgt. Hedar Leonel Turcios Juarez, was deported Monday — marking the seventh spouse or parent of an active-duty military member who was removed from the country.

“I don’t know if I will be able to continue with this,” Turcios Juarez told the AP. “I have to make a plan to make sure I can still fulfill my military responsibilities — but also take care of my family.”

Navy sailor Joshua Aviles — currently serving aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, which earlier this month faced scrutiny for declining living conditions — similarly reported that his father had been detained by ICE. After Aviles’s social media pleas, his father was released from custody Wednesday.

“I don’t know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly being treated like a criminal,” the sailor wrote in his initial post.

ICE also deported more than 160 immigrants to Haiti last week, acting on a June Supreme Court ruling that allowed the Trump administration to end Temporary Protected Status for around 330,000 Haitians and more than 6,000 Syrians.

But polls suggest public approval of ICE’s expanded efforts is dwindling. In early August, the AP and NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that Americans’ approval of Trump’s handling of immigration had dropped by 10 percentage points since the start of his second term, reaching a 58 percent disapproval rate.

text:
By Vince Gasparini

syracuse.com

SYRACUSE, N.Y. — Fifteen county sheriffs across New York state have filed a lawsuit over a state law that bans local law enforcement from cooperating with federal immigration enforcement.

The suit was filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of New York on Tuesday. Among those suing the state are Madison County Sheriff Todd Hood and Oswego County Sheriff Don Hilton, according to court papers.

| SPECIAL REPORT: Find the hidden gaps in your agency’s logistics readiness

Gov. Kathy Hochul is named as a defendant in the lawsuit, alongside Attorney General Letitia James and the state of New York.

The law, dubbed the “Local Cops, Local Crimes Act,” was signed by Hochul in May. The suit was filed Tuesday, the same day the law took effect.

The law prohibits local authorities from entering into formal or informal cooperation agreements with ICE. It also bans local jails, juvenile detention centers and youth detention facilities from holding people on civil immigration charges.

When the bill was signed, Hochul argued that it was necessary due to what she says is the out-of-control nature of the operations being carried out by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The lawsuit argues that the agreements between ICE and the sheriffs are sanctioned by the U.S. Congress and that no state executive has the authority to tell sheriffs — as elected officials — that they cannot participate in the agreements.

Onondaga County Sheriff Toby Shelley was not among the sheriffs named in the lawsuit. Not long after President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, Shelley told syracuse.com | The Post-Standard that he would not comply with the president’s requests to have his deputies work with ICE in their immigration enforcement.

“I took an oath to protect people’s constitutional rights,” Shelley said. “Everything this sheriff’s office does is going to be legal. We’re not going to hold anyone illegally.”

The department also has a policy that goes back at least a decade that bars deputies from questioning people about their immigration or citizenship status.

Hood, however, has not been shy in his support of Trump’s immigration crackdown and mass deportation agenda.

In July 2025, he entered the Madison County Sheriff’s Office into a 287(g) agreement, which allows the Madison County jail to detain people otherwise due for release and hand them over to federal agents for civil immigration violations.

His activism on immigration enforcement, along with opposition to bail reform and other criminal justice reform, landed him a spot as the running mate of Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau County executive and Republican nominee for governor.

In July, the Attorney General’s office warned Hood to end his agreement with the federal government. While he agreed to end the 287(g) as required by the “Local Cops, Local Crimes Act,” he said he still intends to work with ICE and honor its requests to detain and hand over any undocumented immigrants that come into custody at the county jail.

After the Tuesday lawsuit was filed, Hochul and James released a statement saying that the suit is “nothing but a frivolous waste of taxpayer dollars.”

“The courts have already declined to block this law once, and we are confident they will do so again,” the statement reads. “In the meantime, we expect all law enforcement agencies in New York to uphold state law.”

Here are the sheriffs suing the state:

Broome County: Sheriff Frederick Akshar

Cattaraugus County: Sheriff Eric Butler

Cayuga County: Sheriff Brian Schenck

Delaware County: Sheriff Craig DuMond

Franklin County: Sheriff Jay Cook

Fulton County: Sheriff Richard Giardino

Jefferson County: Sheriff Peter Barnett

Lewis County: Sheriff Michael Carpinelli

Madison County: Sheriff Todd Hood

Orange County: Sheriff Paul Arteta

Oswego County: Sheriff Don Hilton

Rensselaer County: Sheriff Kyle Bourgault

Saratoga County: Sheriff Jeffrey Brown

St. Lawrence County: Sheriff Patrick Engle

Wayne County: Sheriff Robert Milby

The agency will sometimes release details of individual arrests, but it only does so voluntarily. ICE doesn’t generally release arrest reports or other similar records. And the people it arrests generally have their cases heard in immigration court, where case files are not open to the public.

Olga Guerra hadn't spoken to her husband, Fidel Romero, since she says federal immigration agents arrested him and a coworker on their way to work in Stamford early Monday morning, leaving his empty truck sitting outside a convenience store.

text:
WASHINGTON, DC — Congresswoman Teresa Leger Fernández (NM-03), Ranking Member of the House Natural Resources Subcommittee on Indian and Insular Affairs, and Congressman Jared Huffman (CA-02), Ranking Member of the House Natural Resources Committee led 18 members of Congress in demanding answers from Interior Secretary Doug Burgum about the Trump Administration’s rushed effort to revoke protections for lands surrounding Chaco Culture National Historical Park.

The Department of the Interior is proposing to revoke Public Land Order No. 7923, which established a 10-mile mineral withdrawal surrounding Chaco Canyon. Revoking the order would reopen these culturally significant public lands to oil and gas leasing and mining activities.

“Chaco Canyon is not just a historical site; it’s a living cultural landscape,” the lawmakers wrote. “The Department’s current fast-tracked efforts to overturn the withdrawal area do not respect the historical, cultural, and spiritual value of Chaco Canyon.”

“The Department’s rushed review undermined the Department’s trust responsibility to Tribal nations and the Tribal consultation process under Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act,” they continued.

The lawmakers’ letter raises serious concerns that the Department failed to fulfill its trust responsibility to Tribal nations and honor Burgum’s public commitment to meaningful consultation. During a June 2025 House Natural Resources Committee hearing, Burgum committed to Leger Fernández to send an official with decision-making authority to conduct individual, in-person consultations with every Tribe with an interest in Chaco Canyon. However, Interior’s own draft Environmental Assessment indicates that the Department moved forward before completing all requested consultations. Several Tribes received only “informational meetings,” while requests to meet with a decision-maker remained unmet.

The Department also provided only 21 days for public comment and held no public meetings before advancing its proposal. Despite that abbreviated process, the public submitted an estimated 300,000 comments.

By contrast, the existing protections were finalized in 2023 following 150 days of public comment, eight public meetings, and years of advocacy by Tribal nations. An archaeological study identified more than 4,730 cultural sites within the protected area.

The lawmakers are asking Burgum to disclose:

● How many Tribal consultations included an Interior official with decision-making authority;

● Why the Department failed to honor Tribal requests to meet with a decision-maker;

● Why Interior published its draft proposal before completing Tribal consultation;

● Whether all requested consultations will occur before the Department completes its review; and

● Why Interior conducted a limited Environmental Assessment instead of a more comprehensive Environmental Impact Statement.

The lawmakers requested answers by Friday, August 28.

The letter was signed by Representatives Teresa Leger Fernández, Jared Huffman, Melanie Stansbury, Gabe Vasquez, Sharice Davids, Betty McCollum, Eleanor Holmes Norton, Mark DeSaulnier, Val Hoyle, Donald Beyer Jr., Judy Chu, Dina Titus, Jesús “Chuy” García, Sylvia Garcia, Rashida Tlaib, Diana DeGette, Julia Brownley, and Raja Krishnamoorthi.

text:
15 New York State sheriffs have filed a lawsuit against Governor Kathy Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James over the stripping of their ability to work with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The lawsuit, filed in federal court and dated Aug. 25, names three Central New York sheriffs as petitioners. Those are Madison County Sheriff Todd Hood, Oswego County Sheriff Don Hilton and Cayuga County Sheriff Brian Schenck.

In late July, Governor Hochul and Attorney General James sent letters to local law enforcement agencies demanding they terminate any agreements with ICE. The letter demanded that they stay in compliance with New York State's "Local Cops, Local Crimes Act."

The legislation was enacted on May 27. It prohibits any local government or law enforcement agency from conducting civil immigration enforcement.

The lawsuit claims that the New York State law conflicts with federal laws. The suit said that, per Congress, partnerships between local, state, and federal agencies are encouraged to enter into written agreements in which local law enforcement assists with the identification, detention and removal of illegal immigrants violating federal law.

The plaintiffs also argued that sheriffs are independently elected, are not subordinate to the governor or attorney general and are permitted to exercise their "own judgment."

"Under the New York Constitution’s guarantees of Home Rule (Article IX) and Separation of Powers, and under the independent status of their office, they possess the authority to make their own judgments about whether and how to participate in the cooperative framework Congress created," the lawsuit said.

On Aug. 17, Madison County Sheriff Todd Hood announced that his office terminated its agreement with ICE. However, additional details of the termination were not released.

The Madison County Sheriff's Office was one of 12 in New York State that received letters from the governor and attorney general demanding that they end their agreements and that they were out of compliance with state law.

Those letters demanded that any agency out of compliance submit proof of termination of its agreement.

The lawsuit seeks the declaration that the "Local Cops, Local Crimes Act" is unconstitutional.
