In total, since Trump’s inauguration last year, ICE has detained over 610,000 people — more than the population of Atlanta, Baltimore, Milwaukee or the entire state of Wyoming.
At times, previous administrations, both Democratic and Republican, have booked hundreds of thousands of people into ICE custody for processing.
But in Trump’s second term, the number of people ICE booked and then held for extended periods of time has ballooned.
And yet ICE detentions, especially long-term, remain among the highest in the timeframe covered by the data.
text:
More than 45,000 people were detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement last month, the highest number since Donald Trump retook office, according to data the Deportation Data Project released Monday.

In total, since Trump’s inauguration last year, ICE has detained over 610,000 people — more than the population of Atlanta, Baltimore, Milwaukee or the entire state of Wyoming.

At times, previous administrations, both Democratic and Republican, have booked hundreds of thousands of people into ICE custody for processing. But in Trump’s second term, the number of people ICE booked and then held for extended periods of time has ballooned.

Last year, more than 270,000 people spent at least a week detained, surpassing any other year since 2012, the earliest in the Deportation Data Project’s archive. However, even as Trump's enforcement upends lives and livelihoods in immigrant communities, the number of people detained and deported falls far short of the president's goal of deporting 1 million people per year.

The Trump administration’s policy is to detain almost all unauthorized immigrants, regardless of their individual circumstances, and to keep them detained as long as it takes for their cases to move through immigration court — often months, or even years.

Both the Biden and Obama administrations oversaw enormous spikes in book-ins to ICE detention amid increases in migrants arriving at the Southern border, including unaccompanied children in 2012 and single adults in 2023. Many of those people were not locked up for long; instead, they were processed and then released to the community — where it is easier to challenge their deportations — while their cases played out in immigration courts.

Since Trump returned to office, border crossings have dropped precipitously. And yet ICE detentions, especially long-term, remain among the highest in the timeframe covered by the data.

The other major difference between today’s immigration detention machine and that of prior administrations, including Trump’s first term, is where and how the arrests and detentions are taking place.

About 80% of people detained since Trump retook office have come from the interior of the country, where they are much more likely to have community ties — families, jobs, homes — than those crossing the border. That’s almost a complete reversal of the practice during the previous two years under President Joe Biden, when 30% of detentions came from inside the U.S.

“What we’re seeing is something unprecedented,” said Caitlin Patler, a public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley who studies immigration. “Going after people where they work, where they pray, in the streets, at the schools. These are these places that in the past you wouldn't really have seen ICE arrests happening at scale.”

César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández, a professor who studies immigration at Ohio State University Moritz College of Law, warned of the lasting impact on a generation of people in the cities hit hardest by Trump’s immigration tactics, like Chicago and Minneapolis.

“People who are detained lose their jobs, lose their homes, lose the money that is needed to pay for food, medical care, school supplies,” Hernández says. “Those are the kind of direct impacts that don’t go away the moment the refrigerator is stocked again, or the electricity is paid.”

Others, who are deported, are not able to return to their homes at all.

“The administration lost a lot of goodwill from a lot of people who thought they were going to remove bad people,” said Sarah Saldaña, who served as director of ICE from 2014 to 2017. “They've done everything to make it look like a lawless-enforcement agency.”

Some people arrested and detained in the last year had already been released from custody by judges during previous administrations with agreements to attend their immigration court hearings.

For many of these people, nothing about their lives or cases has changed to warrant incarceration, said Amy Romero, an immigration attorney with the Lawyers' Committee for Rhode Island, who is representing many people in this situation.

“The only thing that’s changed is we now have an administration that is hell-bent on imprisoning as many immigrants as possible,” she said.

text:
Reports of Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity in several Connecticut communities, including Danbury, Stamford and Bridgeport, are raising concerns among residents and local officials.

Eyewitnesses in Danbury reported seeing federal agents in the city and witnessing arrests in recent days.

Danbury Mayor Roberto Alves said he is angry and concerned about the reported arrests and detentions and the impact they may be having on families.

"There are children who are afraid they're going to get home and their parents aren't there," Alves said. "There are kids who were at home yesterday and a parent never returned."

Connecticut Students for a Dream said it has been working with rapid response groups across the state to gather information about detentions. The organization said its network received firsthand reports from eyewitnesses indicating that at least 21 people were detained, including 16 in Danbury, four in Stamford and one in Bridgeport.

NBC Connecticut has reached out to ICE to confirm those figures but has not yet received a response.

Alves is urging residents to understand their legal rights, including when they are required to open their doors to law enforcement.

"People should know that they don't have to open their door unless that law enforcement agency has a warrant and has a reason to talk to them," Alves said.

Seth Garben of Greater Danbury Area Unites for Immigrants said enforcement activity appeared to increase this week.

"Things really started heating up again yesterday," Garben said.

Video provided to NBC Connecticut by Al Robinson of HatCity Blog appears to show agents wearing vests labeled "Immigration and Customs Enforcement."

Alves said city officials are typically not notified before agents arrive in Danbury.

"They don't let us know if they're going to be here. We don't work with them. They don't work with us," Alves said.

ICE said in response to NBC Connecticut:

For operational security and the safety of our officers, ICE will not disclose or discuss law enforcement operations.

title: Federal Judge Vacates 75-Country Immigrant Visa Ban: What Applicants and Employers ...
description:
A federal judge has struck down the State Department policy that halted immigrant visa issuance for nationals of 75 countries.
The suspension affected both family-sponsored and employment-based immigrant visa applicants processing through U.S. embassies and consulates abroad.
First, consular officers—not the Secretary of State—are charged with deciding whether an individual immigrant visa applicant is eligible under the law.
The court vacated the policy and set aside immigrant visa refusals that were based solely on the 75-country suspension.
That is meaningful relief for many families and workers whose immigrant visa cases were stopped by the 75-country policy.
text:
A federal judge has struck down the State Department policy that halted immigrant visa issuance for nationals of 75 countries. The August 21, 2026 decision in Catholic Legal Immigration Network, Inc. v. Rubio removes a major barrier for families and employment-based applicants who had otherwise qualified for immigrant visas but were refused solely because of their nationality.

The ruling is significant, but it does not mean that every affected case will be approved immediately. It restores individualized visa adjudication. Applicants must still satisfy all statutory and regulatory requirements, and separate restrictions may continue to apply.

What Was the 75-Country Policy?

Effective January 21, 2026, the Department of State suspended immigrant visa issuance for nationals of 75 designated countries while it reviewed screening and vetting policies related to the “public charge” ground of inadmissibility. The affected countries included Brazil, Colombia, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Russia, Jamaica, Nigeria, and many countries across Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Caribbean, the Middle East, and Eastern Europe.

Under the policy, a consular officer could determine that an applicant was otherwise eligible for an immigrant visa and still refuse issuance based solely on the applicant’s nationality. The suspension affected both family-sponsored and employment-based immigrant visa applicants processing through U.S. embassies and consulates abroad.

Several nonprofit organizations, affected applicants, and U.S. citizen sponsors challenged the policy in federal court.

What Did the Court Decide?

U.S. District Judge Jeannette A. Vargas of the Southern District of New York concluded that the nationality-based suspension exceeded the Secretary of State’s authority and violated the Immigration and Nationality Act.

The court emphasized two features of the statutory framework. First, consular officers—not the Secretary of State—are charged with deciding whether an individual immigrant visa applicant is eligible under the law. Second, Section 202(a)(1)(A) of the Immigration and Nationality Act generally prohibits discrimination in the issuance of immigrant visas because of a person’s nationality, place of birth, or place of residence.

The court vacated the policy and set aside immigrant visa refusals that were based solely on the 75-country suspension. As a result, the State Department must return to case-by-case adjudication rather than deny an otherwise eligible applicant merely because the applicant is a national of one of the designated countries.

What the Ruling Means in Practice

For an applicant whose immigrant visa was refused only under the 75-country policy, the decision may create a path for the case to be reconsidered. Applicants should not assume, however, that a consulate will reopen or approve a case automatically. The Department of State must first implement the ruling, and the government may seek appellate review or a stay.

The decision also does not eliminate the public charge ground of inadmissibility. Consular officers may continue to evaluate whether an applicant is likely to become a public charge based on the governing law and the applicant’s individual circumstances. Affidavits of support, household income, assets, job offers, health coverage, and other financial evidence may therefore remain important, depending on the immigrant visa category and the facts of the case.

For employment-based cases, employers and sponsored workers should confirm whether a refusal was based solely on the now-vacated policy or whether the consular officer identified an additional ground of inadmissibility or administrative processing. A refusal supported by another independent legal ground was not necessarily set aside by the court’s order.

Recommended Next Steps

Applicants, sponsoring family members, and employers with affected cases should consider the following:

Review the refusal record. Locate the refusal letter, CEAC status, consular correspondence, and any reference to the 75-country policy or the public charge ground of inadmissibility.

Confirm whether another restriction applies. Nationality-based restrictions under Presidential Proclamation 10998, administrative processing, documentary deficiencies, or a separate inadmissibility finding may still prevent issuance.

Keep financial evidence current. Updated employment letters, tax records, affidavits of support, proof of assets, and other evidence may be requested when adjudication resumes.

Watch for post-specific instructions. Consulates may differ in how and when they reopen or reconsider affected cases. Avoid submitting duplicate applications or paying new fees unless instructed.

Get case-specific advice before acting. The right strategy may depend on the refusal code, visa category, priority date, country of chargeability, and whether the government appeals or obtains a stay.

The Bottom Line

The court’s decision removes the State Department’s blanket nationality-based bar and restores the individualized adjudication required by federal immigration law. That is meaningful relief for many families and workers whose immigrant visa cases were stopped by the 75-country policy.

Even so, the ruling is not an automatic visa approval, and its practical effect will depend on implementation by the Department of State and any further court proceedings. Applicants and employers should review affected cases promptly, preserve all consular records, and obtain individualized guidance before taking the next step.

Because implementation will unfold over the coming weeks and each case presents its own facts, individuals and employers with cases affected by the 75-country policy should seek guidance from qualified immigration counsel to understand how the ruling applies to their specific circumstances.

text:
Shapiro hires ex-Trump admin official to help counter president’s ‘attacks’

Jennifer Higgins, a longtime federal immigration official based in Washington, D.C., is being paid $89 an hour.

This story was originally published by Spotlight PA.

HARRISBURG — Earlier this spring, with no public notice, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro made an unconventional hire: a senior advisor to help him deal with the Trump administration.

Jennifer Higgins, a longtime federal immigration official based in Washington, D.C., was brought on to help Shapiro and state agencies under his jurisdiction map out responses to some of the president’s targeted attacks on Democrat-led states — notably, funding cuts and demands for sensitive or proprietary information.

Higgins is being paid by the hour — an unusual arrangement for a gubernatorial staffer, and one that Shapiro’s office could not immediately explain. State payroll records show she is paid $89 per hour, and Shapiro officials said she works full-time, putting her annual salary at roughly $185,000.

The administration defended hiring Higgins, even though Pennsylvania already spends tens of thousands of taxpayer dollars every year for a federal government liaison.

The governor’s office employs a full-time lobbyist in Washington, D.C., who is paid $177,507 annually. And in theory, Pennsylvania’s two senators act as the state’s de facto protectors in the nation’s capital and run interference with the White House when problems arise.

But Shapiro spokesperson Rosie Lapowsky explained in an emailed statement that an additional person was needed because “the Trump administration’s relentless attacks on the rights and freedoms of Pennsylvanians are reaching into every corner of our Commonwealth.”

Higgins, Lapowsky said, brings “deep expertise and invaluable perspective helping protect Pennsylvanians during this critical moment.” (Higgins did not respond to Spotlight PA’s request to speak with her directly.)

Still, Higgins’ expertise is in the immigration sphere, where she has spent nearly the entirety of her career. The governor’s office acknowledged that Higgins is not directly advising Shapiro on immigration issues, but is part of a larger group of policy officials, lawyers, and others who provide the governor with information on that and other issues facing the state.

Asked for an example of Higgins’ work, Lapowsky said she helped coordinate Shapiro’s response to a Trump administration demand that states turn over commercial driver’s license records containing personal information. Trump officials have pointed, among other things, to crashes involving noncitizen drivers as one reason for the crackdown and have threatened to withhold federal funding if states do not comply.

In August, Shapiro joined a coalition of state attorneys general suing the federal government over the subpoena.

It’s true that, since reclaiming the White House in 2024, President Donald Trump has used the levers of the federal government to punish blue states.

The administration admitted in a federal court filing this summer that it recommended scrapping billions in grants for clean-energy projects based solely on those states’ “political identity,” and whether Trump won the vote in those places in the 2024 election.

Earlier this year, Trump attempted to freeze billions in childcare and social assistance for five Democratic-led states — he had initiated the move following the federal fraud probe involving Minnesota’s social services network — which he later abandoned.

And Politico reported last month that Trump overruled his own emergency management agency to deny federal relief funds to four Democratic-led states.

For his part, Shapiro often talks about how his administration has sued Trump dozens of times to challenge the loss of federal funding. Those suits involve a range of initiatives, from education to natural disasters. The governor’s office also noted that unlike in other states, where attorneys general are handling litigation against Trump, Shapiro’s lawyers are taking on that work in Pennsylvania. Attorney General Dave Sunday, a Republican, has not entered the commonwealth into any lawsuit against the president or his administration.

Many of those suits predate Higgins’ arrival, and were handled by attorneys already on Shapiro’s staff. But the volume of attacks coming from Washington, Lapowsky said, combined with the range and breadth of policies and issues being targeted, necessitated another person to help coordinate plans to respond.

Immigration leadership

Higgins’ role in the Shapiro administration differs significantly from the work that has defined her career.

She started as an immigration officer in the early 2000s, but quickly moved into leadership roles within the federal office that handles asylum applications and screenings and adjudicates refugee applications, according to an online biography.

Shortly after Trump was elected to a first term in 2016, Higgins became the office’s associate director. Some rights groups have highlighted that part of her bio, since she held a leadership position during the implementation of one of the federal government’s most controversial immigration programs.

Officially called the Migrant Protection Protocols (MPP), but better known as Remain in Mexico, the program went into effect in early 2019. It required asylum seekers along the southern border to return to cities in Mexico, many of which are dangerous, while waiting for their immigration cases to be heard in the courts. Previously, those people were allowed to stay in the United States during that waiting period.

The Trump administration sold MPP as a way to thwart people with fraudulent claims from easily entering the U.S. But human rights and immigration groups, as well as multiple news organizations, extensively documented how migrants sent to Mexican border towns faced extreme danger, including kidnapping, assault, and rape. Tent camps were set up to house some of the asylum seekers, but living conditions were squalid, with no running water or electricity.

Human rights groups also noted that access to legal representation was fraught with obstacles, and resulted in higher numbers of cases being denied, sometimes just because migrants did not receive timely notices of their hearings or could not safely reach ports of entry into the country to be present for such hearings.

The office where Higgins held a senior leadership role at the time — the Refugee, Asylum and International Operations Directorate (RAIO) inside the U.S. Department of Homeland Security — was part of the larger apparatus tasked with the MPP’s rollout. Higgins’ level of involvement in the program’s operations is not clear, as the office’s work is subject to high levels of confidentiality. But the office she helped oversee is responsible for, among other duties, conducting asylum screenings and applications, according to its website. Its employees would have been at the front lines of the program’s implementation.

President Joe Biden ended the Remain in Mexico program after defeating Trump in 2020. Since retaking the White House, Trump officials have attempted to revive it but have been blocked by the courts.

During Biden’s presidency, Higgins continued to rise. She became acting chief of staff to then-U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, and within a year was appointed acting director of the department’s vast agency that oversees the legal U.S. immigration system.

Shortly after Trump started his second term, she was replaced.

text:
With immigration arrests spiking last month to all-time highs, a new state law took effect in New York stopping local cops from signing cooperation agreements with Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.

The ban also sets up a confrontation between Gov. Kathy Hochul and her Republican challenger, Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman.

Blakeman is one of two county executives in New York who has so far refused to nullify a cooperation agreement with ICE.

"No county executive should think that they are above the law in the state of New York," Hochul said.

It was a stern warning to Blakeman as the new law went into effect preventing local cops from working with federal immigration agents to advance the Trump administration's mass deportation agenda.

Nassau County is one of only two of the state's 62 counties that have so far refused to comply with the law.

Within minutes of Hochul's remarks, New York Attorney General Letitia James issued subpoenas to law enforcement agencies that either did not confirm plans to unwind their agreements, or whose responses were deemed unsatisfactory.

The subpoenas went out to the sheriff's offices of Broome, Steuben, Nassau and Rensselaer counties, as well as the Nassau County Police Department.

A spokesman for Blakeman said the county executive would have no comment on the subpoenas, but at a recent appearance with President Trump, Blakeman vigorously defended working with ICE to rid the county of what he said were some 2,000 illegal immigrants with criminal records.

"Kathy Hochul, where do you want those guns? What neighborhood do you want to destroy? Where do you want those drugs? What community do you want to destroy? Where do you want those illegal immigrants with criminal records to live? You want it back in New York? We say no," Blakeman said at the time.

Defenders of the law stood in front of the Nassau Police Department to back up Hochul, who wants local police to reduce crime in their neighborhoods.

"Say it loud, say it clear, immigrants are welcome here," they chanted.

Hochul has said law enforcement will assist ICE "only if a real crime has been committed," not on civil immigration matters.

"Because we need local cops hunting down criminals, not kindergartners. Breaking up drug rings, not breaking up families. Arresting gun runners, not grandmas," Hochul said.

The subpoenas issued by James are the first step in forcing Nassau and the others to sever ties with ICE. A spokesperson said that if they don't comply, the next step would be a civil suit.

Last month, ICE agents arrested nearly 50,000 people. That's a 70% increase from February, in the aftermath of two fatal shootings in Minnesota that sparked protests.

title: Chinese Immigrants Led the First Mass Resistance to America's Deportation System - KQED
description:
From 1892-93, Chinese immigrants refused to comply with the requirement to register with their local internal revenue offices.
Yu, a longtime local historian and author, argues the resistance of early Chinese immigrants like her grandfather should be more well known.
Her grandfather arrived in 1881, at age 11 — just one year before the Chinese Exclusion Act banned Chinese laborers from entering the U.S. for a decade.
States, including California, passed laws targeting Chinese immigrants as anti-Chinese sentiment grew, fueled by the narrative that they threatened the nation’s economic well-being.
The 14th Amendment ensured due process and equal protection to everyone, giving Chinese immigrants new grounds to challenge discriminatory state laws.
text:
Connie Young Yu thought she knew a lot about her beloved gung gung. As a young girl, she would listen as her grandfather, Yung Wah Gok, recounted what it was like living through America’s Chinese Exclusion era of the late 19th century. She had heard many stories, like how, as a young boy in San José Chinatown, he’d have to sprint home while white residents hurled rocks at him.

It wasn’t until 1972, when Yu was an adult active in Asian American organizing and scholarship, that her mother shared a surprising piece of his history with her. From the family’s large carved camphor chest in her bedroom, her mother pulled out a neatly folded parchment: It was her grandfather’s chak chee, a certificate of residence that all Chinese people in the U.S. were required to carry, as mandated by the 1892 Geary Act, the successor to the 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act.

Stamped across the top of the document was the word “LABORER.” Below it were his occupation — “cook,” his height — just over 5 feet, 3 inches and identifying marks — “scar on left forearm.” And in the lower left corner was a striking portrait photo of her grandfather at the age of 25.

“I just thought, ‘Gee … that doesn’t look like my gung gung,’” said Yu, now 85, who had known her grandfather as a dignified man who wore suits. “But actually, I really liked that picture in many ways because he looks very determined. Like a young rebel.”

The certificate was issued in May 1894, two years after the passage of the Geary Act, revealing that her grandfather had been one of the tens of thousands of Chinese residents across the country who had resisted the federal government’s demands to register — forming one of the largest campaigns of civil disobedience in U.S. history.

From 1892-93, Chinese immigrants refused to comply with the requirement to register with their local internal revenue offices. If they were caught without a certificate, they faced arrest, detention and deportation as stipulated by the Geary Act, which historians and legal theorists say helped shape today’s U.S. immigration system.

While Chinese immigrants are remembered for constitutional victories, including rulings that established birthright citizenship and strengthened equal protection, they have another legacy: they led a nationwide campaign against the federal government’s expansion of immigration powers. And though they ultimately failed to overturn the Geary Act in court, their resistance challenged the adoption of now-routine practices — calling them “cruel and unjust,” and incompatible with the nation’s constitutional ideals.

Those sentiments are echoed today by immigrant communities across the country, as the Trump administration continues to double down on its deportation efforts.

Yu, a longtime local historian and author, argues the resistance of early Chinese immigrants like her grandfather should be more well known. She co-founded The Geary Act Project two years ago and is now on a mission to collect more certificates — to lay a paper trail of evidence linking the racism experienced by her ancestors to the current administration’s immigration crackdown.

“Our society is under threat, we’re under attack,” she said. “We’re trying to show that the Chinese Exclusion Act was actually a foundation for ICE and the harassment of people of color and immigration detention and deportation.”

Yu said it’s by luck that she was born in the United States. Her grandfather arrived in 1881, at age 11 — just one year before the Chinese Exclusion Act banned Chinese laborers from entering the U.S. for a decade.

“My parents always said, ‘If he had waited until he was 12, you wouldn’t be here,’” Yu said.

When Chinese people began arriving in the U.S. in the late 1840s, there was no federal immigration system. States, including California, passed laws targeting Chinese immigrants as anti-Chinese sentiment grew, fueled by the narrative that they threatened the nation’s economic well-being.

But Reconstruction — the post-Civil War era when constitutional protections were expanded for newly freed Black Americans — changed the landscape. The 14th Amendment ensured due process and equal protection to everyone, giving Chinese immigrants new grounds to challenge discriminatory state laws.

Several Supreme Court justices, along with others who wished to continue excluding Chinese immigrants, pushed for the federal government to take up immigration control, according to Kelly Lytle Hernández, an author and professor of history at UCLA.

“I understand our federal immigration system as being the creation of an effort to skirt the 14th Amendment, to skirt the growth of a multiracial democracy,” she said. ”Reconstruction and Chinese Exclusion are all part of the same story.”

In 1875, the Supreme Court ruled in Chy Lung v. Freeman that immigration was a federal responsibility, while the Page Act established one of the first major federal restrictions on immigration, targeting Chinese and other Asian women.

Seven years later came the Chinese Exclusion Act. Despite the passage of the landmark law, thousands of Chinese laborers and immigrants still arrived. They filed legal challenges to their exclusion, inundating federal courts in San Francisco and frustrating white politicians and residents who wanted to see Chinese immigration come to an end.

As the Chinese Exclusion Act was set to expire in 1892, the federal government realized it needed a way to plug the loopholes of the act, especially as anti-Chinese violence intensified.

“As soon as [white residents] saw that their goals weren’t being met by this experiment in diplomatic control, this is why we see the most violent anti-Chinese incidents happening between ’85 and ’88, not before 1882,” said Alexander Jin, a historian at Dartmouth University.

Vigilante mobs seized Chinese businesses and homes, and rural Chinatowns along the West Coast were set on fire, including Eureka, Antioch, Napa and San José.

Yu’s grandfather was a pioneer of San José’s Chinatown, and she said he shared details of how his community was destroyed in 1887: “The newspaper always said ‘mysterious fire’ … but my grandfather always said the fire was set to drive us out … [they should’ve] asked the Chinese themselves how they felt,” Yu said.

Months before the Chinese Exclusion Act was set to lapse, Santa Rosa lawyer and U.S. House Representative Thomas J. Geary introduced legislation that addressed a question the original act had a hard time answering: how could the government not only restrict newcomers but remove Chinese people who were already living in the country?

The Geary Act became law, extending the Chinese Exclusion Act by a decade and imposing remarkable provisions on Chinese laborers living in the U.S. They had to register with the federal government and obtain a certificate of residence that they had to carry with them at all times or risk up to one year of hard labor in prison and deportation unless they could prove their immigration status with the testimony of two white witnesses.

In other words, the Geary Act provided the U.S. government a way to deport longtime Chinese residents who had entered the U.S. legally. Historians say the law became the precursor to green cards, visas and other forms of surveillance and identification that the federal government uses today.

Though the act was signed into law, it garnered strongly worded protests within Congress, including from Robert R. Hitt, a representative from Illinois.

“Never before in a free country was there such a system of tagging a man like a dog to be caught by the police and examined, and if his tag or collar is not all right, taken to the pound or drowned or shot … Never before was it applied by a free people to a human being with the exception (which we can never refer to with pride) of the sad days of slavery.”

For the Chinese immigrant community, the law was unthinkable and unjust, and the response was swift.

The San Francisco-based Chinese Consolidated Benevolent Association, or the Chinese Six Companies, a powerful coalition that had financed earlier legal victories, asked Chinese residents to each contribute a dollar towards a legal campaign against the law. Meanwhile, in New York, the Chinese Equal Rights League was formed with the sole purpose of overturning the Geary Act.

In addition to applying political pressure and organizing petition drives, the groups organized Chinese residents to challenge the Geary Act through mass noncompliance. The Six Companies distributed leaflets in Chinese communities throughout the country, declaring that “The Geary Act is an unjust law and no Chinese should obey it … They have disregarded our rights and paid no attention to their promise, and made a law to suit themselves, no matter how unjust to us … Let us stand together.”

Russell Jeung, a professor of Asian American studies at San Francisco State University, remarked that spreading these messages across the country was an amazing feat, and demonstrated just how tight-knit and organized the Chinese immigrant population was: “The Chinese networks are in a better position to [raise awareness to] the Chinese community than the American government was … clearly there were networks and newspapers and communication among the community.”

Chinese residents found allyship with different faith communities, particularly Christians. Some white Americans were compelled, in part, by the efforts of people like Jee Gam, a community leader and the first Chinese congregational pastor in America. Gam wrote essays in English for publications, most notably one titled “The Geary Act: From the Standpoint of a Christian Chinese.”

“This Act withdraws some sacred rights such as in the Declaration of Independence are declared to be inalienable,” he wrote. “The right to a free, untrammelled pursuit of happiness, the right of habeas corpus, the right to be adjudged innocent until proven guilty … it is un-American, barbarous and inhuman.”

The call to participate in the civil disobedience campaign was an extraordinary success. Only about 13,000 of the approximately 100,000 Chinese residents in the country registered during the initial registration period. That left the federal government with the challenge of arresting and deporting over 85% of the nation’s Chinese population — something they weren’t prepared or resourced to do.

“Getting 100,000 people to do a thing is hard in itself, but I think the biggest success is making plain the weakness of the federal government,” Jin said. “Through the process of not registering and seeing how much power that had, they were able to find the weaknesses of the system and continue to exploit it throughout the exclusion era.”

On a dining room table in her Los Altos home, Yu fanned out the chak chee’s that she’s been collecting, along with her grandfather’s. Since launching The Geary Act Project, Yu and documentary filmmaker Barre Fong have received and digitized almost 300 certificates.

“Tens of thousands of people were part of the civil disobedience, including my grandfather. They complied, and they felt unity; there was a community because everybody’s behind it,” Yu said, as she carefully picked up the documents. Most of them are men, marked as “laborers,” but there are also ones for women and children.

Almost all of the certificates collected by the project were issued a couple of years after the Geary Act became law. Chinese immigrants only registered after the Supreme Court upheld the law in its ruling on Fong Yue Ting v. United States, a case carefully orchestrated by the Six Companies. They had raised enough money to hire prominent attorneys and chose three unregistered laundrymen in New York to surrender themselves for arrest. The men were ordered to be deported in accordance with the Geary Act, and a lawsuit was initiated claiming the legislation was discriminatory and violated constitutional protections, including the 14th Amendment.

In May 1893, the court announced a 5-3 decision: the Geary Act was constitutional. The ruling extended the federal government’s power to exclude Chinese immigrants and gave it the ability to deport those already living in the U.S. The decision helped cement the plenary power doctrine, which gives the federal government almost unlimited discretion on all aspects of immigration policy and remains a key tenet of U.S. immigration law today.

“Things that seem normal today were actually created at a certain moment in time and for a very specific purpose: to keep Chinese immigrants, or as many as possible, out of the country,” Lytle Hernández said. “ What does it mean that the logic and the language and the rhetoric and the spirit of Chinese exclusion remains written into our precedent and our legal landscape of the immigration regime?”

In Strangers in the Land, author Michael Luo wrote about the news of the Geary Act ruling reaching the San Francisco headquarters of the Six Companies: “In the afternoon, a reporter from the Call found Gee Chong Tone, the secretary of the Six Companies, inside his office surrounded by stacks of telegrams from concerned immigrants across the state and country … he was shocked by the decision. ‘It’s like a man feeling safe being hit between the eyes in the dark,’ he said.”

After the ruling, Geary added more teeth to the law, notably requiring the certificates of residence to include photographs.

“You can not make a verbal description of a Chinaman such as you can make of a white man … All Chinamen look alike, all dress alike, all have the same kind of eyes …” Geary said.

Yu acknowledges the cruelty of the requirement, but as a historian, she also understands the value of having such detailed documentation of the country’s earliest Chinese residents. You know where each person lived and their physical traits, as detailed as “gold filling in upper teeth” or “large wart on nose right side.” There were also portraits of their faces, some of which show indisputable evidence of their hard labor and the stresses of surviving exclusion: the tanned skin from working outside, the wrinkles on their foreheads, the bags under their eyes.

The idea to collect the documents came from a conversation with Yu during a community event, Fong said, shortly after Trump won his second presidential election. There was a “general sense of fear and dread” about the threat facing immigrants, he said, and it felt like the right time to tell a counter-narrative about some of the country’s earliest immigrants.

She also hopes more Chinese American families will search their closets, attics and archives for more certificates — and share them.

“And bring proof of your ancestors’ lives,” she said, with a small smile. “They struggled to be here.”

text:
An Ecuadorian mother and daughter were arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents at a hospital after a car crash in central Florida.

On 20 August, Grace Stephanie Calero Cabanilla, 39, and her daughter, Giulianna Mía Carriel Calero, 19, were involved in a car crash in Poinciana, Florida, according to arrest reports reviewed by multiple news outlets.

According to Jonathan Bravo, Calero Cabanilla’s cousin, who spoke to Newsweek, she was driving to work with her daughter when another vehicle struck the passenger side of their car, in which the pair “almost died” after the car flipped over four times.

Pictures of the crash posted by Bravo on a fundraiser showed a black SUV with damage to both the front and rear.

After Calero Cabanilla and her daughter were transported by ambulance to HCA Florida Poinciana hospital, they were placed in separate rooms, Bravo told Newsweek. He said a Polk county sheriff’s deputy then began asking Calero Cabanilla about her immigration status.

Video posted online by Gia Calero, Calero Cabanilla’s sister, and published by CNN showed the two women embracing in tears on a hospital bed as law enforcement officers attempted to separate them. The video also showed officers with Calero Cabanilla’s hands behind her back as she cried out while they escorted her from the hospital room. A person who appeared to be filming the video could be heard asking: “Where’s the paper? Where’s the arrest warrant?”

In a statement to Newsweek, a Polk county sheriff’s office spokesperson said: “As part of a crash investigation on Thursday, deputies went to the local hospital to speak with the occupants of one of the vehicles … As the deputies were obtaining information from those involved, it was discovered that the driver is in the United States illegally from Ecuador after overstaying an expired visa by several years.”

The sheriff’s office added that it determined Calero had also overstayed her visa, saying: “ICE issued detainers for both women, and after the women were discharged from the hospital, they were taken into custody and transported to the Polk County Jail.” An arrest warrant reviewed by Newsweek showed that neither woman had a criminal history.

The Guardian has reached out to the Polk county sheriff’s office and ICE for additional comment.

Meanwhile, in the fundraiser set up for the pair, Bravo said that Calero Cabanilla has a pending asylum case and a work permit, while her daughter has a visa that is valid until 2030. The Guardian has contacted Bravo for additional comment.

The arrests of the mother and daughter come amid a series of recent ICE arrests that have sparked widespread criticism across the country. Those arrested include the father of a USS Lincoln sailor, who was taken into ICE detention while his son was deployed in the Middle East, though since released, as well as several higher education instructors and researchers in recent weeks.

The arrests have drawn particular criticism in light of Donald Trump administration’s repeated pledge to focus on targeting the “worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens” for arrest and deportation.

title: U.S. standing on human rights is falling fast, driven by failures at home - Los Angeles Times
description:
Listening to politicians, it can be difficult to know how the U.S. government is performing in terms of human rights.
These data raise serious questions about the United States’ commitment to human rights.
Even starting from this poor position, the U.S.’ civil and political rights practices dramatically worsened in 2025.
The Human Rights Measurement Initiative measures nine civil and political rights, and the U.S. significantly worsened on eight of them.
If you ask the human rights experts, the U.S. is clearly not “doing better now than we’ve ever done before.”
text:
Listening to politicians, it can be difficult to know how the U.S. government is performing in terms of human rights.

Some have pointed to a number of potential human rights abuses committed by the U.S. government inside and outside its borders in the past two years.

And yet President Trump recently called the country “the home of freedom” and “the land of liberty,” saying, “We’re doing better now than we’ve ever done before.”

Governments rarely convey accurate information about their own human rights abuses, so the task of measuring them typically falls to advocates and scholars. According to many of the human rights data sources available, the U.S. lags behind most other high-income democracies — countries that are both members of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and classified as high income by the World Bank. The U.S.’ poor performance spans civil and political rights, such as the right to be free from torture and the right to political participation, as well as economic and social rights, including the rights to health and food.

In fact, the U.S. has been a relatively poor performer across many of these rights for quite some time, regardless of the political party in power.

Even accounting for the U.S.’ prior poor practices, however, new data from the Human Rights Measurement Initiative (which I co-founded) show that in 2025 the country’s civil and political rights performance deteriorated even further. These data raise serious questions about the United States’ commitment to human rights.

Recognizing the problems with public reports, we collect information directly from researchers for human rights organizations, human rights lawyers and others, asking them about governments’ practices across several rights and using a statistical model to assess their information and ensure that the resulting metrics are comparable across countries. The result is a robust dataset that includes information previously missing from public reports.

According to the Human Rights Scores dataset, which uses publicly available information to score more than 190 countries on physical integrity rights — such as the rights to be free from torture, killing, forced disappearance and political imprisonment — the U.S. never ranked higher than 81st from 2001 to 2021 or higher than 109th from 2010 to 2021.

Indeed, from 2003 to 2021, the United States’ score was either the worst or the second-worst every year among high-income OECD member states.

The U.S. has also frequently been rated by the Human Rights Measurement Initiative as the worst performer on “empowerment rights,” or the rights to assembly, association, opinion, expression, political participation, religion and belief.

Even starting from this poor position, the U.S.’ civil and political rights practices dramatically worsened in 2025. The Human Rights Measurement Initiative measures nine civil and political rights, and the U.S. significantly worsened on eight of them.

These were not small changes. The U.S. showed the largest decline ever observed for the right to be free from forced disappearance and for the right to freedom of religion and belief.

The U.S. showed the second-largest decline ever observed for the right to be free from arbitrary or political arrest and for the right to opinion and expression.

The U.S. also showed major declines in the rights to be free from torture and extrajudicial killing, and the right to political participation — that is, the right to participate in one’s government via free and fair elections, to take part in public affairs and to have access to public service. U.S. scores likewise fell in the right to assembly and association, which is the right to peacefully gather in public or private and to form or join groups and organizations.

Human rights experts point to several issues that led to these declines. For instance, the U.S.’ worsened scores for the rights to be free from arbitrary detention, disappearance and torture were tied to the expanded use of practices such as incommunicado detention and warrantless arrest by immigration agencies.

While several killings occurred during ICE operations in 2025, the worsened extrajudicial killing score was also tied to the country’s use of airstrikes against boats in the Pacific and Caribbean, which caused the deaths of at least 123 people in 2025 alone.

Other changes enacted in 2025 contributed to large declines in the U.S.’ rights scores, including crackdowns on anti-ICE demonstrations and government pressure on universities, including limits on free speech and class subjects.

Last year also saw threats to television networks over political expression, restrictions on mail-in voting, state measures targeting American Islamic organizations by labeling them “foreign terrorist organizations” and an executive order focused on eradicating “anti-Christian bias.”

Early indicators about 2026 are not promising, with continued abuses by ICE, further killings in international waters and allegations of attempts to use government powers to punish critics. If you ask the human rights experts, the U.S. is clearly not “doing better now than we’ve ever done before.”

text:
All US immigrant visa applications have been paused by the Trump administration as the state department moves to tighten restrictions and limit access to applicants who they deem could end up relying on US assistance, a state department official confirmed Tuesday.

The agency launched the initiative at all embassies and consulates in early August, according to the official and visa appointments had to be adjusted to accommodate “in-depth training”, according to the official. The state department has been working on updated guidance and training since early this year, “to ensure all consular officers are fully equipped to evaluate every visa applicant comprehensively and consistently”, they added.

Financial Times reports that applicants with interviews already scheduled were sent emails that their appointments had been canceled and that they would be informed of a new date and time.

Agency officials claim this will ensure visa applicants will not end up relying on US public benefits. But it’s part of a slate of strategies the Trump administration has employed to crack down on both lawful and undocumented immigration and create a more selective process for who can gain entry into the system.

This week the Trump administration also announced plans to revoke visas from asylum seekers who initially entered the country for tourism or business. Up to 200,000 people currently seeking asylum could be impacted, marking what would end up being the largest mass pulling of visas in the history of the US. The action is being taken in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security.

Under Trump, visa applicants have also faced new restrictions, including review of their social media histories and added costs for processing, the Associated Press reported.

The pause on new visas and training program follows an attempt by Trump to block applications on a similar “public charge” basis, which included a block on applications from 75 countries selected by the administration, which was recently overturned by a federal judge.

“The court made clear that immigration laws cannot be used to justify discrimination,” Joanna Cuevas Ingram, senior staff attorney at the National Immigration Law Center said in a statement last week. “We are determined to ensure every person and family this ban harmed receives appropriate relief and will continue to hold this administration accountable to its obligations under the law.”

In February, a federal judge overturned the president’s attempt to suspend the US refugee system entirely. Federal agents, under Trump, have been allowed to block asylum seekers from entering the US, a move that human rights advocates said undermines international asylum laws.

The latest attempt to restrict access will cause immediate obstacles for those who have lawfully abided by an already challenging process, according to immigration law experts.

A ‌U.S. State Department spokesperson said on Tuesday that it launched a global training initiative at all U.S. embassies and consulates worldwide and that appointments for visa services will be adjusted to accommodate the training.

Trump has pursued an aggressive deportation drive and immigration ‌crackdown that ​includes revocations of visas and green cards ⁠and rejection of applications over ⁠a. range of reasons like political opinions and pro-Palestinian protests against U.S. ally Israel’s assault on Gaza.

He says the crackdown aims to improve domestic security.

The crackdown has faced some legal setbacks. A U.S. judge ​on Friday struck down a Trump administration policy suspending the issuance of immigrant visas to applicants from 75 countries, saying that the ⁠policy exceeded Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s ⁠statutory authority.

The State Department did not specify details on ​the training and its timeline, beyond saying the training aimed to help consular ​officers screen out applicants deemed likely to become dependent on ‌U.S. public benefits and to ensure evaluation of visa applicants “comprehensively and consistently.”

The pause on visa appointments was reported earlier by the Financial Times, which said immigrant visa applicants with scheduled interviews at U.S. embassies and consulates ⁠have received emails that their appointments were being rescheduled and that they would receive future notice of a new date.

title: WA Rep. Randall calls treatment of Tacoma ICE detainees 'absolutely a human rights violation'
authors: Kim Malcolm, John O'Brien, www.kuow.org, kim-malcolm, john-o-brien
description:
She spoke with KUOW’s Kim Malcolm after visiting detainees at the ICE facility, which she’s been doing for 16 months.
Rep. Emily Randall: I went, in particular, to meet with a couple of detainees, including Julián Palacios Obregon, who I've met with before.
I do that because I think it's important for ICE and GEO staff to not always be able to prepare for me coming to visit.
Having medical providers available and having folks be able to access health care seem to be two different things, and denying people access to health care when they are in the custody of the U.S. government is absolutely a human rights violation.
I have heard about the potential sale of the GEO facility to ICE, to the U.S. government.
text:
The Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma is one of the largest immigration detention centers in the United States, and it’s in U.S. Rep. Emily Randall’s district.

The facility holds over 1,500 people, most of whom are being detained indefinitely. Randall (D-WA) represents Washington's 6th Congressional District, covering the Olympic and Kitsap peninsulas and most of Tacoma. She spoke with KUOW’s Kim Malcolm after visiting detainees at the ICE facility, which she’s been doing for 16 months.

This interview has been edited for clarity.

Kim Malcolm: I understand you've visited this facility 11 times since May of last year. Why did you visit today?

Rep. Emily Randall: I went, in particular, to meet with a couple of detainees, including Julián Palacios Obregon, who I've met with before. We're following up on his case and wanting to make sure that he's receiving health care and the treatment in the facility that he needs, as well as getting a sense of what the legal updates are with his asylum claim.

He's been held there since December 2024, after he declared he was seeking asylum at the port of entry at Sumas. What are you hearing from ICE about why they've held Palacios Obregon for so long?

They haven't been very engaged in giving us answers. Our casework team is working with his legal representation to provide support. We have asked some questions of ICE and GEO [the private company that operates the facility] staff in the facility, but they don't ever really have any information on individual asylum cases.

You say you're concerned about his health.

I am. He has been fighting an antibiotic resistant bacterial infection that's really wreaking havoc on his digestive system. He told us today that he hasn't received any antibiotic treatment for six months, even though he had another positive test two months ago. He's finally been scheduled for a medical procedure. It’s scheduled the same day as his next asylum hearing.

A judge has ordered them to find a way to accommodate both needs, which are both essential needs, long-awaited medical care and access to the justice system. We asked today if they had a plan. Neither of the staff members we talked to knew of one, but they said they would follow up for us.

Congresswoman, you have faced obstruction and delays when you've tried to visit the Tacoma facility previously. How open would you say your access is now?

We alternate announced and unannounced visits. I do that because I think it's important for ICE and GEO staff to not always be able to prepare for me coming to visit. Today was a scheduled, announced visit. On those visits, I try to meet with as many detainees as possible. It's easier if we tell them ahead of time that we're coming.

A little over a week ago, I was at the facility with Dr. Maxine Dexter, my fellow congresswoman from Oregon. We went in response to a hunger strike, and at first, were told that we wouldn't be able to enter the facility. But after running it up the chain and waiting about an hour, we were able to go in and take a tour.

While the courts have said multiple times that Section 527 of the Department of Homeland Secruity Appropriations Act requires unfettered oversight access to members of Congress, there are still sometimes barriers, even if it's just a long wait time or misunderstanding among staff.

Rep. Dexter from Oregon is a physician. She has called the facility “a human rights failure.” What can you tell us about the conditions that you witnessed there and what you heard from people you talked to?

The biggest complaint is definitely the access to medical care. And while there are medical staff on site at the facility, the ability for individuals to get meaningful access to health care is still very difficult. We met last week with someone who requires catheters but is only given like six a day. So, if he needs to use the bathroom more than once, he has to wash out his catheters, which is not standard of care. There are folks who have diabetes and are not having their blood sugar monitored regularly. There are individuals who need access to regular health care, but if they don't sign up for sick call and wake up at 5:30 in the morning to present the next day for care, then they aren't going to get it.

Having medical providers available and having folks be able to access health care seem to be two different things, and denying people access to health care when they are in the custody of the U.S. government is absolutely a human rights violation.

The GEO Group has the private contract to run the facility. That contract runs out at the end of October. We're hearing reports that the company is considering selling some of their detention facilities. Have you heard anything recently about a contract extension or a sale of the facility? What would you like to see happen?

I have heard about the potential sale of the GEO facility to ICE, to the U.S. government. While I also have concerns about private for-profit detention facilities, my concern with this sale is that it would be a no-bid contract that would be meant to enrich the owner, the CEO of GEO, who is an active Trump supporter.

We've seen cases of this over and over in this administration, the most corrupt administration in the history of our government. I think it is our duty to report on what's happening, to ensure that the public knows. Just like the reflecting pool, which is a much lower-stakes no-bid contract, we are seeing this government make choices that are in the worst interest of the American people and in the best interest of their donors and supporters and themselves.

We're heading into the midterm elections, and immigration policy is one of the most divisive and high-profile issues that voters are looking at right now. The Trump administration's deportation agenda is even being criticized by some Trump supporters. What do you think Congress can realistically achieve on immigration reform while the country is so divided?

There are about three weeks of voting days scheduled between now and the November election, so I don’t have a lot of faith that we'll be able to accomplish anything in that short period of time. But I do think it's our duty to keep trying, to keep working with folks who are disillusioned by this administration's choices, who were told that the priority of the Trump administration would be to arrest and deport the worst of the worst criminals, but who are now actively going after grandmothers and parents and green card holders and American citizens in the streets.

This is an unpopular immigration agenda, and it's unpopular not just among Democrats. It's unpopular amongst independents and Republicans. And so I'm going to keep showing up to the facility, but also in the halls of Congress to offer to work with my colleagues to find a pathway in which we have a well-funded immigration system that allows us to process requests for asylum, process visa applications, process folks at the border humanely and safely, so that our country's best intentions, the vision of our country as a place where we accept the tired and the hungry, yearning to be free, is upheld.

Before I let you go, what's another issue you're focused on that you think your constituents need to know about?

I hear over and over about people’s ability to afford their lives, to not have to work two or three or more jobs to be able to afford health care and housing and child care. It's a concern of business owners, who are trying to find folks to work in their companies, and it's a concern of individuals who are just trying to make ends meet. And it's a concern of so many immigrant families who come here for the promise of an economy that is people-focused.

But what's not making this country more affordable, what's not lowering the cost of housing, food, gas, health care, is continuing to give billions of dollars in unchecked money, a blank check, to ICE to lock up human beings and deny them health care and to deny them their human rights. That's not making our country more affordable, and I believe we should be focused on making it easier for folks to build their future.

text:
A federal court of appeals this week issued a significant pro-immigration ruling that relies on a recent landmark opinion from the U.S. Supreme Court about the power of administrative agencies.

In June 2024, the nation's high court announced the end of the "administrative state" in the opinion in the case of Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo. The 6-3 majority opinion eliminated so-called "Chevron deference," a long-standing precedent that provided a framework for when and how the judiciary should defer to an agency's interpretation of a federal statute.

Now, in the aftermath of Loper Bright, judges are no longer constrained by an agency's interpretation of a statute.

Love true crime? Sign up for our newsletter, The Law&Crime Docket, to get the latest real-life crime stories delivered right to your inbox.

For several decades, the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) viewed a section of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) as something of a double-edged sword for certain immigrants.

On Monday, a unanimous panel on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit decidedly smoothed down one of those edges.

In a 23-page opinion, the panel overturned precedent governing the immigration consequences of a vacated criminal conviction.

For years, the BIA said there were effectively two different kinds of vacated convictions. One kind of vacatur favored immigrants. Another kind of vacatur disfavored immigrants. Under Chevron deference, courts were forced to accept the agency's interpretation of the statute in question: 8 U.S.C. §1182(a)(2)(A)(i).

"Under that framework, a conviction vacated because of a substantive or procedural defect in the underlying proceedings no longer qualifies as a conviction for immigration purposes, while a conviction vacated for rehabilitation, immigration hardship, or another reason still does," the appellate court opinion explains. "Many courts deferentially accepted that distinction."

The 4th Circuit is now taking a fresh look at the statute.

The opinion explains that the BIA previously created the distinction in applying the statute "that sought to balance policy priorities." This distinction, the opinion further explains, was based "on the state court's reason for vacating" any given conviction.

In the present case, Lizbeyde Yanez Piedra was once convicted of marijuana possession — but that conviction was later vacated and the underlying charge against her was dismissed.

The Trump administration argues the pre-Chevron understanding of the statute — which is still advanced by the BIA — controls.

This understanding is simply not supported by the text of the statute, the appellate court determined.

"Start with the text," the opinion reads. "Section 1182(a)(2)(A)(i) makes inadmissible 'any alien convicted of' a controlled-substance offense … the disputed question is not whether she was once convicted. It is whether she is an 'alien convicted of' the offense."

The appeals court answered the question in the negative.

"Yanez Piedra argues that her vacated conviction for possession of marijuana does not make her an 'alien convicted of' a controlled-substance violation," the opinion reads. "We agree. The Board's reason-for-vacatur framework cannot govern because it conflicts with the statute's best reading."

Rather, the statute refers to what it calls "the legal-status reading," the panel says, which is a reading that "rests on the view that [the statute] describes a current characteristic of the alien."

The panel uses a few examples to explain its reading:

[T]he term "convicted" is acting as a past participle. Consider how other past participles—like "married," "licensed," or "employed"—might be understood in various contexts. If a restaurant extends a military discount to "any person married to an active-duty service member," we would not expect a soldier's ex-wife to receive a discount. If an airline limits its pilot applications to "any person licensed to fly commercial airplanes," a person whose license has lapsed should not expect a callback. And if a company provides a year-end bonus to "any person employed full-time by the company," the company need not give a bonus to a part-time employee who used to work full-time.

"In each example, the text and context of the policy suggest that the relevant characteristic must currently apply," the opinion goes on. "We read the plain language of §1182(a)(2)(A)(i) the same way: 'any alien convicted of' a controlled-substance offense raises a legal-status question."

The court also explicitly rejects the BIA's policy-focused bifurcation.

"The Board's framework for analyzing vacated convictions may make good policy, but it is not the result of good statutory interpretation," the opinion continues. "Because Yanez Piedra's drug conviction has been vacated, she is not now an 'alien convicted of' a controlled-substance offense."

The court takes the opportunity to note that its opinion is a stark departure from the past in the post-Loper Bright landscape.

"For decades, Chevron deference restricted courts from exercising their duty 'to say what the law is,'" the opinion reads. "Newly freed from that restraint, courts now exercise their independent judgment about the best meaning of statutes. The practical change will often be modest. But other times, a fresh read will mark a sharp break with past practice. This is that type of case."

text:
A second witness to a fatal shooting in Houston by a federal immigration agent has been ordered released from custody after more than a month in detention.

Daniel Tirado Pantoja was one of three passengers riding in a work van when the driver, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican national who ran a homebuilding business, was shot July 7. The Department of Homeland Security has said Salgado Araujo, who had lived without legal status in the U.S. for 35 years, had “weaponized his vehicle” and that the officer fired on him in self-defense.

U.S. District Judge Alfred Bennett in Houston ordered Tirado Pantoja released after finding that he had no criminal record and was neither a flight risk nor a danger to the community, according to court records.

“We’re very glad that Mr. Tirado is going to be reunited with his family,” said Ross Miller, an attorney for Tirado Pantoja.

Tirado Pantoja and another passenger, Jose Trinidad Rojas Pliego, have disputed accounts given by DHS about the confrontation with agents with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

They said the agents were never in front of the ICE vehicle and that Salgado Araujo had put vehicle in park as the agents were shooting. Tirado Pantoja also has said the agents’ vehicle hit them from behind and then again on the driver’s side.

Rojas Pliego was already released from detention last month. DHS did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Tuesday about the judge’s ruling.

Victor Salgado, the brother of the man killed, was also in the van and remains in custody. He also has asked a judge to order his release.

Ronaldo Salgado, Salgado Araujo’s son, had said in social media post after the shooting that his father was on his way to work, picking up his workers, when the shooting occurred. He said his father was a hardworking man and was in the process of getting a work permit.

text:
The U.S. Department of Justice filed a lawsuit Tuesday in federal court against the Franklin County Municipal Court, alleging the court is blocking federal immigration agents from arresting undocumented immigrants at the courthouse.

In a news release, the DOJ said the complaint challenges the new courthouse rule that purports to shield immigrants from being detained at or around the courthouse and to impose criminal and civil liability for violations.

The rule, enacted in March, states “no individual shall be subject to a civil arrest while present in the courthouse for the purpose of attending a court proceeding or conducting other lawful court business.”

The rule does allow civil arrests pursuant to a judicial warrant issued by a judge.

The lawsuit names Presiding Judge Jessica D'Varga and the court's head of security Enoch White.

A spokesperson for the court or the city of Columbus did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The DOJ states in the lawsuit that since the rule took effect, ICE has made no civil immigration arrests at the municipal court and "has had to devote additional personnel, surveillance, vehicles, equipment, and overtime to arrests elsewhere."

"Those at-large arrests are less predictable and can expose officers, the public, and arrest subjects to greater risk than a targeted arrest in a screened, controlled setting," the statement said.

The court faced calls from the public to change rules that allowed such arrests since the start of President Donald Trump's second administration. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials have arrested immigrants at the courthouse in the past year, including for routine traffic violations.

The lawsuit estimated ICE has arrested at least twelve individuals at the municipal court in recent years.

"Today the [d]epartment sued yet another local entity that seeks to thwart the will of Congress by regulating when and where [f]ederal law enforcement does its job, all in the name of protecting criminal aliens who violate our [n]ation’s laws,” Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward, Jr. said in a statement “No more. This Department of Justice will not sit idly by while state and local government seek to undermine federal immigration enforcement.”

The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio, contends the rule is an illegal attempt to regulate the federal government and that the rule threatens the safety and effectiveness of federal operations.

The DOJ said in a statement that conducting an arrest at or near a courthouse often reduces the risk of flight and potential safety risks to the public, law enforcement officers, and subjects themselves due to the enhanced security screenings in place at courthouses.

"Franklin County Municipal Court’s rule runs counter to common sense and endangers the broader community by attempting to eliminate safe places for law enforcement officers to act," the statement said.

While ICE made limited arrests at the courthouse, ICE conducted Operation Buckeye in Columbus before this rule went into effect throughout the community. The agency said it arrested over 200 people in this community-wide raid.

ICE began arresting Haitian refugees stripped of protections under the Temporary Protected Status in Springfield last week. Columbus also has a sizable population of Haitians and could be targeted like Springfield.

The lawsuit, however, doesn't target the Franklin County Court of Common Pleas, which has a similar rule restricting ICE activity in the courthouse.

The legal argument the DOJ leans on in the lawsuit is the federal government's authority over immigration law. The lawsuit argues the Immigration and Nationality Act authorizes federal immigration agents to rely on administrative warrants from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security or even no warrant at all.

The DOJ is asking the federal court to declare that the courthouse rule violates the supremacy clause of the U.S. Constitution and therefore is unlawful and unenforceable. In addition, it wants the court to issue an order preliminarily and permanently enjoining the Franklin County Municipal Court from enforcing this rule against the federal government.

text:
The father of a US navy sailor who has been deployed in the Middle East for a record-breaking nine months on the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier has been released from immigration detention, according to his family.

His arrest sparked intense backlash after the Associated Press reported that his son was entering his ninth month on the Lincoln with the navy when his father was detained. The carrier had just set a US military record for uninterrupted time at sea and has raised concerns about supply shortages and deteriorating mental health among those serving onboard.

Luis Manuel Aviles, 48, was arrested on Saturday after leaving his house to take his car to the mechanic, according to his wife, Argelia. She said her husband, a handyman in Key West, Florida, had a permit to work in the US. Originally from Nicaragua, he has lived in the US for 19 years.

Aviles’s arrest was the latest in a string of high-profile immigration arrests of the immediate family members of enlisted US soldiers as part of Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown. Elected officials recently launched a congressional investigation into the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) practice.

Aviles’s son, Joshua, posted on Facebook on Tuesday that his father had been released from federal immigration custody. An immigration judge dismissed Aviles’s case on Monday, just hours after he was booked into an immigration detention center in Miami, according to Department of Justice records.

The DHS didn’t offer comment to clarify why Luis Manuel Aviles was arrested – or subsequently released.

Margaret Stock, an immigration attorney for military families, called the rapid succession of filed and dismissed charges “super unusual”.

Joshua said in a Facebook post on Saturday that he had been working 12-hour days without a break since the USS Abraham Lincoln left US shores in November. The US navy confirmed that Aviles is enlisted and serves onboard the Lincoln, where his physically demanding duties include moving aircraft on the ship.
