text:
ALBANY — Several New York sheriffs are planning to file a lawsuit challenging a new state law that took effect Tuesday and bans congressionally authorized agreements governing civil immigration enforcement coordination between local, state and federal agencies.

Rensselaer County Executive Steve McLaughlin and Sheriff Kyle Bourgault issued a joint statement late Monday saying they would be parties in a federal lawsuit that they said would be filed “in just hours.” On Tuesday morning, McLaughlin said the lawsuit would “be filed today.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The litigation is being planned as Gov. Kathy Hochul held a news conference Tuesday morning at the Capitol touting “her new law to stand against ICE overreach.”

“We’ve worked hard to drive down crime … to record lows, and that includes working with ICE to track down and apprehend criminals,” Hochul said. “Once they’re convicted and do their time, we work with ICE to ensure they’re deported. And I’ll repeat that New York state will never become a sanctuary for criminals. But at the same time, we’re not talking about criminals, and we will not sit idly by when ICE commits atrocities on our streets.”

The law is intended to prevent local government entities and police or correctional agencies from entering into formal agreements with the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Those agreements allow the local agencies to operate as immigration officers or to detain someone who is being held solely for civil immigration violations.

Several New York sheriff’s departments have pledged to end their formal agreements with ICE and to no longer house migrants in their jails if they are facing only civil immigration charges. But sheriffs in several other counties, including Madison, Wayne, Broome and Rensselaer counties, have pledged to oppose the law. Hochul said Tuesday that two of New York’s 62 sheriff’s departments have not informed her administration about whether they will comply with the law.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“Let me be clear: any police department or sheriff’s office that disobeys this law, that maintains any agreement with ICE, will face legal action,” Hochul said. “And to those suing us, those trying to block the implementation of this law, (you) tried before and failed. Our law has been already upheld by courts. But if you’re trying it again, I say bring it on. Courts have already spoken, but I’m confident we’ll win again.”

Hochul was flanked by several New York police chiefs whose departments do not have agreements with ICE, including Albany police Chief Brendan Cox and Kingston police Chief Egidio F. Tinti.

“Effective policing depends on trust, and that trust is eroded when local law enforcement is asked to do federal civil immigration enforcement,” Cox said. “Trust directly impacts public safety. When that trust is broken, when residents fear calling the police, when victims stay silent, when witnesses refuse to come forward, we all become less safe. It’s that simple.”

The federal statute that authorizes the agreements — Section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act — was added to the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, which was adopted during the administration of President Bill Clinton. The federal legislation was amended in 2002 to authorize the secretary of the Department of Homeland Security — which was created after the 9/11 terrorist attacks — to enter into written agreements with state and local agencies “so that qualified personnel can perform certain functions of an immigration officer.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

McLaughlin and Bourgault said in their statement that their “participation in the 287(g) program means we screen any non-citizens brought to our jail to ensure they are not wanted for crimes elsewhere, the same as we do for any citizen brought to the facility. This ensures a person wanted for a dangerous crime is not released into our communities and neighborhoods.”

The state law banning the agreements is also being challenged in a pending lawsuit filed by the U.S. Department of Justice against the state of New York in June.

Last month, U.S. District Judge Mae A. D’Agostino issued a temporary injunction in that case blocking the state from enforcing another part of the law that went into effect this year that prohibits any law enforcement officers — local, state or federal — from concealing their identity with masks while interacting with the public and requiring them to display clear identification. The law was intended to specifically target federal ICE agents.

But D’Agostino’s 51-page ruling also rejected the Justice Department’s request for a temporary injunction to block the portion of the law that bans what are known as 287(g) agreements between U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and 12 New York police agencies. Those agreements allow local officers to be deputized to help with detaining migrants targeted for deportation, including making arrests and holding them in county jails, in exchange for federal funding.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

D’Agostino concluded that the law prohibiting those agreements does not impede federal immigration enforcement activities.

She said the Termination Act “seeks only to control whether New York and its localities voluntarily engage in certain cooperation with federal authorities. The United States has also failed to show, at this stage, that the Termination Act likely discriminates against the federal government.”

The new state law will not prevent local or state law enforcement agencies from assisting federal immigration agencies with the apprehension or detention of someone who has been accused of committing a crime. The new law also allow those agencies to apprehend or detain someone facing a civil immigration violation if a warrant for their arrest has been issued by a judge — which many agencies are interpreting as including a federal immigration judge.

But the law will not end the detention in New York’s local jails of migrants facing deportation proceedings. Those who are charged with federal crimes — it can be a misdemeanor federal offense to evade a checkpoint when crossing a U.S. border — are routinely held in local jails that have contracts with the U.S. Marshals Service.

Data obtained by the Times Union from U.S. District Court in New York’s Northern District, which includes roughly 310 miles of international border with Canada, shows that 1,118 people were charged with unlawful entry after crossing the U.S. border with Canada during Trump’s first administration. During President Joe Biden’s administration, 1,098 people were charged with the same offense in the 32-county district that stretches from Kingston to west of Syracuse.

The highest annual number of arrests for that misdemeanor offense in northern New York during Trump’s first term was 608 cases in 2019. Under Biden, the highest annual number of arrests for that offense in northern New York was in 2022, when 604 people were arrested. The number of prosecutions for illegal entry has declined in the Northern District during Trump’s second term, with eight prosecutions docketed in U.S. District Court in the first three months of this year.

At Tuesday’s news conference, Hochul declined to say whether she believes police should contact ICE if they arrest a migrant who may be in the U.S. illegally for an unrelated crime.

“I want the system to work the way it’s been working successfully. This does not change this. This simply says local cops, local crimes,” Hochul said. “I want local police 100% focused on doing the great work they’re doing in keeping our communities safe.”

'Serious crimes'

In June, New York filed a federal lawsuit against President Donald J. Trump’s administration in anticipation of a feared showdown with White House Border Czar Thomas Homan over the new state statutes, which are intended to prevent or sharply limit the ability of state and local police agencies to assist with federal immigration enforcement. The U.S. Department of Justice filed its own lawsuit in federal court around the same time, challenging the constitutionality of the statutes.

Barring an appeal, D’Agostino’s decision paused New York’s mask ban but kept in place the new law requiring local police agencies to end their contracts with ICE. It’s unclear what civil penalties any agencies that defy the law will face.

The new state laws will not prevent local or state law enforcement agencies from assisting federal immigration agencies with the apprehension or detention of someone who has been accused of committing a crime. The new laws also allow those agencies to apprehend or detain someone facing a civil immigration violation if a warrant for their arrest has been issued by a judge — which many agencies are interpreting as including a federal immigration judge.

In addition, while Hochul has for years suggested that state and local law enforcement agencies could still assist federal agencies in matters involving “serious crimes,” the new state statutes — and policies already implemented by State Police — do not define a “serious” crime. The governor has also said repeatedly that crossing a U.S. border without authorization is “a civil violation” and “not a crime,” but that is misleading.

While it’s true that crossing the U.S. border for the first time by evading a checkpoint is a civil violation, it is also a misdemeanor crime under federal law and has been routinely prosecuted by the Justice Department. And reentering the U.S. without authorization after being deported is a felony under federal law.

It’s unclear how many individuals facing civil immigration violations may have also crossed the U.S. border without authorization.

The Times Union reported last year that State Police frequently assist federal immigration authorities and contact them during investigations in which they encounter people suspected of entering the U.S. illegally.

In the wake of the new laws recently enacted in New York that officials contend will limit the ability of state and local agencies to assist with federal immigration enforcement, State Police have not issued any new directives changing their policies.

The last directive was issued in November, when Deputy Superintendent Darrin S. Pitkin issued a memorandum to all State Police employees instructing that no one may “make referrals to federal authorities in cases where they develop information of suspected civil immigration violations unless there is reason to suspect a violation of a criminal law.”

But that guidance conflicts with the policies that have been outlined by Hochul and implemented by State Police, which enable police to assist immigration authorities in cases involving a crime, including an immigration crime, which could involve someone entering or reentering the U.S. illegally, even if they have not been charged with any other crime.

The New York State Sheriffs' Association issued guidance to its members this summer noting that the restrictions under New York’s new laws ban “most state and municipal employees from using public resources, on-duty time, or facilities for immigration enforcement but the ban does not apply to local correctional facilities, nor to local police officers (e.g., sheriffs and deputies), peace officers (or correction officers) … nor their civilian staff.”

text:
The Donald Trump administration is launching a second attempt to set an extremely high fee for H-1B visas for highly skilled foreign professionals. It plans to publish a proposal in the Federal Register on Tuesday to impose a $103,265 charge when applying for the visa, despite a court rejecting a similar plan in June.

If approved, the new fee would apply to H-1B visa petitions subject to an annual cap. That program, created by Congress, currently grants up to 65,000 visas of this type to foreign professionals and 20,000 to workers who hold a U.S. master’s degree, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in the proposal. The payment would be in addition to existing fees, it added.

H-1B visas have been a target of the president since he returned to the White House in January 2025, because the program, he claims, has been “deliberately exploited to replace, rather than supplement” the country’s skilled workforce. That rationale underpinned the measure he enacted in September of last year that imposed a $100,000 charge when applying for the visa. About 20 states sued the government to try to block it from taking effect, and in June federal judge Leo Sorokin of Massachusetts sided with them, finding it to be a disguised tax. At the time, total fees to apply for an H-1B visa ranged from nearly $1,000 to about $7,600.

“The defendants [the federal government] argue that the required $100,000 payment is a ‘regulatory payment’ that does not amount to a tax. This is mere ipse dixit. Defendants offer no definition for what constitutes ‘a regulatory payment,’ cite no cases or statutes employing the term, and advance no reasoned argument explaining how this term encompasses something different than a tax or a penalty,” Sorokin wrote in his June decision. “In any event, the manner in which a particular payment is labeled does not determine whether the payment can be viewed as an exercise of Congress’s taxing power, because what matters is the substance and application of the payment, not its designation,” he added.

The government appealed and asked to stay Sorokin’s ruling while the case was further reviewed. But an appellate court declined to do so.

Potential impact of restricting H-1B visas

In this new attempt, the administration argues that charging just over $100,000 per visa application would help “recoup” part of the cost of administering the legal immigration system. That, it says, would help avoid a possible judicial block like the one that halted the prior plan.

“This fee would serve as a dedicated revenue mechanism to help recover a portion of the federal government’s costs of administering the lawful immigration system, including activities carried out by DHS, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ), the U.S. Department of State (DOS), and the U.S. Department of Labor (DOL),” the official document states.

When challenging the previous fee in court, the states suing said a charge of that magnitude would complicate hiring teachers for elementary schools, high schools, and colleges, which would “exacerbate existing teacher shortages.” They added that the impact could also be felt in the health sector, affecting the ability to provide adequate services and raising costs for state health insurance programs.

Under the new proposal, the fee would not apply to H-1B petitions from employers who are currently exempt from the annual cap, such as nonprofit research organizations.

The plan is part of a much broader effort in which the U.S. government has removed immigration benefits that protected thousands of migrants from deportation and has stepped up an offensive to expel undocumented people on a large scale, including those with no serious criminal records.

text:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Customs and Border Protection announced today the establishment of four Customs Enforcement Areas, expanding its enforcement jurisdiction from 12 to 24 nautical miles in designated waters adjacent to South Florida, Southern California, Puerto Rico, and the Gulf Coast of Texas.

Smuggling organizations have exploited the outer edge of traditional customs waters by positioning vessels beyond the 12 nautical mile boundary, transferring illicit cargo at sea, and coordinating landings along remote shorelines. The new designations strengthen CBP’s ability to counter those tactics and align its customs enforcement authority in these areas with the 24-nautical mile U.S. contiguous zone.

“The ocean is not a safe haven for cartels and smugglers,” said Rodney Scott, Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection. “These designations give our agents the room to act sooner and stop threats before they reach the American people. If you are moving drugs, contraband, or people toward our shores, expect us to find you.”

The establishment of these CEAs supports the Administration’s efforts to secure U.S. borders and strengthen customs enforcement. The designations comply with Executive Order 14165, Securing Our Borders, by enhancing operational control in areas facing ongoing maritime smuggling threats, and are consistent with Executive Order 14411, Strengthening Customs Enforcement, which directs the Department of Homeland Security to take action to bolster enforcement of customs laws.

Within the four Customs Enforcement Areas, CBP’s Air and Marine Operations will work with the U.S. Coast Guard and other federal partners to detect and interdict vessels used by cartels, foreign terrorist organizations, and other criminal networks to move people, narcotics, and contraband toward the United States. The designations provide more consistent customs enforcement authority across these waters and support the investigation and prosecution of maritime smugglers.

title: The United States' human rights practices are taking a nosedive - The Conversation
description:
In the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections, how is the U.S. government performing in terms of human rights?
Even accounting for the U.S.’s prior poor practices, however, new data from the Human Rights Measurement Initiative shows that in 2025 the country’s civil and political rights performance deteriorated even further.
As a human rights scholar who has been measuring human rights practices for 20 years – and as one of HRMI’s co-founders – I believe this data raises serious questions about the United States’ commitment to human rights.
Further, the Trump administration has changed one of the most important sources of human rights information, the U.S. State Department’s Country Reports on Human Rights Practices, to contain more bias in favor of the administration’s foreign allies and less information on human rights abuse overall.
Even starting from this poor position, the U.S.’s civil and political rights practices dramatically worsened in 2025.
text:
In the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections, how is the U.S. government performing in terms of human rights? Listening to politicians, it can be difficult to know.

On one hand, some have pointed to a number of potential human rights abuses committed by the U.S. government inside and outside its borders in the past two years.

On the other hand, while marking the United States’ 250th anniversary this year, President Donald Trump called the country “the home of freedom,” “the land of liberty” and “the most extraordinary, most exceptional, most incredible nation ever to exist on the face of the earth.”

“We’re doing better now than we’ve ever done before,” he said.

So which is it?

According to many of the human rights data sources available, the U.S. lags behind most other high-income democracies – countries that are both members of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and classified as high income by the World Bank. The U.S.’s poor performance spans civil and political rights, such as the right to be free from torture and the right to political participation, as well as economic and social rights, including the rights to health and food.

In fact, the U.S. has been a relatively poor performer across many of these rights for quite some time, regardless of the political party in power.

Even accounting for the U.S.’s prior poor practices, however, new data from the Human Rights Measurement Initiative shows that in 2025 the country’s civil and political rights performance deteriorated even further.

As a human rights scholar who has been measuring human rights practices for 20 years – and as one of HRMI’s co-founders – I believe this data raises serious questions about the United States’ commitment to human rights.

How are rights practices measured?

Governments rarely publish accurate information on their own human rights abuses, so the task of measuring them typically falls to advocates and scholars.

Historically, most international measures of civil and political rights have depended on public reports from the U.S. State Department, Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch or news organizations.

However, these reports cannot cover every human rights violation that experts know about, especially in countries with low government transparency or high levels of repression.

Thus, data produced using those sources will show fewer abuses than those that have actually occurred and will be more accurate about some places than others. Further, the Trump administration has changed one of the most important sources of human rights information, the U.S. State Department’s Country Reports on Human Rights Practices, to contain more bias in favor of the administration’s foreign allies and less information on human rights abuse overall.

Since 2017, HRMI has used a different approach. Recognizing the problems with public reports, we collect information directly from researchers for human rights organizations, human rights lawyers and others, asking them about governments’ practices across several rights and using a statistical model to assess their information and ensure that the resulting metrics are comparable across countries. The result is a robust dataset that includes information previously missing from public reports.

Today, HRMI’s civil and political rights dataset covers 62 countries, with more added every year.

How does the US compare?

According to the Human Rights Scores dataset, which uses publicly available information to score more than 190 countries on physical integrity rights – such as the rights to be free from torture, killing, forced disappearance and political imprisonment – the U.S. never ranked higher than 81st from 2001 to 2021 or higher than 109th from 2010 to 2021.

Indeed, from 2003 to 2021, the United States’ score was either the worst or the second-worst every year among high-income OECD member states, which include the United Kingdom, Japan and New Zealand.

The Human Rights Scores dataset has not been updated past 2021, but HRMI’s data collected since that time suggests that the pattern has continued.

Among the six high-income OECD countries on which HRMI currently collects data, the U.S. has been the worst performer for physical integrity rights since 2017.

It has also frequently been rated as the worst performer on “empowerment rights,” or the rights to assembly, association, opinion, expression, political participation, religion and belief.

What changed in 2025?

Even starting from this poor position, the U.S.’s civil and political rights practices dramatically worsened in 2025. HRMI measures nine civil and political rights, and the U.S. significantly worsened on eight of them.

These were not small changes. Measured against every significant change HRMI has recorded since 2017, the U.S. showed the largest decline ever observed for the right to be free from forced disappearance and for the right to freedom of religion and belief.

The U.S. showed the second-largest decline ever observed for the right to be free from arbitrary or political arrest and for the right to opinion and expression.

The U.S. also showed major declines in the rights to be free from torture and extrajudicial killing, and the right to political participation – that is, the right to participate in one’s government via free and fair elections, to take part in public affairs and to have access to public service. U.S. scores likewise fell in the right to assembly and association, which are, respectively, the rights to peacefully gather in public or private and to form or join groups and organizations.

What caused the scores to fall?

Human rights experts raised several issues that led to these declines. For instance, the U.S.’s worsened scores for the rights to be free from arbitrary detention, disappearance and torture were tied to the expanded use of practices such as incommunicado detention and warrantless arrest by ICE and other immigration-related agencies.

While several killings occurred during ICE operations in 2025, the worsened extrajudicial killing score was also tied to the country’s use of airstrikes against boats in the Pacific and Caribbean, which caused the deaths of at least 123 people in 2025 alone.

Other changes enacted in 2025 contributed to large declines in the U.S.’s rights scores, including crackdowns on anti-ICE demonstrations and government pressure on universities, including limits on free speech and class subjects.

Last year also saw threats to television networks over political expression, restrictions on mail-in voting, state measures targeting American Islamic organizations by labeling them “foreign terrorist organizations” and an executive order focused on eradicating “anti-Christian bias.”

text:
BOSTON (WWLP) – The Healey-Driscoll Administration released new model policies, procedures and guidance to assist K-12 schools and child care programs in responding to civil immigration enforcement.

The resources give educators and early education providers step-by-step instructions on protecting student information and managing requests from federal immigration agents ahead of the 2026–2027 school year.

The release comes as state officials implement the PROTECT Act, which generally prohibits civil arrests on school grounds and child care premises without a judicial warrant or judicial order. Under the law, covered educational facilities must adopt formal policies governing interactions with civil law enforcement by Sept. 1, 2026, or the first day of the 2026–2027 school year, whichever is earlier. The statutory protections apply regardless of whether an individual school or program has finalized its internal policy.

The Department of Elementary and Secondary Education released specific model policies and procedures for school districts, charter schools and educational collaboratives. The resources establish steps for designating designated school and district points of contact, involving legal counsel, reviewing judicial warrants and orders, documenting interactions with civil law enforcement and notifying parents or guardians if an agent requests access to a student or student records. Additionally, the department provided procedures for alerting school communities when civil law enforcement agents are confirmed on school grounds while protecting individual privacy, updating student emergency contact lists and sharing policy details with families.

Elementary and Secondary Education Commissioner Pedro Martinez said the framework builds on prior guidance issued by the state. “This important work builds on guidance that the administration issued last year, clarifies how schools should respond and reinforces the need for communication with families,” Martinez said. “I know that our school communities want to keep students safe and we will work with districts to help them implement the PROTECT Act.”

Education Secretary Dr. Steve Zrike emphasized the role of practical instructions for school personnel. “Students, children and families across Massachusetts deserve to feel safe when they walk through the doors of their school or child care program,” Zrike said. “These new resources give schools and early education and care programs clear, practical guidance to implement the PROTECT Act and ensure educators and providers know how to respond to civil immigration enforcement.”

For early education providers, the Department of Early Education and Care issued guidance covering licensed child care centers, family child care homes, school-aged child care programs and group care facilities. The policies outline procedures for assigning staff points of contact, handling enforcement requests and documenting all interactions with immigration officers.

Early Education and Care Commissioner Amy Kershaw noted the administration’s focus on maintaining welcoming early education settings. “Children and families deserve to feel safe and supported when accessing high-quality early education and care,” Kershaw said. “The PROTECT Act reflects the Healey-Driscoll Administration’s and EEC’s continued commitment to supporting safe, welcoming early education environments and ensuring programs have the resources, guidance and support they need.”

To support implementation in early education, the agency partnered with the Massachusetts Office for Refugees and Immigrants to offer Know Your Rights training. The training covers immigrant and refugee rights, legal resources and guidelines for interactions with law enforcement.

Cristina Aguilera, executive director of the Office for Refugees and Immigrants, explained the objective of these tools. “Every child in Massachusetts should be able to go to school or child care feeling safe, supported and focused on learning and every family should be able to access these essential services without fear,” Aguilera said. “By making sure early education and care providers have clear information and practical tools, we can help them better support immigrant and refugee families and respond appropriately when immigration enforcement issues arise.”

The model policies stem from the PROTECT Act, landmark state legislation signed by Gov. Maura Healey earlier this month. The law limits civil arrests in courthouses, schools, child care programs and nonpublic areas of health care facilities. It also restricts state and local participation in civil immigration enforcement, expands guardianship options for families if a parent is detained or deported and creates a state civil rights remedy for constitutional violations.

Healey noted that the new guidance puts statutory protections into daily practice. “As families prepare for the new school year, every child should feel safe walking into their classroom and every parent should feel confident dropping them off,” Healey said. “The PROTECT Act makes clear that schools and child care programs are places for children to learn and grow, not places for ICE to target families.”

State legislative leaders supported the publication of the implementation materials. Senate President Karen E. Spilka praised the swift rollout of the guidance. “Today we are putting a core principle of the PROTECT Act into action: no family should fear that a normal day at school or day care can be disrupted by President Trump’s ICE agents,” Spilka said. “The Senate led on this legislation to protect Massachusetts students and families and today’s guidance does exactly that.”

House Speaker Ronald Mariano stated that the measures protect educational settings from unwarranted disruption. “Since the beginning of President Trump’s second term, dangerous and illegal actions taken by federal immigration agents have immigrants in Massachusetts living in fear as they go about their daily lives, including when they bring their children to school,” Mariano said. “These measures are about ensuring that the Commonwealth is doing everything it can to preserve schools as safe spaces for learning, rather than allowing them to become opportunities for warrantless harassment and detainment.”

Attorney General Andrea Campbell stated that her office will work alongside state partners to ensure compliance across Massachusetts. “Every child deserves to learn and grow in a safe, welcoming environment – and every family deserves to know that we will protect them from aggressive tactics employed by ICE that do nothing to enhance public safety,” Campbell said. “My office will continue to work with our partners across the state to ensure these important protections are understood and upheld across the Commonwealth.”

The new framework builds on previous executive actions taken by the administration earlier this year. In January, Healey signed Executive Order 650 to limit civil immigration enforcement in nonpublic areas of state facilities and prohibit new 287(g) agreements without a public safety need. In May, the administration issued broader statewide guidance for schools, child care centers and higher education campuses to prepare staff for potential visits by federal immigration officers.

Covered schools and child care programs must have their required policies in place by Sept. 1, 2026, or the first day of the 2026–2027 school year, whichever occurs earlier. State agencies will continue working directly with school districts and early education providers to assist with policy adoption and staff training.

text:
CARY, N.C. (WTVD) -- A Cary woman and permanent U.S. resident is being held in immigration detention in Georgia after what her family believed would be a routine check-in with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), according to relatives and an attorney.

Teja Vasamsetty said she watched her mother, Venkata Vasamsetty, taken into custody during an ICE appointment in Charlotte.

"This is probably the lowest point in my life, honestly," Teja Vasamsetty said.

She said she remains focused on the moment her mother was detained.

"Standing there begging them, just saying, why are you taking her?" she said.

According to her family, Venkata Vasamsetty moved to the United States from India in 1999 and became a permanent resident in 2013. She built a life in Cary, worked as a Wake County substitute teacher, and raised her family there.

After returning to India in 2022, Venkata Vasamsetty became ill during the pandemic and was unable to return to the United States for several months. Her family said the Department of Homeland Security later accused her of abandoning her Green Card because of the delay. The family said that case was dismissed in May.

Teja Vasamsetty said her mother still had a scheduled ICE check-in in Charlotte that had been postponed until August. She accompanied her mother to the appointment, expecting it to be uneventful.

"It just keeps playing in my head: this will just take 30 seconds. They took her into a room and then put shackles on her, and she screamed," she said.

Since her detention, Venkata Vasamsetty has been held at a detention center in rural south Georgia, according to her family. Her daughters have traveled there as they seek her release and say they are concerned about her health because she has diabetes.

"She's deteriorating, and so my motto for the last two weeks has just been I need her out alive," Teja Vasamsetty said.

Immigration attorney Trey DeBrine of Sivaraman Immigration Law said cases like this are unusual for someone who is a permanent resident and that people are typically given notice to appear.

"Instead, what happened was she was detained at the check-in, and that is something that was meant to really surprise her and her family," DeBrine said.

ALSO SEE | Pregnant woman held for weeks in ICE custody after immigration lawyer scam

In a statement to ABC11, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson acknowledged that Venkata Vasamsetty had a Green Card but said she was "alleged to have later abandoned her status by violating her residency conditions."

The spokesperson also said, "Vasamsetty will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending the outcome of her removal proceedings."

The case has also drawn attention from Democratic U.S. Rep. Deborah Ross of North Carolina, who criticized the detention.

"I talked with her family in Georgia just this week; it is wrong what the government is doing to her. She needs to get out, and she needs to get out now; the entire community is behind her," Ross said.

Teja Vasamsetty said her family has been encouraged by support from people in Wake County.

"She is a grandmother, she's a special ed teacher, she's followed all the rules her entire life, she's not a criminal, and she doesn't check any of the boxes, so she's coming home," she said.

Venkata Vasamsetty's family said she is scheduled to have a bond hearing in Georgia on Thursday morning and hopes she will be released.

text:
(NewsNation) — The Department of Homeland Security is again proposing that U.S. employers seeking to fill specific jobs with foreign-born workers rather than an American be assessed a six-figure application fee.

DHS officials are seeking to collect a $103,265 fee for all HB-1 visa applications, including those eligible for an advanced degree exemption, officials announced Monday. The plan was announced just less than three months after a federal judge blocked DHS from collecting a $100,000 fee for the visas previously sought by the Trump administration.

The fee was introduced, the proposed legislation says, to ensure that American companies are “less likely to hire an H-1B worker over a qualified and highly-skilled American.” The legislation cites a working paper from the National Bureau of Economic Research that found H-1B workers earned about 15% less than American co-workers.

The proposed fee would be required to be paid at the time of the filing of the application, officials said, and would be paid in addition to the normal costs associated with the H-1B visa. The revenue generated by the proposed application fees would be used to recover a portion of the federal government’s costs spent administering the lawful immigration system, according to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

DHS estimates the proposed fee would generate approximately $8.8 billion annually, based on a projected annual volume of 85,000 H-1B cap-subject petitions.

These costs include adjudication of immigration benefits, fraud detection and national security vetting, systems modernization, records and fee collection operations, immigration court operations, consular visa processing, labor standards enforcement, and interagency coordination.

Under the proposed rule, the additional fee would not apply to H-1B petitions that are not subject to the cap, such as petitions filed by certain nonprofit research organizations, governmental research organizations, and institutions of higher education, USCIS officials said in announcing the new plan.

The number of cap-subject H-1B visas (or grants of status) issued annually is limited to 65,000, with an additional 20,000 for aliens who have earned a master’s or higher degree from a U.S. institution of higher education.

In June, Massachusetts U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin agreed with a group of Democratic-led states that the administration exceeded its authority, and the fee usurped Congress’s power to set immigration policy and taxes.

Sorokin wrote in his decision that the proposed fee is a tax, regardless of how federal officials attempted to define it.

USCIS officials said in June that DHS officials “strongly disagree” with the ruling that denied a stay on the fee proposal. Officials said that they would comply with the court’s ruling while it considered next steps but said it plans to collect the payment if the order was ever lifted.

A USCIS spokesperson did not respond directly to NewsNation’s inquiry about what prompted the second push for the six-figure fee proposal, directing a reporter to the released news release.

However, David Bier, the director of Immigration Studies and Selz Foundation Chair in Immigration Policy at the Cato Institute, argues that the proposed visa fee would result in the intended benefit of generating revenue for DHS. Instead, he called the reasoning “a bizarre justification for the policy.”

“The government itself told the court that the $100,000 fee was ‘arguably prohibitive’ and ‘does not raise revenue’,” Bier said in a statement issued to NewsNation. “Even if it did raise revenue, that would not make it legal because immigration fees can only be imposed to recover the costs of adjudication and naturalization services.”

“And because this is a filing fee, employers would have to pay it with no guarantee that USCIS will approve the petition. Almost no one will risk more than $100,000 with no guarantee of approval.”

President Donald Trump signed a proclamation in Sept. 2025, adding a $100,000 fee for all new H-1B visa applications. The fees are typically paid for by the sponsoring employer, and Trump administration officials have characterized the plan as an initiative to encourage companies to hire Americans rather than foreign-born employees.

NewsNation reporting partner “The Hill contributed reporting to this story

title: DHS conducted far-reaching surveillance during Minnesota ICE surge, court documents show - NPR
description:
The revelation was part of a motion filed in federal court just a few days before the service, as part of an ongoing conspiracy case against ICE protesters.
According to government documents, an undercover DHS agent attended a meeting of ICE protesters at Prince of Peace in February.
He's far from the only person caught in the wide-reaching surveillance web spun by the federal government.
Sergio Manancero manages La Doña Cerveceria, a brewery in Minneapolis where an undercover agent attended a meeting in January, according to court documents.
A DHS agent testified to the grand jury that it showed other organizations the defendants in the conspiracy case were affiliated with, according to the motion.
text:
On a recent Sunday morning at Prince of Peace Lutheran Church in Roseville, Minn., Steve Sylvester, the interim pastor there, had an unusual announcement to make.

Standing at the altar, he told his mostly elderly congregation that the Department of Homeland Security had surveilled their church during the federal immigration enforcement surge that happened in the state last winter.

The revelation was part of a motion filed in federal court just a few days before the service, as part of an ongoing conspiracy case against ICE protesters.

According to government documents, an undercover DHS agent attended a meeting of ICE protesters at Prince of Peace in February. The agent captured the license plates of people there, and then compiled dossiers including their names, addresses, and information about their families and jobs, according to the motion.

"It feels weird. It feels like I'm living in 1950s Eastern Europe," Sylvester told NPR. "I don't know that it feels frightening or daunting. It just feels completely out of place and inappropriate."

He's far from the only person caught in the wide-reaching surveillance web spun by the federal government.

Surveillance at churches, schools and libraries

For months, the documents show, federal agents secretly made recordings of meetings held at churches, libraries, restaurants and schools around the Twin Cities. They infiltrated private group chats, sought the financial records of national labor unions, and gathered information on community members who had not been accused of any crimes.

"Quite honestly, it was breathtaking," says Rachel Levinson-Waldman, who directs the Liberty and National Security Program at the Brennan Center for Justice. "Just the scope of what was being revealed in terms of how deeply it had gone, how many government resources were being devoted to this."

Cody Sanders, interim pastor at University Baptist Church in Minneapolis, says his first reaction was surprise, then anger, when he heard that an undercover agent wore a wire to a self-defense class held at his church this past May.

"I do imagine people will look over their shoulder a little more and wonder, 'Is there someone here who's trying to gather information?' Or when they see a strange car in the parking lot," Sanders says. "I hope we can resist the kind of suspicion that this is likely to generate."

Sergio Manancero manages La Doña Cerveceria, a brewery in Minneapolis where an undercover agent attended a meeting in January, according to court documents.

"I would understand why they would send somebody to that meeting, considering it was open to anybody that wanted to come because they were probably trying to figure out whether or not protesters were going to do something more serious against their agents," Manancero says.

"Do I think the government spying on us in that way is maybe bad? Yes," he said. "Am I surprised that they did it? No."

Manancero says organizers at the event were planning a lawful ICE protest. In a way, he says, he finds it almost beneficial that DHS agents witnessed it firsthand to see that nothing suspicious was taking place.

During another meeting at a public library, an undercover agent allegedly told a person there that he worked in construction and could build items for more "direct action," and that he didn't mind going to jail.

Privacy and free speech concerns

Levinson-Waldman, of the Brennan Center, says the federal government has broad authority under the Fourth Amendment to gather information on people, though other laws do impose limitations. There isn't enough information yet to determine whether the surveillance in Minnesota was legal, she says.

Regardless, Levinson-Waldman says, "Just because something's legal doesn't mean that it aligns with people's sense of what is ethical or what they're comfortable with having the government doing."

She says the tactics described in the documents seem to break from decades-long norms and guidelines. They remind her of COINTELPRO, the domestic counterintelligence program run by the FBI, which began in the 1950s and ended in the early 1970s.

As part of that operation, agents conducted intense surveillance on organizations it deemed subversive, including the Communist Party, the Black Panthers and civil rights leaders including Martin Luther King, Jr., and Malcolm X.

The abuses of that program, Levinson-Waldman says, led to a series of reforms, including tighter guidelines at the Justice Department on investigative techniques.

The government defended its actions in a court filing on Friday, saying it did not target the thousands of peaceful protesters in Minnesota.

Instead, it said it targeted the people who were ultimately charged in the conspiracy case. Prosecutors say they were planning activities not protected by the First Amendment, like setting up blockades at the federal building outside of Minneapolis that served as ICE headquarters during the surge.

According to the government, the surveillance conducted was "standard law enforcement practice."

Aaron Terr, director of public advocacy with the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, says the investigative tactics described in the court motion also raise First Amendment concerns, because this type of surveillance can also sweep up people engaged in perfectly lawful activity.

As part of its investigation, the documents show, DHS obtained the financial records for several nonprofits and labor unions, including the Service Employees International Union and the Communications Workers of America. In its response, prosecutors said requesting these records was "within the authority" of the agency.

"These reports raise the question of whether the government is investigating crimes or investigating political movements," Terr says. "When officials are infiltrating political meetings, recording protesters' license plates and examining years of financial activities by these mainstream advocacy groups, it raises the question, do they have actual evidence of criminal activity here?"

One government document presented to grand jurors shows a PowerPoint slide depicting a web of 18 organizations with the label "The Conspiracy." A DHS agent testified to the grand jury that it showed other organizations the defendants in the conspiracy case were affiliated with, according to the motion.

They included a local teacher's union, a bicycle repair shop, and the Minnesota affiliate of the AFL-CIO, a large federation of labor unions. In a statement, Minnesota AFL-CIO President Bernie Burnham said the government is "bringing back McCarthyism."

In its response to the court motion, the government said that it did not actually argue that the AFL-CIO or any other organizations shown in the web were part of the conspiracy.

Terr says the image communicates a troubling idea: Be careful who you associate with.

"The consequences of that are that many Americans may be afraid to attend a protest, support an advocacy organization, because they don't want to become the target of a government investigation," he says.

In a statement, DHS told NPR it does not comment on the existence or status of ongoing investigations. The agency directed NPR to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Minnesota, which also declined to comment.

MANHATTAN (WABC) -- A new state law in New York prohibiting local police agencies from cooperating with federal immigration enforcement takes effect Tuesday, setting up a potential legal showdown between the state and Nassau County, which has not yet committed to complying with the measure.

The legislation, known as the Local Cops Local Crimes Act, bars local government agencies from entering into or maintaining agreements with Immigration and Customs Enforcement to carry out civil immigration enforcement and detain immigrants in local jails.

According to state officials, 13 counties had such agreements in place when Gov. Kathy Hochul signed the measure into law in May. Eleven counties said they would end those arrangements by the deadline, but some counties, including Nassau, are still weighing their options.

Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, who is running for governor, has said the county is considering whether to comply with the law. One of the key questions is whether Nassau could challenge the statute in court, arguing it infringes on local governing authority. Another unresolved issue is whether New York could withhold federal funding flowing to counties that refuse to comply.

Gov. Hochul is scheduled to address the new law during a 10 a.m. news conference.

text:
A federal judge says Florida International University’s protest policy likely won’t withstand judicial scrutiny in a lawsuit filed by students punished after protesting ICE.

The ruling came Sunday, less than two weeks before a university-imposed deadline for the students to make a “video reflection” on the policy that prohibited their protest, and less than two weeks after they filed suit.

Judge Jacqueline Becerra, a Joe Biden-appointee to the U.S. District Court in the Southern District of Florida, issued the preliminary injunction.

The judge found a substantial likelihood the students, members of a group called ICEBreakers, would succeed on the merits, the standard for a preliminary injunction.

FIU students file federal lawsuit over ICE protest clampdown

The suit stems from a March 13 anti-ICE protest during a public event with FIU President Jeanette Nuñez and retired pro baseballer Alex Rodriguez.

Students stood up in the audience, turned around, and faced the crowd while wearing shirts urging, “ICE OFF FIU.”

Becerra wrote that “over sixty years of First Amendment precedent supports” the students.

“In short, when all is said and done, and for at least sixty years, the standard has been the same: student speech cannot be curtailed unless it materially disrupts the educational mission or involves substantial disorder or invasion of the rights of others,” Becerra wrote.

Becerra pointed to Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District in her 28-page filing. That U.S. Supreme Court decision held that students and teachers do not “shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate.”

High school and elementary school students in that case wore black armbands to protest the Vietnam War, and the Des Moines school district suspended the older kids.

“Any discussion of a student’s freedom of speech in public schools certainly begins, and perhaps ends,” with Tinker, Becerra wrote.

The details

Per the lawsuit, the FIU students, a group of no more than 15, left the auditorium on their own after less than five minutes. The students remained silent and the conversation on stage continued throughout.

FIU charged the students with misconduct, contending they violated the school’s “expressive activities” policy.

The university, to “protect health, safety, and welfare and prevent disruption of university activities,” prohibits inside university buildings “protests, parades, marches, picketing, demonstrations, and other similar expressive activities” under the policy.

“Formally, the ruling prevents FIU from enforcing its policy against only members of ICEBreakers, but the court’s reasoning makes clear that it would be unconstitutional if enforced against anyone else as well,” the ACLU said in a news release.

The university demanded the students produce a two-minute video reflecting upon the regulation by Sept. 4. Failure to do would would get them barred from registering for classes or receiving diplomas.

“Blocking this regulation means students can start the fall semester without fear of being punished for peacefully protesting,” Max Fondren, president of the ICEBreakers student group, said in a news release. “Our work to end FIU’s cruel and unnecessary decision to deputize campus police as ICE agents will continue.”

The students are represented by the ACLU of Florida and Community Justice Project.

“FIU’s discomfort with our message does not override our right to protest against the university’s 287(g) agreement — nor will it get us to stop,” Andrew Caro, another of the seven charged students, said in the news release. “Our protest did not derail the event, nor did it impact anyone else’s rights. It was non-disruptive and fully protected speech.”

I, and my colleague Representative Chuy Garcia from Illinois, are so honored to stand with you at the opening of this PanAmerican Congress.

text:
Good morning. Buenos días. Bom dia.

I’m Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal, representing the Seventh Congressional District in Washington State and a proud immigrant: the first and only Indian American woman to serve in the House of Representatives and one of only two dozen naturalized citizens in Congress. I, and my colleague Representative Chuy Garcia from Illinois, are so honored to stand with you at the opening of this PanAmerican Congress.

Many of you have traveled great distances, some at personal risk, because you know how urgent this moment is. Thank you for everything you are doing to lift up and fight for working people and poor people in your countries and across the hemisphere.

We all face similar forms of opposition to our progress, from authoritarians and dictators trampling on human rights and international laws, to misinformation and disinformation designed to undermine the free and fair elections of our countries, to the growing inequality and the capture of our economies by billionaires and giant corporations that throttle our peoples’ human rights, dignity, and futures.

This is exactly why the PanAmerican Congress is so important at this moment. The challenges we face require a shared hemispheric response, a response based on listening and learning from each other, on collaboration, the rule of law, and respect for sovereignty; and on shared strategies to take on the growing threat of fascism and right-wing actors in all our countries.

The Trump administration’s catastrophic reframing of the Monroe Doctrine in a new and super-sized vanity ploy called the Donroe Doctrine reasserts the failed and flawed concept of US dominance in the hemisphere. It dangerously attempts to justify US intervention, economic coercion, military pressure, and unilateral operations, often in violation of our own US Constitution and international law.

Just last week, we made our opposition to this doctrine clear in a letter that I led, with 10 of my colleagues, including Representative Garcia and Senator Bernie Sanders, demanding answers from Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the use and scope of these efforts—all completely unauthorized by Congress—and incredibly vast.

Dozens of lethal, extrajudicial strikes on boats in the Caribbean and Pacific Ocean carried out by the US military over the past year. Joint operations with partner militaries that have led to the bombing and detention of civilians. The kidnapping of a sitting head of state in Venezuela. The imposing of an illegal fuel blockade on top of a longstanding, illegal embargo against Cuba, that inflicts terrible collective punishment on the Cuban people—something that I have emphasized over and over again in the two Congressional delegations I have led to Cuba. Tariffs and sanctions deployed to shield political allies of the US president from prosecution. And US interference in other sovereign nations’ elections, including endorsing favored candidates, and pardoning a convicted narcotrafficker on the eve of an election.

This is an old and dangerous playbook of intervention and regime change that carries the same severe costs. It holds contempt for democratic institutions, hostility toward migrants and the poor, a willingness to criminalize dissent, and an economic vision that serves corporations and billionaires first and working families last. And most dangerously, it is being propped up and furthered by the economic, military, and political might coming straight from the White House but not authorized by Congress or approved by the people.

That is exactly why we are here. The far right is coordinating across nations, and so must we. Not only must we share effective strategies of opposition, but also our solutions of proposition: a shared vision that lifts up and puts power back in the hands of the people. A real partnership between our nations of collaboration and cooperation to solve the global challenges of climate change, labor rights, public health, migration, and economic prosperity for all. An understanding that military might, dominance, and aggression are tools of the oppressor, but diplomacy and respectful multilateral and bilateral relationships are the only tools to bring about lasting peace.

As a long-time organizer for justice speaking with awe and respect to a room full of people who have led transitions from dictators to democracies, and brought strength and power to peoples’ movements across the hemisphere, I can say that strength emerges most in times of crisis. What terrifies our opponents most is that our ideas are truly popular and we refuse to give up.

Across the United States, majorities of Americans reject the outright cruel kidnapping and disappearing of immigrants by ICE, and instead are clamoring for humane immigration reforms. Majorities reject billionaires and corporations who want to steal our clean air, water, and energy and instead demand that we respect our core value as human beings. Majorities reject spending taxpayer dollars on bombs abroad and instead demand universal healthcare and housing. Majorities are responding to a call that our people should thrive—not just barely survive.

Ad Policy

And in late July, one of our last actions before breaking for August recess was to pass my War Powers Resolution in the House, with every Democrat and several Republicans supporting an end to the war in Iran. We won’t stop there—we intend to pass Representative Velázquez’s Cuba War Powers Resolution when we get back, as well as other legislative actions to take on this administration’s unconstitutional actions.

Most hopeful is that we stand poised to retake control of the House of Representatives in November, and possibly even the Senate. From New York to New Jersey, Florida to Pennsylvania, Colorado to California, and Michigan to Minnesota, incredible progressive champions are winning elections despite tens of millions of dollars poured into those races for their opponents. We are so pleased to welcome some special guests of the US delegation, soon-to-be members of Congress: Chris Rabb from Pennsylvania, Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez from New York, and Adam Hamawy from New Jersey.

Thank you to the organizers of the PanAmerican Congress for having the vision to see that our collective action is the only way forward. And thank you to all of you for demanding change and insisting on democratic institutions by the people and for the people, built jointly across the hemisphere, not imposed north to south.

This is our time. Let’s use it to build power for the people across our hemisphere. Thank you.

text:
SCARBOROUGH — Six-year-old Ivana has back-to-school jitters.

Even though she loves math, she’s nervous about learning how to add and subtract digits in the thousands in second grade.

And she keeps having nightmares about immigration agents coming to arrest her.

“Me and my family were being separated into different jails like the one where Daddy is,” she said on Thursday.

It started when her father, Jonas Manywa, a 42-year-old immigrant from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, was detained at the Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Scarborough.

It’s been 20 days since Ivana and her 3-year-old sister Eliana saw him — in handcuffs as an ICE agent shut an office door.

They cried and tried to push their way into the room where he was being held after being detained during a routine check-in.

“I want daddy,” Eliana cried as she tried to open the door, her mother Alaise Seguro recounted in an interview in French a couple weeks later. “Daddy is inside. I want daddy.”

Eliana was pulled away as she clung to her father’s neck. Manywa didn’t have a chance to say goodbye or drive Ivana to her first day of school on Monday.

Manywa was transferred to Plymouth County Correctional Facility in Massachusetts the same day. A judge is now giving ICE until Friday to prove it complied with regulations and that Manywa should not be immediately released, according to court documents.

If the judge decides he was improperly arrested, Manywa could come home. Or, he could be deported to Cameroon — a country he’s never been to — where he’s worried he’d be shot at the airport.

Manywa’s case is one of several reports of someone detained during a routine immigration appointment at the ICE processing facility in Scarborough. And it isn’t the first time he’s been detained, either.

He was held for seven months after a drunken-driving charge. In the year in a half since, he said he’s cooperated with regular check-ins and was in the process of applying for asylum. Then ICE arrested him again without warning.

He will go wherever ICE chooses to deport him, he said, as long as it doesn’t put him at risk of the violence or death he came to the U.S. to escape. He wants to be granted a “fear interview,” or a chance to explain that he could face violence in Cameroon, too.

“They will kill me before I even arrive,” he said in French during a recent phone interview from the detention facility.

NAVIGATING THE PROCESS

A couple of years ago, a judge ruled that Manywa met the criteria for withholding of removal, a status often given to immigrants seeking asylum who have a nonviolent criminal record.

Under previous presidential administrations, people with this status were allowed to stay in the U.S. indefinitely because they couldn’t be deported to their home country. But the Trump administration changed the policy to consider deporting people under that status to a third country whose government is willing to take them.

Spokespeople for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not respond to a request for information about Manywa’s case, including why he was detained.

Manywa has retained an attorney, Amelia Lynn Ritenour, who declined to comment on his case.

The presence of federal immigration enforcement in Maine surged at the beginning of the year, when more than 200 people were arrested in less than a week in what ICE dubbed “Operation Catch of the Day” — with a stated goal of detaining 1,400 people in Maine.

ICE has remained in the state. In June, immigration advocates reported a rising number of calls to a hotline and steadily climbing reports of enforcement and detentions.

It’s not clear how many people ICE has detained to date in Maine. Spokespeople for ICE did not immediately respond Monday to questions asking for that number.

This past year, ICE grew its Maine staff by 44%, and people continued to be picked up by federal agents on the street, at work or at home. In July, a newly recruited ICE agent in Biddeford shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who didn’t have a criminal history and wasn’t the agents’ intended target.

Manywa and his family are Banyamulenge, a Tutsi minority ethnic group primarily from the South Kivu province.

Thousands of civilians in the Democratic Republic of Congo were killed and hundreds of villages destroyed in a wave of violence that began in 2017. Local militias, joined by Burundian rebel groups with Rwandan support, have vowed to expel or eliminate this ethnic group, according to an article in The Conversation.

Manywa spoke out against the violence on social media and in the newspapers. He said he was arrested and kidnapped multiple times, and people threatened to kill him and his family every day.

They fled to the U.S. in 2022 when they secured a visa to treat Ivana’s left kidney. The family of three then started the asylum-seeking process, and Manywa’s two younger daughters were born in the U.S., making them citizens. Manywa’s case was separated from his wife’s and Ivana’s, who are still seeking asylum.

“At least I will live,” Manywa thought when he moved to the U.S. “At least my children will live.”

A SEPARATED FAMILY

Weeks after her father was detained, Ivana holds a small yellow wooden block in her palm while sitting on a leather couch in the family’s dimly lit living room. Her younger sister tracks her every movement.

“Bippity boppity boop,” Ivana says, making the block disappear by quickly tucking it between her shoulder blade and the couch cushion. Ivana feigns disbelief. Eliana giggles.

“Magic,” Ivana says.

Their mother, Alaise Seguro, sobs next to them, pulling at her hair as her head hangs in her hands.

Seguro’s phone rests on the arm of the couch, her husband’s voice echoing on speaker.

They’re used to doing everything together, even bathing the children.

Now, he calls a few times a day: in the morning around 9:30, in the afternoon at 1 and 3 and in the evening around 8, an automated voice first announcing that an incarcerated individual is trying to place a call.

Manywa can talk in 30-minute increments, sometimes for up to an hour, listening to the kids playing in the background and asking his wife about them. At night, he sings to the girls, and tells them stories about his adventures back home.

An automated voice alerts the end of each call.

A ROUTINE APPOINTMENT

Manywa drove to the ICE facility in Scarborough with Ivana and Eliana in the back seat for a routine check-in with immigration officials on Aug. 5. It normally takes a couple of minutes — he presents his identification and then is sent on his way. He’s never had any problems before.

But that day, they didn’t ask for his ID. Instead, he said an agent asked why his children were there. He brings them everywhere, like grocery shopping.

The agents told him to call his wife so she could pick up the kids, he said. That’s when he could tell something was wrong.

Seguro was at the hospital with baby Jaya, their 9-month-old daughter.

The agent didn’t give him enough time to explain what was happening, he said, not that he had any answers. They kept asking what was taking her so long. “I think they’re going to arrest me,” he remembered telling his wife over the phone.

They held Manywa in a separate room from his children. He said he offered to drive back to his house with ICE agents so that his kids wouldn’t have to see him get arrested. But the agents put him in handcuffs as they watched.

Afterward, Seguro and her three children waited outside in the parking lot for 30 minutes. She cried. She had her husband’s keys, but said she doesn’t have a driver’s license or permit. Manywa earned most of their income, working as a certified nursing assistant at the Maine Veterans’ Homes in Scarborough. How would they manage without him?

Protesters who regularly gather at the ICE facility gave Seguro and her children a ride home. Community members visit the family to offer help and donate items. She said a local church is helping them pay rent.

But they can’t give them everything the family needs, Seguro said.

“With the children and the baby, it’s very difficult,” she said.

Eliana dreams about the arrest every night, her mother said. “She was traumatized by the actions she saw in front of her,” Manywa said.

DETAINED A SECOND TIME

Ivana asked her mother if her father will be gone for a long time — like last time.

Manywa said he recognized Plymouth County Correctional Facility when he was brought there with handcuffs around his hands and feet three weeks ago. He had been there before, just over a year and a half ago.

In 2024, police arrested Manywa for driving under the influence. He didn’t know about the legal blood alcohol limit in the U.S., he said. And he didn’t get into an accident.

At the end of July that year, ICE agents arrested him when he drove to Hannaford to buy milk for the children. They said he was in the country illegally, and they didn’t listen when he tried to explain he had a Social Security number and a work permit, he said.

He spent five days in the Cumberland County Jail, a few months in Rhode Island, and a few more months at Plymouth County Correctional Facility until he was released in February 2025.

Manywa said ICE told him then that as long as he didn’t break any laws, they would leave him alone.

Since then, Manywa frequently communicated with ICE via email and checked in at the facility in Scarborough every few months. He said he did everything they asked.

He never thought he’d end up in Plymouth again.

MISSING THEIR FATHER

The children don’t fully understand where their father is.

Eliana knows that he’s not there to give her a big hug after he gets home from work or read her a story before bed. She knows he’s in jail, but she’s too young to really grasp what that means, her mother said. She knows it’s a place they put people, and she can’t see him anymore.

Eliana pretends to be a starfish, making snow angels in the dining room while her father tells her mother about the conditions he’s being held in.

He has a sinus infection, made worse by the air conditioning, he says, and he sustains himself on bread and milk, unable to eat anything else.

Eliana bounces up and peeks through the fluttering translucent curtains to watch the sun.

“I wait for the morning,” he says, because he has trouble sleeping.

Eliana picks up a paper airplane and tosses it to her sister.

“My back hurts,” he says. “My ribs hurt.”

Eliana rolls a spikey yellow ball to her sister.

“I am dying, little by little,” he says.

Ivana, the big sister, knows about ICE. She knows that their presence means staying home from school and hiding. She knows that her father was taken because they are immigrants.

Eliana and Ivana don’t play with other kids anymore.

On a sticky Thursday afternoon, they entertain each other in the dining room. They twirl like ballerinas, Ivana gracefully, with all of her weight held delicately on one foot, the other pointing behind her.

Eliana teeters behind her, stumbling, but happy to be like her big sister. They both love the color pink, and practicing their splits on the vinyl flooring.

They ask to kiss and hug their dad all the time.

“I believed in the United States,” Manywa said. “I considered it a country that respects human rights.”

But now, he sits and worries that his children will always remember him in handcuffs.

“It is not the country I thought it was,” he said.

text:
WASHINGTON — The Department of Homeland Security is planning to drastically increase the fee for hiring high-skilled foreign workers within the United States to $100,000, according to a preview of a proposed rule published Monday.

The administration noted in the Federal Register that it plans to use the fee to “serve as a dedicated revenue mechanism to help recover a portion of the federal government’s costs of administering the lawful immigration system, including activities carried out by DHS” and the departments of Justice, State and Labor.

Currently, it costs anywhere from $2,000 to $5,000 for an employer to hire a highly skilled foreign worker through the H-1B visa program. Congress created the program in the 1990s and visas are capped annually at 65,000, with an additional 20,000 for foreign workers who graduate with a masters or doctoral degree from a U.S. institution.

A federal judge in June struck down the Trump administration’s attempt to increase the H-1B visa to $100,000 for foreign workers hired outside the U.S.

Workers on a temporary H-1B visa work in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, medicine or education.

Employers use the H-1B program to hire foreign workers who have a minimum of a bachelor's degree for up to three years, but the temporary visa can be extended for up to six.

Last year, the Trump administration imposed a one-time $100,000 H-1B visa fee to employers in an effort to prevent high-skill jobs going to foreigners instead of U.S. citizens. However, the program is used to fill high-skill jobs that are difficult to fill with American workers.
