text:
In February, the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit held in Buenrostro-Mendez v. Bondi that noncitizens who entered the US unlawfully, however long ago, remain “seeking admission” under 8 U.S.C. Section 1225(b)(2)(A) and must sit in detention without a bond hearing while they fight removal. Last month, the Seventh Circuit in Cirrus Rojas v. Olson held the opposite: Deeming a longtime resident an applicant for admission doesn’t make him one seeking it, so Section 1226(a) governs and a bond hearing is available. The Ninth Circuit agreed the same day, over a dissent, in Rodriguez Vazquez v. Bostock.

The Trump administration adopted the mandatory-detention reading in July 2025. That September, the Board of Immigration Appeals made it precedent in Matter of Yajure Hurtado. Seven circuits currently reject it; only the Eighth Circuit’s Avila v. Bondi has joined the Fifth. District judges reportedly have rejected the policy in more than 9,300 rulings, and three certiorari petitions are pending.

Review is a question of vehicle and timing, not whether it will happen; until the justices act, the ability even to ask for bond depends on where the government holds the client.

Two Readings

The dispute runs through one deeming clause. Section 1225(a)(1) provides that a noncitizen present in the US who hasn’t been admitted “shall be deemed for purposes of this chapter an applicant for admission.” Section 1225(b)(2)(A) then mandates detention of “an alien seeking admission” who isn’t “clearly and beyond a doubt” entitled to be admitted.

For the Fifth Circuit, the deemed status does all the work. An applicant for admission is necessarily seeking admission — like a college applicant who is still seeking admission after filing, Judge Edith Jones wrote in Buenrostro-Mendez. On that reading, Section 1226(a)’s bond regime is left mainly for admitted noncitizens who later became deportable. Three decades of contrary practice couldn’t override the text. On the 1996 statute’s purposes, Jones was blunt: “Congress’s purpose matters far less than what it wrote.”

The panel split, with Judge Dana Douglas warning in dissent that under the government’s reading, “for purposes of immigration detention, the border is now everywhere.” Rehearing was denied in April, and the petitioners have gone to the US Supreme Court.

The Seventh Circuit answered in Cirrus Rojas v. Olson that a legal fiction travels only as far as its text. Congress defined “applicant for admission” but left “seeking admission” undefined, so ordinary meaning controls. Jaciel Cirrus Rojas — in the country since 2018 and pursuing asylum and related protection, not lawful entry — isn’t seeking admission in any ordinary sense, and deeming him an applicant doesn’t “conjure a fictional intent to seek admission,” Judge Joshua Kolar wrote.

Structure agreed: The 2025 Laken Riley Act’s expansion of Section 1226(c)’s detention list would be pointless if Section 1225 already required detaining every unlawful entrant, and Congress never funded the mass detention now read into a 1996 catchall. Judge Diane Sykes dissented, siding with the Fifth and Eighth Circuits, saying that the statute classifies people like Cirrus Rojas as constructively seeking admission.

A Second Front

Even where Buenrostro-Mendez governs, the fight has moved rather than ended. In Sosnava Rodriguez v. Ortega, a Fifth Circuit panel accepted the statutory holding on July 2 but ruled that the Due Process Clause forbids holding long-term residents beyond 90 days without an individualized custody hearing. Eight days later, on its own motion, the full court vacated that decision and ordered rehearing en banc. On July 21, it stayed the district court judgments. It will decide whether detainees in Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi keep a constitutional route now that the statutory one is closed.

The Seventh Circuit saw the same problem. Two immigration judges found Cirrus Rojas neither a flight risk nor a danger, yet the government insists on confinement, the purposeless deprivation Zadvydas v. Davis warns against.

A parallel due process question is already at the Supreme Court. In June, the justices granted certiorari in Genalo v. Black on whether a bond hearing is constitutionally required once Section 1226(c) mandatory detention becomes “unreasonably prolonged,” and if so, whether the government must justify it by clear and convincing evidence. The US Solicitor General has petitioned from losses in the Sixth Circuit (Raycraft v. Lopez-Campos) and Second (Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha), telling the Supreme Court that Lopez-Campos is the better vehicle because it also squarely presents the due process issue.

What to Preserve

For habeas counsel with detained clients, geography controls, so move fast. Habeas corpus runs against the immediate custodian in the district of confinement under Rumsfeld v. Padilla as courts apply it to immigration detention, so the client’s circuit of confinement supplies the law — not the removal venue — and a transfer can flip it overnight.

Circuit precedent closes the statutory route to bond only in the Fifth and Eighth Circuits. There, case-by-case parole under Section 1182(d)(5)(A) is the remaining valve: Request it and paper the denial. File the 28 U.S.C. Section 2241 petition promptly; jurisdiction attaches at filing.

Build the bond record everywhere, including where Yajure Hurtado forecloses relief. Request the hearing. When the immigration judge disclaims jurisdiction, document the denial and seek danger and flight findings from the habeas court. In Cirrus Rojas, the two immigration judges’ findings anchored the court’s constitutional concerns. Winning the statutory fight yields a hearing, not release. The burden at that hearing stays on the noncitizen.

Plead both in every petition: Section 1226(a) governs, and prolonged detention without an individualized hearing violates the Fifth Amendment. National Immigration Project advisories collect what remains open in the Fifth and Eighth Circuits and under the Sosnava stay.

Finally, paper the government’s conduct. Bond cancellation notices, stated intentions to re-detain, and unilateral stays of bond orders under 8 C.F.R. Section 1003.19(i)(2) all figured in Cirrus Rojas; that conduct kept his appeal alive after release. Build the same file whenever custody shifts mid-litigation.

For nearly 30 years, five administrations of both parties read these statutes the same way. Whatever the Supreme Court decides, the interim rule is clear: Liberty pending removal depends on the map. Counsel’s job is to have the record ready when it is redrawn.

text:
HARRISBURG — Earlier this spring, with no public notice, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro made an unconventional hire: a senior advisor to help him deal with the Trump administration.

Jennifer Higgins, a longtime federal immigration official based in Washington, D.C., was brought on to help Shapiro and state agencies under his jurisdiction map out responses to some of the president’s targeted attacks on Democrat-led states — notably, funding cuts and demands for sensitive or proprietary information.

Higgins is being paid by the hour — an unusual arrangement for a gubernatorial staffer, and one that Shapiro’s office could not immediately explain. State payroll records show she is paid $89 per hour, and Shapiro officials said she works full-time, putting her annual salary at roughly $185,000.

The administration defended hiring Higgins, even though Pennsylvania already spends tens of thousands of taxpayer dollars every year for a federal government liaison.

Email address

The governor’s office employs a full-time lobbyist in Washington, D.C., who is paid $177,507 annually. And in theory, Pennsylvania’s two senators act as the state’s de facto protectors in the nation’s capital and run interference with the White House when problems arise.

But Shapiro spokesperson Rosie Lapowsky explained in an emailed statement that an additional person was needed because “the Trump administration’s relentless attacks on the rights and freedoms of Pennsylvanians are reaching into every corner of our Commonwealth.”

Higgins, Lapowsky said, brings “deep expertise and invaluable perspective helping protect Pennsylvanians during this critical moment.” (Higgins did not respond to Spotlight PA’s request to speak with her directly.)

Still, Higgins’ expertise is in the immigration sphere, where she has spent nearly the entirety of her career. The governor’s office acknowledged that Higgins is not directly advising Shapiro on immigration issues, but is part of a larger group of policy officials, lawyers, and others who provide the governor with information on that and other issues facing the state.

Asked for an example of Higgins’ work, Lapowsky said she helped coordinate Shapiro’s response to a Trump administration demand that states turn over commercial driver's license records containing personal information. Trump officials have pointed, among other things, to crashes involving noncitizen drivers as one reason for the crackdown and have threatened to withhold federal funding if states do not comply.

In August, Shapiro joined a coalition of state attorneys general suing the federal government over the subpoena.

It’s true that, since reclaiming the White House in 2024, President Donald Trump has used the levers of the federal government to punish blue states.

The administration admitted in a federal court filing this summer that it recommended scrapping billions in grants for clean-energy projects based solely on those states’ “political identity,” and whether Trump won the vote in those places in the 2024 election.

Earlier this year, Trump attempted to freeze billions in childcare and social assistance for five Democratic-led states — he had initiated the move following the federal fraud probe involving Minnesota’s social services network — which he later abandoned.

And Politico reported last month that Trump overruled his own emergency management agency to deny federal relief funds to four Democratic-led states.

For his part, Shapiro often talks about how his administration has sued Trump dozens of times to challenge the loss of federal funding. Those suits involve a range of initiatives, from education to natural disasters. The governor’s office also noted that unlike in other states, where attorneys general are handling litigation against Trump, Shapiro’s lawyers are taking on that work in Pennsylvania. Attorney General Dave Sunday, a Republican, has not entered the commonwealth into any lawsuit against the president or his administration.

Many of those suits predate Higgins’ arrival, and were handled by attorneys already on Shapiro’s staff. But the volume of attacks coming from Washington, Lapowsky said, combined with the range and breadth of policies and issues being targeted, necessitated another person to help coordinate plans to respond.

Immigration leadership

Higgins’ role in the Shapiro administration differs significantly from the work that has defined her career.

She started as an immigration officer in the early 2000s, but quickly moved into leadership roles within the federal office that handles asylum applications and screenings and adjudicates refugee applications, according to an online biography.

Shortly after Trump was elected to a first term in 2016, Higgins became the office’s associate director. Some rights groups have highlighted that part of her bio, since she held a leadership position during the implementation of one of the federal government’s most controversial immigration programs.

Officially called the Migrant Protection Protocols (MPP), but better known as Remain in Mexico, the program went into effect in early 2019. It required asylum seekers along the southern border to return to cities in Mexico, many of which are dangerous, while waiting for their immigration cases to be heard in the courts. Previously, those people were allowed to stay in the United States during that waiting period.

The Trump administration sold MPP as a way to thwart people with fraudulent claims from easily entering the U.S. But human rights and immigration groups, as well as multiple news organizations, extensively documented how migrants sent to Mexican border towns faced extreme danger, including kidnapping, assault, and rape. Tent camps were set up to house some of the asylum seekers, but living conditions were squalid, with no running water or electricity.

Human rights groups also noted that access to legal representation was fraught with obstacles, and resulted in higher numbers of cases being denied, sometimes just because migrants did not receive timely notices of their hearings or could not safely reach ports of entry into the country to be present for such hearings.

The office where Higgins held a senior leadership role at the time — the Refugee, Asylum and International Operations Directorate (RAIO) inside the U.S. Department of Homeland Security — was part of the larger apparatus tasked with the MPP’s rollout. Higgins’ level of involvement in the program’s operations is not clear, as the office’s work is subject to high levels of confidentiality. But the office she helped oversee is responsible for, among other duties, conducting asylum screenings and applications, according to its website. Its employees would have been at the front lines of the program’s implementation.

President Joe Biden ended the Remain in Mexico program after defeating Trump in 2020. Since retaking the White House, Trump officials have attempted to revive it but have been blocked by the courts.

During Biden’s presidency, Higgins continued to rise. She became acting chief of staff to then-U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, and within a year was appointed acting director of the department’s vast agency that oversees the legal U.S. immigration system.

Shortly after Trump started his second term, she was replaced.

text:
CHICAGO (WLS) -- A crash involving immigration agents and a pickup truck near the Stevenson Expressway led to an arrest and drew protesters, elected officials and community activists to the scene Monday, raising questions about how the arrest was carried out.

Illinois State Police confirmed that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents were inside a second vehicle involved in the incident, which occurred on the Damen Avenue off-ramp of Interstate 55 shortly before 11:30 a.m. State police said no injuries were reported.

ABC7 Chicago is now streaming 24/7. Click here to watch

The circumstances surrounding the arrest remain unclear. Activists and local officials questioned what appeared to be agents' decision to use their vehicle to stop a blue pickup truck on a busy expressway off-ramp.

Kevin Amaro of the Southwest Side Rapid Response Team said he was traveling on I-55 moments before the crash.

"I saw five to six cars, speeding really fast," Amaro said.

Amaro said he pulled over after witnessing the aftermath and briefly spoke with the man being detained.

"He quickly asked me, 'Do you have a phone? Can you call my family and please let them know. Call them,'" Amaro said.

According to Amaro, the man was taken away before he could obtain any additional information.

As news of the incident spread, more people gathered near the off-ramp, where the damaged ICE vehicle had been towed.

Baltazar Enríquez of the Little Village Community Council said community members sought information from agents at the scene.

"We asked one of the agents, 'Why were you following him?'" Enríquez said. "He responds 'Oh, he had a DUI warrant.' But we don't know yet if this is true."

Ald. Julia Ramirez, whose 12th Ward includes parts of the area, also responded to the scene. Ramirez said she was concerned about the potential for tensions to escalate as protesters gathered.

"Last year, there was tear gas and rubber bullets, and I was really worried about that occurring," Ramirez said. "And I decided to bring a staffer along, so we could be on the scene to potentially de-escalate."

Ramirez said she has not been able to verify the reason for the arrest but questioned the manner in which it appeared to have been conducted.

"The ICE vehicle was pinned alongside that vehicle. Super dangerous. We're talking about the expressway," Ramirez said.

The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately responded to requests for comment.

text:
AUSTIN (KXAN) — The family of 5-year-old Liam Tadeo, the boy detained by ICE alongside his father in Austin earlier this month, is voluntarily deporting to Mexico, the family’s immigration attorney told KXAN.

Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, that attorney, said despite a statement from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) noting that “ICE will place the children with a safe person the parent designates,” DHS has not allowed Liam to be released to his mother. His mother, Maria, is not a legal United States citizen either, Lincoln-Goldfinch confirmed.

“Victor (the father) has asked for Liam to be released to his mother since the moment of their detention and DHS will not allow Maria to just go pick Liam up. And the risk is that Liam would be placed into ORR custody as an unaccompanied migrant child,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

ORR is the Office of Refugee Resettlement, the agency that takes custody of unaccompanied migrant children.

KXAN reached out to DHS about claims the agency would not release Liam to his mother. They largely sent us the same statement they sent us last week, which you can read below.

“It feels like when you go to someone’s house after a sudden death has occurred and there’s a wake or a gathering and everybody is just stunned. That’s what it feels like after a detention like this. Liam’s mom, Maria, is desperate and distraught, being separated from her child and worrying about his well being,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

How we got here

Liam and his father were detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Austin on Sunday, Aug. 16, according to a GoFundMe post from the family. They were taken to the Dilley detention facility near San Antonio.

“Liam wanted to go to play soccer so his dad took him to a soccer game and while they were out … the truck that they were in was pulled over by ICE, who immediately asked them their legal status,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson confirmed ICE arrested Victor Martinez Nieto, the father, during a traffic stop in Austin. He is an undocumented immigrant from Mexico.

DHS said ICE has arrested the man before, in late 2025 in Hutto.

“He accepted voluntary departure and was removed from the country on February 12, 2026. Martinez Nieto illegally reentered the country at an unknown time and place after being removed,” the DHS spokesperson said.

DHS said Martinez Nieto and his son will remain together in ICE custody “pending removal.” The spokesperson also added:

“Parents have a choice if they want to be removed with their children or ICE will place the children with a safe person the parent designates. This is consistent with past administrations’ immigration enforcement.

The Dilley Detention Center is retrofitted for families. Children have access to teachers, classrooms, and curriculum booklets for math, reading, and spelling. All of this is generously funded by the U.S. taxpayer. Adults with children are housed in facilities that provide for their safety, security, and medical needs.

Being in detention is a choice. We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App. The United States is offering illegal aliens $2,600 and a free flight to self-deport now. We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return.“

text:
An explosive report has revealed that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries held a secret meeting with Trump administration power broker Jared Kushner to find “common ground” with the far right in the past weeks — as he made statements that could isolate the left-wing members of the House Democratic Caucus.

The New York Times reported on Sunday that the two recently met in a space offered by a mutual friend in New York City, citing two people familiar with the meeting and another who was briefed on it. The meeting covered a broad range of topics for the two men who have been in contact since collaborating on a criminal legal system reform bill in Donald Trump’s first term.

The meeting appears to be an acknowledgement that Democrats are expected to win control of the House this November, and that Jeffries is likely to become speaker.

One theme of their conversation was to find “common ground” on issues like housing, the high cost of living, and immigration. On those topics, Kushner suggested that Jeffries meet with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.

The report did not specify whether the two came to any agreements on those topics. However, it comes as the Trump administration’s war with Israel on Iran is drastically raising prices across all sectors — a war that Jeffries has opposed, but in a relatively muted way.

It also comes as the Trump administration has pursued extreme policies on immigration. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) have arrested and detained a record number of people in Trump’s second term, conducting raids targeted at Democratic-leaning areas, while officials are also meting out harsh punishments for anyone opposed to the mass deportation campaign.

Many Democratic voters oppose ICE and Trump’s raids. But, as outrage spread over the administration’s ICE crackdowns earlier this year, Jeffries only said he would advocate for minor reforms to the agency’s conduct — and refused to whip against the DHS funding bill earlier this year.

Republicans downplayed the meeting after it sparked furor on the right, with House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) saying that Kushner is “not really directly involved in the admin, at least in the day-to-day in the White House” — though he has served as a representative of the Trump administration in critical affairs like in negotiations with Israel over colonialist plans for Gaza and the war on Iran.

Facing fierce criticism from the report of the meeting, meanwhile, Jeffries said in a statement that the Republicans’ “extremist approach” to governance in this Congress “will be met with forceful opposition.”

“In every conversation that we have with the Trump administration, we will continue to make it explicitly clear that the affordability crisis is not a hoax and nothing short of transformational policy change is acceptable,” Jeffries said.

However, it is “transformational policy change” that Jeffries has worked to oppose and obstruct from left-wing members of his caucus.

For instance, last week, Jeffries said that, despite his support in previous years, he now opposes Medicare for All during an interview on NBC. He said, instead, that Democrats are working to “make health care affordable” for all, without specifying how. Other priorities that may be championed by progressives — like impeachment of Trump or his cabinet, abolishing ICE, or cutting aid to Israel — have also gotten the cold shoulder from Jeffries in recent weeks.

In the NBC interview, Jeffries would not say whether or not he believes that democratic socialists have a place in the Democratic Party — despite multiple Democratic Socialists of America members holding seats in his caucus and others running for highly contested seats in Congress. In June, Jeffries put distance between himself and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist, saying that Mamdani has “work to do” to placate more centrist members of Congress.

Election deniers are back on the ballot. In most swing states, at least one major Republican candidate has questioned or outright denied the results of the 2020 US presidential election, which Donald Trump lost to Joe Biden.

While voters in swing states have previously largely rejected candidates who denied election results, Republicans running for statewide offices across much of the country are trying again.

In Arizona, gubernatorial candidate and US representative Andy Biggs voted against certifying his own state’s election results. In Wisconsin, Republican gubernatorial hopeful Tom Tiffany similarly voted against certifying the 2020 results as a US representative for his state.

Candidates for governor in Pennsylvania and Michigan have cast doubt on the validity of the 2020 results. And some swing state Republican candidates for secretary of state have questioned or denied election results.

Governors sign off on state election results, issuing certificates to the presidential electors of whichever candidate wins. They can call for investigations or special sessions, and use their bully pulpit to cast doubt on election results. Secretaries of state are meanwhile the chief election officials in most US states, overseeing voting systems and advising the local jurisdictions that run elections. They usually play a role in certifying election results, too.

In 2020, Trump pressured governors and secretaries of state, alongside a host of state and local officials in several swing states, to withhold their signatures in a broad campaign to overturn his loss. Swing state governors and secretaries of state refused to stall or impede their states’ results.

But if election deniers or skeptics are elected to these key statewide roles, they would be in office in 2028, raising apprehension that they may refuse to sign off on results, or succumb to pressure from Trump and his allies, should Republicans lose.

title: US plans mass visa revocation for asylum seekers - DW
description:
If carried out, it would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history.
What did the State Department say about revoking visas?
Trump official slams visa use Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau criticized the use of tourist and business visas as a path to asylum claims.
Who has been impacted by Trump's immigration crackdown?
Despite campaigning largely on illegal immigration, the administration has also tightened legal immigration pathways, including through new, costly fees for certain work visa applicants.
text:
United States President Donald Trump's administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of foreigners who applied for or are currently seeking asylum in the country, the State Department said in a statement on Monday.

It didn't say how many visas would be affected, but the Associated Press put the number at up to 200,000, citing State Department documents ‌and ​two US officials. If carried out, it would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history.

What did the State Department say about revoking visas?

The State Department is expected to announce the revocations in the coming weeks, targeting so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 to holders who have sought or are now seeking asylum. These visas are generally issued for business travel, tourism, family visits or medical care.

"We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently," State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said, referring to the Department of Homeland Security.

He declined to give a specific number, saying the count "remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis."

Officials said the revocations would not necessarily lead to immediate deportation. Most people with pending asylum cases would instead be recategorized, losing their status as business or tourism travelers, according to officials who spoke to AP on condition of anonymity.

Trump official slams visa use

Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau criticized the use of tourist and business visas as a path to asylum claims.

"People in the US and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims," he wrote on social media platform X, adding, "Asylum isn't supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law."

He separately alleged that the US immigration system "has long been swamped by frivolous asylum claims" and cited the case of a Colombian national who entered the US on a tourist visa in 2015 before applying for asylum.

Applicants for B1 and B2 visas are currently required to affirm they will not seek asylum and to demonstrate intent to return to their home countries. It remains unclear how many current visa holders have actually filed for asylum.

Who has been impacted by Trump's immigration crackdown?

The move is the latest in a series of visa restrictions under Trump's second term, which has included expanded social media vetting, new bond requirements, and outright bans on visa issuance for citizens of certain countries.

The State Department said it has revoked roughly 175,000 visas over the past 18 months, citing reasons ranging from criminal convictions to public criticism of US policy, particularly regarding the Middle East. The administration has also targeted "birth tourism," and has repeatedly sought to end birthright citizenship. Courts, including the Supreme Court, have rejected those efforts.

Rights groups have criticized the broader immigration crackdown, arguing it has infringed on free speech and due process rights while creating an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities who could face racial profiling. The administration maintains the crackdown is intended to strengthen domestic security.

Despite campaigning largely on illegal immigration, the administration has also tightened legal immigration pathways, including through new, costly fees for certain work visa applicants. Several aspects of the crackdown are facing ongoing legal challenges.

Acosta, held at the Cascade County Detention Center, is a possible class member in a lawsuit filed against Cascade County, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and other federal officials by Upper Seven Law.

In signed declarations, a couple of other potential class members said they passed out while in custody, including one who was held in the back of a hot truck.

One said he was threatened by a Customs and Border Patrol agent.

“A CBP agent put me in his car and told me that he wanted me to run so that he could use his gun on me,” said Jonny Hernandez Antunez in court records. “ … I was terrified.”

The lawsuit alleges U.S. Customs and Border Patrol and Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials are arresting people without warrants and detaining them without evidence they are a flight risk or danger to their communities, contrary to the U.S. Constitution or laws of the country.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office acknowledges government agents made arrests without warrants, but it argues the government issued warrants after the arrests, and in one court filing, it argues the plaintiffs are in the United States without legal permission.

The press team for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not respond Monday to an email with questions about the circumstances outlined in the declarations filed in federal court.

A federal judge earlier ordered the release of Jesus Verde Hernandez from the Cascade County Detention Center, and last week he ordered the release of Adrián Espinoza De La Cruz and his 9-year-old child from a facility in Havre.

In both cases, U.S. District Court of Montana Judge Brian Morris found federal authorities violated the constitutional rights of the petitioners, including by not having warrants ahead of time.

The judge said he found the “lack of regard” for the parent and child “particularly disturbing.”

Cascade County Sheriff Jesse Slaughter earlier said the county detention center is simply the contract facility for the detainees.

Monday, Upper Seven senior staff attorney Andres Haladay said the firm has identified at least 41 members of the potential class, and at least 38 remain in custody. A hearing on the petition to release the others is scheduled to take place this week.

In the meantime, Upper Seven filed declarations of three people who are possible class members in the case. Here are two summaries of the experiences described in the declarations.

From the declaration of Acosta:

Acosta, 26, lives in Phoenix, Arizona, with his wife and child, who are U.S. citizens. He hasn’t been convicted of any crimes. The family was headed home after a vacation in North Dakota and stopped at a gas station in Sidney. They were looking for the clinic because his wife, who is diabetic, didn’t feel well. Acosta went into the gas station to buy food for his son, and a local sheriff’s officer showed up and said CBP would arrive. But CBP didn’t, and the sheriff’s officer handcuffed him and took him to jail. Acosta passed out in a cell and believes he hit his head after experiencing a panic attack. He was taken to a medical center, a CBP agent was there, and his wife tried to explain they were getting papers completed because they are married. The CBP agent arrested him without a warrant, the affidavit says. Later at a CBP station in a different town, another CBP agent kicked him to get his attention, and he still has pain in his back. The CBP agent said if Acosta talked to anyone, including an attorney, he would have to stay in jail. The CBP agent also said Acosta needed to sign documents to either voluntarily depart or stay and see a judge. The agent told Acosta, “If you don’t sign, I’m going to sign it for you.” Acosta said he didn’t know if the agent actually signed, and if he did, which option he chose for Acosta. He said he was never presented with a warrant or given the chance to call a lawyer. Eventually, he was taken to the Cascade County Detention Center, where he faced threats from other inmates and feared for his life and the life of an 18-year-old who was also detained and smaller than others being held. “There are a lot of people in Cascade who pick on the weak and pound on their cell windows.”

From the declaration of Antunez:

Antunez is 26 and has lived in the United States for seven years. He lives in Butte with his fiance and six-month-old son. His fiance has postpartum depression, and he cares for her and their son. He and his brother were passengers in a car with his friend, and CBP pulled them over, and three other trucks surrounded them. The CBP agent who came to the car didn’t tell them why they were pulled over. Thirteen or 14 agents were on the scene and put waist shackles and handcuffs on them. Antunez asked to take his gastritis medication with him but agents refused. A CBP agent told him he wanted him to run so that he could use his gun on Antunez, and the agent said the same thing to the others. “My wife knows people who have been killed by CBP. I was terrified,” Antunez said. He said agents never showed him a warrant or asked questions about his ties to the community. He was asked to sign a document he couldn’t read and was later told it was a voluntary departure form. Antunez and the others were held at a weigh station for three or four hours without being allowed to go to the bathroom. They were put in the back of a truck that was like a box and “very hot.” “I began hitting the wall of the box, asking for more air. At some point, my heart began to beat really fast. I felt the guy sitting next to me pour water on my head. … I believe that I passed out from the heat.” Later at a CBP station, he again was denied his medication. Agents asked him to sign more documents, but they only showed him the signature portion of the documents. After agents talked to him, they gave him a card with his rights written in Spanish. “There was only one rights card for all of us being held there.” He was transported to the Cascade County Detention Center, where he shares a cell with a couple of people who have criminal charges. He asked a third time for his medication but did not receive it.

The press team for the Department of Homeland Security did not respond Monday to the experiences described in the declarations, but in an earlier email from DHS, a spokesperson for Customs and Border Patrol said Espinoza De La Cruz admitted to illegal immigration and “accepted voluntary return for himself and his minor child.”

The email said Espinoza De La Cruz was “placed into supervised release” with ICE, Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

“We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure by utilizing the CBP Home app to receive a free flight home and $2,600,” the CBP spokesperson said in the email.

In January 2026, the Department of Homeland Security announced President Donald Trump was starting his second year of “making America safe again and continuing mass deportations.” A news release said “illegal aliens” who signed up to self deport through the CBP Home application would receive the flight and $2,600 “exit bonus.”

“More than 2 million illegal aliens have made the decision to self-deport,” the news release said.

The press team did not respond to a follow-up question Friday about how many people in Montana have received $2,600 checks.

text:
A sailor deployed aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln said his father was detained by immigration authorities in Florida over the weekend, while the sailor was at sea in the Middle East nine months into his deployment.

Luis Manuel Aviles Roa, 48, was detained Saturday shortly after 11 a.m. in Key West, Fla., where he lives. His wife, Argelia Aviles, told the Associated Press that he was arrested after leaving home to take his car to a mechanic.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) confirmed the arrest, telling Military.com on Monday that the suspect "entered the country illegally on an unknown date and location" and will remain in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement proceedings, or ICE, custody pending removal proceedings.

The circumstances of Aviles' immigration status are disputed. His family said he is originally from Nicaragua and has lived in the United States for about 19 years. He works as a repair man and holds a work permit, a Social Security card, and a driver's license.

He was reportedly waiting for a green card to be approved.

Word Reached Son at Sea

Joshua Aviles, the man's son, said he learned of the detention while deployed aboard the Lincoln. He described his sentiments in a Facebook post.

"I've been deployed for over nine months, out at sea in the Middle East aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, fighting for a country that has given me everything," he wrote. "I just got a call that my dad was taken by ICE."

He described his father as a hardworking and humble man, saying he was doing everything he could to secure his release.

"I love you with all my heart. Please stay strong. I'm coming home, Dad," he wrote.

Joshua Aviles told NBC News he has limited internet access at sea and described the strain of working while worrying about his father.

A stepsister, Katty Delgado, told the network that she knew of no arrest history or criminal allegations against Aviles.

DHS 'Simply Enforcing Laws'

DHS defended the arrest as a matter of law.

“Having a family member in the military is not a free pass to violate our nation’s laws," a DHS spokesperson told Military.com. "Military service by an immediate relative does not automatically grant parole, lawful status, or immunity from immigration enforcement.

“We are simply enforcing the laws passed by Congress. This administration does not pick and choose which laws to enforce."

The detention comes amid a broad expansion of immigration enforcement under President Donald Trump, which has included the arrests of relatives of other service members. Trump has backed the enforcement effort and his administration's approach.

Joshua Aviles' deployment aboard the Lincoln was extended by the war against Iran. Relatives of sailors aboard the carrier have described reports of shortages of clean water, food and supplies, along with low morale, during the prolonged deployment.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said claims about conditions aboard the ship have been "completely misrepresented."

The Navy said Saturday that the Lincoln had left the Middle East and was headed for the West Coast, which could take a month or more.

text:
The Trump administration unveiled a proposal on Monday to codify an unprecedented fee of more than $100,000 for cap-subject H-1B petitions for highly skilled foreign workers, replacing a charge first imposed by presidential proclamation last year that has thus far been blocked by a federal court.

The Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule would charge $103,265 as an additional fee for every H-1B petition subject to the annual statutory cap, including petitions eligible for the advanced-degree exemption.

The worker visas are heavily relied on in the tech, education and research industries.

The fee would be used to cover the federal government’s costs of administering the legal immigration system, including actions carried out by DHS and the Department of Justice, Department of State and Department of Labor.

FEDERAL JUDGE STRIKES DOWN TRUMP’S $100K H-1B VISA FEE, RULING IT AN UNCONSTITUTIONAL TAX

"The proposed H‑1B fee is intended to recover the costs incurred across the federal government to adjudicate, vet, and support lawful immigration programs that otherwise must be funded by taxpayers," U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services spokesperson Zach Kahler said in a news release.

The fee, which was first temporarily imposed by President Donald Trump's administration last year, was blocked by a federal judge in June in an order that barred the federal government from collecting the money.

An appeals court is reviewing the judge's decision while a different court considers whether a challenge to the fee by a major business group was properly rejected.

The temporary fee increase expires next month, one year after it was issued. The proposed rule by DHS was posted for public inspection Monday and is scheduled to be published in the Federal Register on Tuesday. It would make the $103,265 fee permanent.

The charge could be finalized by the end of the year.

The H-1B program allows U.S. employers to hire foreign workers with training in specialty occupations, with 65,000 of these visas offered annually under the regular cap.

Another 20,000 are offered for workers with a master’s degree or higher from a U.S. institution, generally granted for up to three years but typically extendable to a total of six years. Those visas typically came with fees between $2,000 and $5,000 before Trump's order, according to Reuters.

The proposed fee would apply to all cap-subject H-1B petitions, including petitions filed for some foreign students already in the United States seeking to change to H-1B status. It would not apply to cap-exempt H-1B petitions; routine extensions for current H-1B holders generally are not subject to the annual cap.

Trump has argued that the H-1B program is abused by many companies who replace American workers with cheaper foreign labor. But business groups and many U.S. companies have contended that the program is needed to address a lack of qualified American workers for certain jobs and to allow American firms to bring in the most skilled workers to support the U.S. economy.

According to court filings, about 70 employers had paid the $100,000 fee on a total of 85 visa applications as of late February.

The fee is being challenged by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce of Democratic-led states and a coalition of labor unions and employers.

The Trump administration has also ordered increased vetting of H-1B applicants and proposed a new visa selection process that would favor higher-skilled and better-paid workers.

By Daniel Wiessner

Aug 24 (Reuters) – President Donald Trump’s administration on Monday released a proposed regulation to codify an unprecedented fee of more than $100,000 on new H-1B visas for highly skilled foreign workers that has been blocked by the courts.

The fee, first temporarily imposed by Trump last year, dramatically raises the cost of visas that ​are heavily relied on in the tech, education and research sectors.

A federal judge in June ruled that the ‌fee was illegal and blocked the Trump administration from collecting it. A Boston-based appeals court is reviewing that decision while a different court considers whether a judge properly rejected a challenge to the fee by a major business group.

Trump’s temporary fee increase expires in September, one year after it was issued. The proposed rule by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, posted in the Federal Register on Monday, would make a fee of $103,265 permanent. It ‌could ​be finalized by the end of the year.

The H-1B program allows U.S. employers to ⁠hire foreign workers with training in specialty ⁠fields and offers 65,000 visas annually, with another 20,000 for workers with advanced degrees, approved for three to six years. Those visas typically came with fees between $2,000 and $5,000 before Trump’s order.

The fee would not apply to visas granted to foreign citizens already in the United States on student visas, who make up a large share of new H-1B recipients, ​or to renewals of current visas.

DEBATE OVER VISA PROGRAM

Trump, a Republican, and other critics of the H-1B program say it is abused by many companies who replace American workers with cheaper foreign labor. But business groups and many individual companies have said ⁠the visa program is needed to address a lack of qualified American ⁠workers for some jobs and to allow U.S. businesses to recruit top talent.

About 70 employers had ​paid the $100,000 fee on a total of 85 visa applications as of late February, according to court filings.

In imposing the fee, ​Trump invoked the president’s power under immigration law to restrict the entry of certain foreign nationals who ‌would be detrimental to U.S. interests.

The fee is being challenged by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, the largest U.S. business lobbying group, Democratic-led states and a coalition of unions and employers. Those lawsuits could be amended to challenge the rule proposed this week once it is finalized.

LEGAL CHALLENGES MOUNT

The lawsuits claim that Trump’s power to restrict entry does not allow him to override the law that ⁠created the H-1B visa program. The states and groups that sued also say that the Homeland Security Department cannot impose fees, taxes or other means to generate revenue for the United States without permission from Congress.

The Trump administration has maintained that the fee ⁠is not a traditional tax and that ‌courts have little power to question the president’s authority to restrict entry into the country.

Amid ⁠Trump’s broader immigration crackdown, employers last year registered for about 344,000 H-1B visas, down more ​than 25% ‌from 2024 and fewer than half of the 794,000 visas sought in 2023, according to ​data from U.S. ⁠Citizenship and Immigration Services.

The Trump administration has also ordered enhanced vetting of H-1B applicants and proposed a new visa selection process that would favor higher-skilled and better-paid workers. Earlier in August, the Department of Homeland Security in a separate rule added fees of up to $4,500 to applications to extend the stay of H-1B workers or to transfer employees based in other countries to the United States.

(Reporting by Daniel Wiessner in Albany, New York; Additional reporting by Daphne Psaledakis and Susan Heavey in Washington; Editing by Andy Sullivan, Alexia ​Garamfalvi, Matthew Lewis and Chizu Nomiyama )

Summarizes ICE Directive 11032.4 and related detention standards governing the custody and care of pregnant, postpartum, and nursing people;

Analyzes recent decisions granting relief and identifies features common to successful petitions;

Outlines four principal claims: violation of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), violation of the Accardi doctrine, denial of procedural due process, and denial of substantive due process (unconstitutional punishment and deliberate indifference to serious medical needs).

Addresses the government’s anticipated arguments opposing release; and

Provides, as Appendix B, a model habeas petition, with highlighted text to be adapted to the facts of a given case and the controlling precedent of the relevant circuit.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin lashed out at the politicians in Virginia and Maryland, saying their sanctuary policies elevate the needs of illegal immigrants above Americans' safety.

"The brave men and women of ICE are hard at work every single day getting these dangerous illegal aliens out of our country. Over the course of just two weeks in Virginia and Maryland, they arrested sexual assailants, kidnappers, drunk drivers, robbers, and gang members,” Mullin said. “While sanctuary politicians in Virginia and Maryland keep putting the needs of illegal aliens over the safety of the American people, the Trump Administration will always put American citizens first. By arresting and removing illegal aliens from our communities, we will make America safe again.”

SEE ALSO: Fairfax prosecutor accused of stonewalling Congressional illegal immigration investigation

DHS said most of the operation was focused on the D.C. suburbs in Virginia and Maryland, but extended to other regions in both states.

Virginians For Safe Communities President Sean Kennedy is a public safety watchdog and a member of the Fairfax County Criminal Justice Advisory Board. He told 7News this operation was crucial.

"It's impressive and heartening to see ICE was able to pick up these individuals, many of them who have violent and sexually predacious criminal records that they need to come off the street," Kennedy said.

ICE officers made the following arrests in the D.C. suburbs:

German Mejia-Baires, arrested in Manassas, Virginia: alleged MS-13 gang member from El Salvador, who had previously been convicted for driving while intoxicated, driving on a suspended license, and illegal re-entry. He had also been arrested for felony malicious wounding and shoplifting.

Julio Hector Carranza-Rojano, arrested in Manassas, Virginia: from Mexico, previously convicted for sexual battery, driving while intoxicated, and hit-and-run.

Angel Gabriel Ortiz-Hernandez, arrested in Alexandria, Virginia: from Guatemala, criminal history includes arrests for rape of a mentally incapacitated victim and TWO counts of aggravated sexual battery of an incapacitated victim.

Rowan Andrew Brown, arrested in Alexandria, Virginia: from Jamaica, previously convicted for identity theft, kidnapping adult, and illegal re-entry, and an arrest for fraud.

Mauricio Antonio Barrera-Navidad, arrested in Hyattsville, Maryland: alleged MS-13 gang member from El Salvador, whose criminal history in El Salvador includes robbery, use and illegal possession of firearms, two counts of illicit association with illegal group (MS-13), and disorders and resistance.

"Of the 1,328 illegal aliens arrested, almost 400 have either been convicted or charged with crimes in the United States," DHS said. "ICE officers made these arrests despite the sanctuary policies of many of the counties throughout Virginia and Maryland."

DHS said members of criminal street gangs like MS-13, 18th Street Gang and Tren de Aragua were arrested as part of the operation.

"Once again, our officers are out in the streets arresting and removing criminal alien offenders from American communities - this time in the Washington, D.C. area,” said ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations Acting Assistant Director Patricia Hyde. “Our officers are the best in the world at finding people who do not want to be located. That’s exactly what we did throughout the course of this operation. Removing these criminal alien offenders from Virginia and Maryland neighborhoods makes for much safer communities, and that is exactly what the men and women of ICE work to accomplish every day across our great nation.”

This operation comes as some local prosecutors have come under fire for having policies mandating they do not cooperate with ICE, or have dropped charges for those who would go on to commit other crimes.

"We have a number of instances where individuals were accused of rape and were convicted later of misdemeanor assault and battery. That's unacceptable. Those people are not minor misdemeanor criminals," Kennedy said. "It sounds like ICE basically is not allowing that to happen and they're going to take these people out of the country."

ICE has these detainees in their custody, and is moving forward with the deportation process.

"If they're in ICE custody, and ICE doesn't release them, then these individuals will be deported after they get their hearings in immigration court," Kennedy said. "These are all preventable crimes. And at the end of the day, they all should have faced justice. They didn't face justice, so they're going to face deportation."

text:
The Wisconsin Department of Justice (DOJ) has joined 19 other states, including the commonwealths of Massachusetts and Virginia, in a lawsuit pushing back against the Trump administration’s attempts to attach immigration enforcement requirements to federal grants supporting state and local public safety efforts.

“Threatening to cut funding that supports law enforcement if states don’t agree to unlawful conditions is an abuse of the Trump administration’s authority,” Attorney General Josh Kaul said in a statement. “This funding should be distributed to the states, not improperly used as a bargaining chip.”

The lawsuit states that the grant programs, which have been active for decades, “provide more than a billion dollars to States annually to address some of the most serious threats to the safety of their residents: from gang violence to drug trafficking to sexual assault to all kinds of violent crimes.” The funds, which are enacted by Congress, are used “to assist more than 8.5 million crime victims; pay more than 200,000 claims for losses suffered by crime victims; and fund ongoing criminal justice and public safety operations, such as drug task forces, crisis intervention programs, and youth recidivism reduction efforts, in all 50 states and over 1,000 local government units nationwide,” the lawsuit states.

Under President Donald Trump, states which depend on these funds have been advised to either cooperate with Trump’s immigration priorities or face losing access to those funds. Calling this a “brazen attempt to manipulate critical funding for law enforcement and crime victims to strong-arm States into supporting the Administration’s civil immigration policies,” the lawsuit asserts that the Trump administration is running afoul with governing principles of the United States: that a federal agency “has no power to act … unless and until Congress confers power upon it.” Since Congress has the power of the purse, it decides what criteria executive branch agencies — like the Justice Department — must use when awarding grants, the suit argues.

The lawsuit also accuses the Trump administration of not considering how denying these grants would undermine public safety across the country. “Action by this Court is urgently needed,” the lawsuit states, asserting that it is illegal for the administration to impose these conditions on the public safety grants.

In a press release, the Wisconsin DOJ said Monday that last year the Trump administration declared that states wouldn’t be able to access Victims Crime Act funds unless they cooperated with the administration’s hardline deportation agenda, affecting $1.3 billion in grants.. A coalition of states sued and the administration reversed its action and released the money.

This year, however, the immigration conditions have been applied funding for juvenile justice and law enforcement, and amount to over $6 million in Wisconsin alone — a loss of $3.2 million in grant assistance, $2.1 million for a crisis intervention program, and $800,000 for juvenile justice and delinquency prevention, according to DOJ.

Although 20 sheriff offices across Wisconsin partner with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) through the 287(g) program, many communities have mixed relationships with the controversial federal agency. Some police departments may still cooperate with immigration enforcement even without an official 287(g) program. Others have policies prohibiting officers and jails from participating in immigration enforcement.

text:
A federal agency's refusal to release records related to longstanding immigration fraud allegations involving Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., is fueling new questions about whether federal enforcement proceedings could be underway.

News organizations have sought records related to allegations surrounding Omar's 2009 marriage to Ahmed Nur Said Elmi. Critics have long alleged the marriage was part of an immigration fraud scheme and have claimed Elmi was Omar's brother.

Omar has denied those allegations, which have not been proven.

According to the response discussed on The National News Desk, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement declined to release requested records under the Freedom of Information Act, commonly known as FOIA, citing concerns that disclosure could interfere with "enforcement proceedings."

Washington insider Armstrong Williams said the language deserves attention but cautioned against treating the exemption itself as proof of wrongdoing.

"The public deserves transparency, but we should not confuse a FOIA exemption with evidence of guilt," Williams said.

Federal agencies can withhold certain law enforcement records under FOIA when releasing them could reasonably be expected to interfere with enforcement proceedings. Such a response does not, by itself, establish that Omar is the subject of an investigation or that the underlying allegations are true.

Asked whether the response could indicate an active federal investigation involving a sitting member of Congress, Williams said those associated with the matters under scrutiny should take the situation seriously, while stopping short of drawing a definitive conclusion.

"I think Omar and anyone associated with her in these programs have cause for great concern," Williams said. "I'll leave it at that."

The controversy comes as Omar continues to face scrutiny from political opponents over her personal history and other matters. She has consistently denied allegations that her marriage to Elmi involved immigration fraud.

The interview then shifted to a separate controversy involving political polling after a 21-year-old college graduate reportedly created a fake polling operation, complete with fabricated results and a website, that was subsequently cited within political and media circles.

Williams said the episode should serve as a warning to journalists, campaigns and voters about accepting polling data without examining how it was produced.

"It is a devastating indictment of the political media ecosystem," Williams said.

"A poll without transparent methodology should never be treated as news," he added.

Williams said legitimate polling can provide valuable information about public opinion, but argued that promoting numbers without verifying the methodology risks influencing voters rather than simply measuring their views.

"When campaigns and journalists promote convenient numbers without verification, and that's what happened, it begins shaping opinions instead," Williams said.

"They're shaping opinions, not news," he added.

The discussion also turned to reports of a private meeting between Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump's son-in-law and former senior White House adviser, and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., with the midterm elections approaching.

Williams characterized the meeting as "strategic outreach" and suggested both sides have reasons to maintain lines of communication as control of Congress remains at stake.

"Kushner understands that the Democrats could possibly capture the House, making Jeffries the speaker," Williams said.

A Democratic takeover of the House could significantly alter the balance of power in Washington, potentially giving the party control of congressional committees and investigative authority during the second half of Trump's term.

Williams also argued Jeffries is confronting pressure from the progressive wing of his own party, particularly in New York.

"The meeting expresses both their vulnerability," Williams said.

He suggested the conversation could reflect an effort to identify areas where the Trump White House and Democratic congressional leadership might eventually cooperate if Republicans lose control of the chamber.

"I think they've come to the realization that they have to find a way to cooperate," Williams said, adding that Trump could need to establish a working relationship with Jeffries if he becomes House speaker.

With the midterms little more than two months away, the three developments highlight different uncertainties hanging over Washington: unanswered questions surrounding federal records, renewed skepticism about political polling and behind-the-scenes conversations that could take on greater significance depending on which party controls Congress.

For now, the ICE response does not establish wrongdoing by Omar or confirm that she is personally under federal investigation. But the agency's invocation of an enforcement-related FOIA exemption is likely to keep scrutiny of the longstanding allegations alive as reporters and lawmakers seek additional information.

text:
The Trump administration is preparing to revoke business and tourism visas from up to 200,000 migrants who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum in the U.S. on a rolling basis — a move that would trigger the largest mass visa revocation ever, The Associated Press reported Monday.

The State Department is expected to announce the revocation, in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), of B1 and B2 visas issued since 2016, according to two U.S. officials and department documents obtained by the AP.

“We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told The Hill.

Pigott declined to comment on the number of visa revocations and said that the “number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis.”

The officials told the AP that revoking the visas will not result in immediate deportation, with pending asylum cases recategorized to no longer be for business or tourism travelers.

“People in the U.S. and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims,” Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau wrote on social media Monday. “Asylum isn’t supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration laws; rather, it’s supposed to provide a narrow safe harbor for persons persecuted because of their ‘race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.'”

Landau added that the asylum system “has long been swamped by frivolous asylum claims, meaning that it takes years to adjudicate whether applicants are actually entitled to asylum—during which time they can typically work, have children, and otherwise put down roots in our country.”

Current B1 and B2 visa applicants are asked to affirm that they will not apply for asylum and prove that they plan to return to their home countries.

President Trump has sought to ramp up restrictions on visas for asylum applicants since he returned to the White House last year. Since then, the State Department has revoked about 175,000 visas for people convicted or accused of various crimes, as well as for those who have spoken out against U.S. policies in the Middle East.

text:
(CN) — A Ninth Circuit panel dealt a setback to an agricultural workers’ union on Monday after it lifted a preliminary injunction prohibiting Border Patrol agents from detaining people without reasonable suspicion they violated immigration laws.

U.S. District Judge Jennifer Thurston, a Joe Biden appointee, imposed the preliminary injunction in April 2025. But the Department of Homeland Security, arguing the United Farm Workers of America didn’t have standing to pursue its class action challenging sweeps in California’s Central Valley to detain and arrest farm workers in violation of their Fourth Amendment rights.

Siding with the government, the three-judge panel determined in their 4-page-ruling “the district court considered only plaintiffs’ allegations of past harm. Although past harm may support standing to seek damages, it does not, on its own, establish standing to seek prospective injunctive relief."

The United Farm Workers also needed to show impending future injury for a preliminary injunction, the panel ruled, finding no traction to the union’s claims during oral arguments that the department’s practice of routinely violating its clients’ Fourth Amendment rights was evidence of future injury.

“We agree and remand to the district court for the limited purpose of addressing standing,” the three-judge panel wrote, siding with the federal government. “The district court considered only plaintiffs’ allegations of past harm. Although past harm may support standing to seek damages, it does not, on its own, establish standing to seek prospective injunctive relief.”

While the Ninth Circuit’s order lifts the preliminary injunction, it does not affect the plaintiffs’ underlying claims.

“Without assurance of standing, we lift the preliminary injunction, but if new allegations of harm arise during the pendency of this remand, nothing precludes the district court from considering additional requests for relief,” the Ninth Circuit panel wrote.

The Border Patrol’s sweeping immigration operation, dubbed Operation Return to Sender, hit Kern County, California, and the surrounding areas frequented by agricultural workers between Jan. 7-9 last year — just a few days before Donald Trump took office for a second term.

In their complaint, the United Farm Workers describe the operation as a fishing expedition that dispensed with reasonable suspicion and relied on racial profiling instead. They say the operation swept up nearly 200 people in an unlawful dragnet in an attempt to get as many people to voluntarily deport themselves back to Mexico.

The union also says the Border Patrol agents arrested and bussed them to a station in El Centro, California, without regard to probable cause of flight risk. Among the 40 people who were sent back to Mexico, most had lived in the United States for years, they say.

The unanimous panel included Senior U.S. Circuit Judge Mary Schroeder, a Jimmy Carter appointee; U.S. Circuit Judge Morgan Christen, a Barack Obama appointee; and U.S. Circuit Judge Danielle Forrest, a Trump appointee.

The University of California, Davis estimates that there are about 900,000 agriculture workers in California annually. The vast majority are Latino.

Spokespersons for the government did not respond to requests for comment. Representatives from the United Farm Workers and the American Civil Liberties Union, also representing the plaintiffs, did not respond to requests for comment either.

text:
The Trump administration is again seeking to impose a payment for highly skilled worker visas, this time leaving out visas for educational institutions, nonprofits and governmental research organizations.

The Department of Homeland Security filed a notice Monday outlining its plan to charge a $103,265 fee for H-1B visa petitions. In June, a federal judge stopped the Trump administration from charging $100,000 for workers entering the country under the program, which President Donald Trump said had been abused by technology companies.

DHS is justifying the fee as a way to raise revenue for the costs of administering the legal immigration system. The department estimates it will get $8.8 billion annually and said in the notice submitted to the Federal Register that companies seeking to hire H-1B workers have a greater capability to absorb the cost.

“The scope of the proposed fee increase in this rule is significant,” the notice states. “DHS proposes this cost shifting approach with an emphasis on the ability-to-pay principle for determining user fees. Petitioners for H-1B cap-subject nonimmigrant workers generally are required to have the resources necessary to pay the worker(s) for whom the petition is filed.”

Trending

Up to 65,000 H-1B visas are available per year, plus 20,000 for those who have advanced degrees or higher from universities in the country. The fees would apply to everyone applying for those slots, but DHS chose to exempt employees who would be working for higher education institutions and nonprofit and government research organizations.

“Because this is a filing fee, employers would have to pay it with no guarantee that USCIS will approve the petition,” David Bier, director of immigration studies at the libertarian think tank Cato Institute, said in a statement. “Almost no one will risk more than $100,000 with no guarantee of approval.”

DHS’s proposal comes after a federal judge ruled against the fee Trump imposed through a proclamation, labeling the cost a tax that the president didn’t have authority to put in place.

U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin of Massachusetts also found that the fee violated federal statute because the department did not go through the required rulemaking procedures, such as filing a notice, as it did Monday.

“Defendants’ failure to undergo notice-and-comment rulemaking was not [a] harmless error,” Soroking wrote in a June order. “These additional procedures could have altered Defendants’ decision to impose an unconstitutional tax on the H-1B program or, at the very least, required Defendants to consider the impact of the $100,000 payment obligation on regulated entities.”

The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals declined to reinstate the fee last month.

Twenty states sued the administration in December, claiming they would lose vital workers such as teachers, nurses, physicians and researchers as a result of the fee.

text:
Gov. Greg Abbott has asked a federal judge to reject Minnesota's effort to force the extradition of an immigration officer arrested in Texas, saying he has "serious concerns" about whether the officer is actually a fugitive from justice.

Abbott said state officials are still investigating whether Christian Castro, who is being held in Cameron County Jail, can be classified as a fugitive because he didn't flee Minnesota but was apparently reassigned to Texas by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Minnesota is also seeking a court order keeping Castro in custody beyond Thursday for fear he would "flee and avoid prosecution." In Texas, people awaiting extradition cannot be held longer than 90 days. Castro was arrested in Cameron County on May 29 on a warrant issued by a Minnesota court.

Abbott, in a brief filed on Monday, asked the judge to deny the request, noting Castro's freedom would have "no effect on the Governor's ability to issue a warrant to extradite."

"The ninety-day period limits pre-warrant detention; it does not impose a ninety-day deadline on the Governor to approve or deny the demanding State's request," Abbott told the court.

Both sides are due to appear for a Tuesday hearing in Brownsville regarding Minnesota's request.

Cameron County Sheriff Manuel Trevino said in a court filing last week that he "must follow state law" and release Castro on the 90th day - unless the court orders otherwise.

Abbott's response came nearly a week after Minnesota officials filed a federal lawsuit to compel the extradition of Castro, who faces four counts of second-degree assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime after allegedly injuring a Venezuelan man earlier this year during Operation Metro Surge - a massive immigration crackdown in Minneapolis - and lying about what occurred before the shooting.

The Monday filing is in line with a comment Abbott made at an unrelated news conference last week, during which he said he doesn't trust Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz "on anything, let alone something like this."

In particular, Abbott's filing says it appears Castro did not flee Minnesota but instead returned to Texas to fulfill his job obligations, citing media reports quoting the ICE officer's defense attorney.

The governor has instructed interim Texas Secretary of State Robert Howden - who was a senior adviser to Abbott before taking on the role - to investigate Castro's circumstances and whether he should be turned over to Minnesota's custody.

"Based on publicly available information indicating that Mr. Castro was compelled to return to Texas on orders of the federal government, I have serious doubts that the prerequisites for extradition have been met," Abbott wrote in a July 31 letter to Howden.

Howden's report is still pending, so Abbott has not decided on the extradition request, according to the Monday court filing. Howden's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

"Once the Secretary of State concludes his investigation, the Governor may conclude that the statutory requirements for extradition are satisfied, or he may conclude that they are not," the filing said. "Either way, Governor Abbott is entitled to see that deliberative process through and is entitled to the presumption of regularity afforded to government acts."

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison's office declined to comment immediately but said it will respond in court.

The case started Jan. 14 when Castro allegedly fired into an occupied home in Minneapolis and struck Julio Sosa-Celis in the leg. The ICE officer was later accused of falsely stating that Sosa-Celis and another man attacked him with a shovel and a broom, according to court documents.

The Hennepin County Attorney's Office announced its charges against Castro on May 18, and the Texas Rangers helped arrest him in Cameron County later that month.

Walz quickly sent Abbott an extradition request - a process that typically sees prompt cooperation between the two states, according to the lawsuit. But in this case, Minnesota officials said they had to send letters urging Abbott to sign the paperwork before suing him on Aug. 18.

"Abbott's refusal to extradite Castro is unconstitutional and violates federal law and Texas law," Ellison said in a statement about the lawsuit.

Abbott shot back later that day during an unrelated news conference.

After expressing his distrust of Walz, the Texas governor pointed to a wide-ranging welfare fraud scandal in Minnesota that the Trump administration used to justify Operation Metro Surge. This crackdown also led to the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens by federal immigration officers.

"While they're making demands, I got a demand of my own, and that is: It's time for Minnesota to step up and repay the United States of America and Americans for all the fraud that they have committed in their state under federal programs," Abbott said last week.
